themes.name: AI Safety
themes.description: Work on monitorable-by-design architectures, ground-truth-free agent evaluation, safe autoformalization, agent harm measurement, and privacy auditing of fine-tuned models.

themes.name: Interpretability and AI Safety
themes.description: Work on chain-of-thought faithfulness, sandbagging detection, and governance-ready evidence for model decisions, probing whether model explanations and evaluations can be trusted.

themes.name: Computer Vision

themes.name: Model Editing and Interpretability
themes.description: Techniques that inspect or modify model internals, such as reading and writing neural network weights to fix behavioral failures.

themes.name: Robot Learning from Egocentric Human Data
themes.description: Multiple papers (ActiveBridge, Ego2Real, EgoLoAF, Any2Act) leverage egocentric human demonstrations to scale robot skill acquisition, with varying use of tactile sensing, affordance cues, and executor-centric representations.

themes.name: Agent Security and AI Safety
themes.description: Security vulnerabilities in deployed coding-agent permission and authorization systems, including compaction-induced and policy-rewriting attacks.

items.title: On Potentiality and Actuality Of Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.32991v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Foundation models are built through large-scale pretraining, often followed by post-training, and are then adapted to specific tasks and behaviors. But, does the adaptation add truly new capabilities, or the base model already holds it? We decompose the update induced by different adaptations into a component shared across all inputs and a residual that varies with the input. We find that the shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that learns a constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. We call this the potentiality principle of foundation models: the base model already contains the capacity needed for task-specific expertise. To adapt to a new task, the model just needs to be actualized, i.e., pushed in a certain direction via a constant, input-independent shift. We show the implications of this principle on parameter-efficient adaptation, steering, and convergence across models, and how it explains the neural thickets phenomenon.
items.author: Fabian Gr\"oger, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbi\'c
items.summary: This paper asks whether post-training adaptation adds new capabilities or whether the base model already contains them, decomposing adaptation updates into a shared component and an input-varying residual. The finding is that a per-layer constant vector shared across all inputs reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning for most gains, which the authors call the potentiality principle. This has implications for how we think about what fine-tuning actually does and could simplify adaptation.
items.reasoning: Conceptually striking result with credible authors (including Maria Brbic) suggesting base models already hold most task capacity and adaptation mostly surfaces it. If the findings hold broadly, this reshapes understanding of fine-tuning and enables extremely cheap adaptation, though generality across model families and task types needs confirmation.

items.title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability
items.content: arXiv:2611.31271v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) allows language models to verbalise multi-step rationales before producing their final answer. While this technique often boosts task performance and offers an impression of transparency into the model's reasoning, this position paper argues that rationales generated by current CoT techniques can be misleading and are neither necessary nor sufficient for trustworthy interpretability. We analyse faithfulness as whether CoTs are not only human-interpretable but also reflect the model's underlying reasoning well enough to support responsible use. By synthesising evidence from prior work, we systematically show that verbalised chains are frequently unfaithful, diverging from the critical hidden computations that drive a model's predictions. As CoT is increasingly relied upon in application domains, including high-stakes ones such as medicine, law, and autonomous systems, we further argue that this unfaithfulness is not taken seriously enough in these settings: our analysis of 1,000 recent CoT-centric papers finds that approximately 21.7% explicitly treat CoT as a load-bearing interpretability technique, building pipelines or safety arguments that would not hold if CoT is unfaithful to the model's actual reasoning. They include papers in high-stakes domains that heavily hinge on such interpretability claims. Building on prior work, we make three proposals: (i) avoid treating CoT as being sufficient for interpretability without additional verification, (ii) adopt rigorous methods that assess faithfulness for downstream decision-making, and (iii) report such assessments alongside any interpretability claims based on CoT, while continuing to use CoT for its communicative and monitoring benefits.

items.title: Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2611.32539v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection. The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.

items.title: Medical Image Segmentation Is Now Just Another Coding Task
items.content: arXiv:2611.31673v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: For decades, every new medical image segmentation task has needed an expert, a dedicated architecture, and a framework such as nnU-Net. This is no longer the case: medical image segmentation is now just another coding task. Given only a task description, labeled data, and a CPU (with no segmentation framework, no pretrained weights, and no human in the loop), four off-the-shelf coding agents built segmenters for 13 tasks across four imaging modalities within hours, an ability that has emerged rather than been built. On the nine 2D tasks, their best programs reach 99% of the Dice of a GPU-trained nnU-Net. Like any code, a segmenter improves by being revised and checked, so we ask how far the same agents can improve their own segmentations and what unlocks further gains. On unseen cases there is no reference, so the agents inspect renderings of their own predictions: this alone lifts the worst tenth of cases by 0.09 Dice and cuts boundary error (HD95) by almost a quarter. Far more is within reach. Told the true Dice of each attempt, the same agents improve in all 14 matched pairs, rescue 85% of failed masks instead of 30%, and surpass the GPU-trained nnU-Net on average, by producing better masks rather than by choosing among them. What unlocks these gains is a quality signal, which neither visual inspection, nor more rounds, nor a quality estimator trained by the agents themselves yet supplies: we call this the quality blind spot. The ability to build and to repair is already present; the next advance will come not from another segmentation model, but from reference-free quality estimation that coding agents can call.
items.author: Shuheng Cao, Ruiqi Chen, Qizhen Lan, Edward Wang, Xiyun Hu, Yilei Wang, Juqy Chen, Weilin Huang, Anhong Guo
items.summary: The paper shows that off-the-shelf LLM coding agents can autonomously build medical image segmentation pipelines from just a task description and labeled data, with no pretrained weights or human involvement, matching 99% of nnU-Net Dice scores on 2D tasks across 13 tasks and four imaging modalities. This suggests a paradigm shift where specialized segmentation frameworks and expert tuning may be replaced by agentic code generation and self-revision.
items.reasoning: The finding is striking and practically significant: it demonstrates an emergent capability of coding agents to automate an entire specialist ML engineering workflow, with strong empirical evaluation against the de facto standard (nnU-Net) across multiple modalities. The breadth of tasks, clarity of the claim, and implications for both medical imaging practice and agentic AI applications elevate its importance, though reliance on GPU-trained baselines only for 2D tasks and unanswered questions about self-improvement limits temper the score.

items.title: Interpreting a recent acceleration in pretraining loss
items.content:
OpenAI recently published the base-model log-perplexity of 13 models it has trained since GPT-3.5, measured on a fixed held-out dataset sourced from its own codebase. It shows a very striking acceleration in pretraining loss: since early 2026, it has been falling about seven times faster than it was from 2022 through 2025.

If the current pace holds, OpenAI would cover the drop in log-perplexity from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.1, which took three years, in about six and a half months. This acceleration is even more striking because progress in loss should get harder over time: text is never perfectly predictable, so the loss can’t fall below some floor, and gains typically become smaller as models approach it. Under standard scaling laws, each tenfold increase in compute buys a smaller drop in loss than the last, so naively we would expect progress in loss to slow down over time (see figure below).1

Among METR staff there remains active discussion on how to interpret this dramatic acceleration in pretraining progress, and how to reconcile it with the lack of a comparable acceleration in benchmark scores of OpenAI’s models, e.g. as reflected in Epoch’s ECI.

Concretely, it remains arguable how much this new information should change our forecasts of future AI capabilities. The following considerations are important:

- It is possible that the data released overstates true progress in pretraining, e.g. through various types of overfitting. More data would help substantially here.
- It is possible that benchmark scores are the best measure of real-world capabilities, and pretraining perplexity is only informative as an input. This implies the new data showing acceleration in pretraining progress would not substantially change our forecasts of future capabilities. 2 However, to the extent that AI contributed to the acceleration in pretraining, this gives us a sign of AI’s likely future contribution to all parts of the model-training pipeline. 3
- It is possible that pretraining perplexity reflects a fundamentally deeper measure of model capability than the typical benchmarks used to evaluate models. Many AI researchers treat pretraining perplexity in this way, and expect that OpenAI’s rapid acceleration in pretraining will be followed by an acceleration in capabilities measured by real-world impact. 4

There remain substantial disagreements on how much this information should modify our projections of the future path of capabilities, and METR does not have a consensus view on this. Some interpretations imply that OpenAI’s data on acceleration in pretraining should make us expect a broad-based acceleration in real-world AI capabilities over the next six months.

To our knowledge, no frontier developer had previously published how the pretraining loss of its successive frontier models has changed over multiple years on a fixed held-out dataset. This information is typically considered highly commercially sensitive. However, we think publishing information about pretraining loss is very valuable for informing the public about the prospect of AI R&D acceleration. We encourage all AI developers to do the same, as Microsoft has since done for its own models using OpenAI’s dataset, and to share additional context that would let external researchers better understand the degree of acceleration, what’s driving it, and whether we should expect it to continue and/or compound.5

The following would be especially informative:

- Log-perplexity on other held-out datasets. Loss measured on a single corpus may not capture progress on other kinds of text. OpenAI’s plot, for example, reports loss on a corpus sourced from its own internal codebase. Recent recipes or data could help on that kind of text (e.g. coding) more than on others, or small parts of the codebase could have leaked into training data. Log-perplexity on other very different held-out datasets (e.g. a corpus of books) would be informative about the robustness of this trend. 6 Eventually, these held-out corpora could be maintained by a third party, making it possible to compare trends in pretraining loss across AI developers.
- The rough date that the pretraining run ended for each model. Plotting models at their public release dates may not capture when pretraining progress happened: log-perplexity is a property of the base model, and base models could be finished months before release. If the lag between the end of the pretraining run and model release shrank over time, the acceleration in loss would be smaller than the plot suggests (and vice versa). More importantly, knowing the lag helps us determine how much AI uplift contributed to the pretraining gains: regardless of when a model was released, we can’t attribute its pretraining gains to AI agents if its pretraining happened when researchers barely used AI agents.
- How pretraining compute, labor spending, and experiment compute changed over time. Lower pretraining loss could be attributable to a number of factors: for example, increased training compute, increased labor or experimental compute spending, or increased uplift from AI assistance. Some of these factors imply that we should expect the growth to be a one-time spike, while others imply that we should expect it to continue; if it is substantially attributable to AI uplift, the acceleration could compound. To understand this, it would be helpful to have a sense of how these resources were growing in the relevant time period.

- One way to see this is to convert log-perplexity into “effective compute”: the compute that a single fixed recipe would need to reach a given loss value. If we assumed that all of OpenAI’s models are on the same scaling law with irreducible loss between 0.3 and 0.6, effective compute would have grown roughly 8 to 10 times faster since early 2026 than in 2022–2025, measured in orders of magnitude per year. However, that assumption is unrealistic, since newer recipes likely follow different scaling laws. ↩︎
- For example, architectural changes that spend more computation per token, such as looped transformers, might lower perplexity more than they improve downstream capabilities, since standard models could reach similar capabilities after post-training by reasoning in a chain of thought. ↩︎
- A footnote in OpenAI’s post is consistent with AI playing a small role at the start of the acceleration, but a larger role currently: “We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI.” Similarly, METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic found that the acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors, but estimated that “a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.” ↩︎
- A related argument why this data on pretraining acceleration should modify our forecasts of real-world capabilities is that our scales of capability, such as ECI, MCI, and time horizon, are sensitive to delicate statistical assumptions, or rely heavily on a few benchmarks that are close to saturation. ↩︎
- Many other kinds of information would also help, but we have focused on a few numbers that we expect companies already collect and should be relatively simple to share. ↩︎
- The other held-out datasets should date from before 2022, so that they don’t contain any AI-generated text. Ideally, they would cover a variety of text types, such as code, scientific writing, and prose, to show how much of the trend on the original held-out set reflects progress on code specifically. ↩︎

  • The rough date that the pretraining run ended for each model. Plotting models at their public release dates may not capture when pretraining progress happened: log-perplexity is a property of the base model, and base models could be finished months before release. If the lag between the end of the pretraining run and model release shrank over time, the acceleration in loss would be smaller than the plot suggests (and vice versa). More importantly, knowing the lag helps us determine how much AI uplift contributed to the pretraining gains: regardless of when a model was released, we can’t attribute its pretraining gains to AI agents if its pretraining happened when researchers barely used AI agents.
  • How pretraining compute, labor spending, and experiment compute changed over time. Lower pretraining loss could be attributable to a number of factors: for example, increased training compute, increased labor or experimental compute spending, or increased uplift from AI assistance. Some of these factors imply that we should expect the growth to be a one-time spike, while others imply that we should expect it to continue; if it is substantially attributable to AI uplift, the acceleration could compound. To understand this, it would be helpful to have a sense of how these resources were growing in the relevant time period.
  • One way to see this is to convert log-perplexity into “effective compute”: the compute that a single fixed recipe would need to reach a given loss value. If we assumed that all of OpenAI’s models are on the same scaling law with irreducible loss between 0.3 and 0.6, effective compute would have grown roughly 8 to 10 times faster since early 2026 than in 2022–2025, measured in orders of magnitude per year. However, that assumption is unrealistic, since newer recipes likely follow different scaling laws. ↩︎
  • For example, architectural changes that spend more computation per token, such as looped transformers, might lower perplexity more than they improve downstream capabilities, since standard models could reach similar capabilities after post-training by reasoning in a chain of thought. ↩︎
  • A footnote in OpenAI’s post is consistent with AI playing a small role at the start of the acceleration, but a larger role currently: “We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI.” Similarly, METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic found that the acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors, but estimated that “a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.” ↩︎
  • A related argument why this data on pretraining acceleration should modify our forecasts of real-world capabilities is that our scales of capability, such as ECI, MCI, and time horizon, are sensitive to delicate statistical assumptions, or rely heavily on a few benchmarks that are close to saturation. ↩︎
  • Many other kinds of information would also help, but we have focused on a few numbers that we expect companies already collect and should be relatively simple to share. ↩︎
  • The other held-out datasets should date from before 2022, so that they don’t contain any AI-generated text. Ideally, they would cover a variety of text types, such as code, scientific writing, and prose, to show how much of the trend on the original held-out set reflects progress on code specifically. ↩︎

items.title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA
items.content: arXiv:2611.32823v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
items.content: arXiv:2611.33102v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived rather than freshly generated rollouts, but this leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy: maximum likelihood on the archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.
items.author: Jiayi Sheng, Jingwen Gu, Guanning Zeng, Zhaoyi Zhou, Stefano Viel, Qianqian Wang, Fahim Tajwar, Andrea Zanette

The authors show that naively replaying old rollouts causes catastrophic collapse, explain why, and demonstrate that maximum likelihood on the archived rollouts — replayed in their original order — surprisingly recovers much of the RL training benefit.
items.reasoning: A conceptually striking result with broad implications for RL post-training pipelines: it suggests rollout logs are a valuable, reusable asset and offers a simple remedy to a collapse phenomenon. items.title: Lit Up but Not Needed: Scoped Lesions Show Where Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts Depend on Their Experts
items.content: arXiv:2611.31576v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cognitive neuroscience learned that an activation map is not a map of necessity. Regions that light up during a task are not always needed for it, and only lesions reveal which ones are. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) vision-language models come with an activation map for free, since the router records which experts respond to image and text tokens, and recent work reads modality-specialized experts off this map. We bring the lesion. In Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, Kimi-VL-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3 to 12% of the experts are vision-exclusive: image tokens route to them at up to five times the uniform rate and text tokens almost never. In Qwen3-VL they receive a quarter of all image-token routing, and lesioning all of them costs less than one percentage point on average over eight perception benchmarks and free-form OCR, no more than lesioning a random set of the same size. In Kimi-VL and Gemma-4 the lesion also costs no more than a random set. Scoped lesions, which remove an expert set only at image positions or only at text positions, then show where the models do depend on their experts. In Qwen3-VL, silencing every expert at every image position costs 3 points, against 45 at text positions, where the dependence sits in dual-use experts that text-only tasks need as well. Across models the image-side dependence is 2 to 3 points in Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL and 26 in Gemma-4. Reading text in images is the one ability that needs image-position experts in every model. The exclusive experts receive informative patches, produce outputs of ordinary size, and stay inert under sensory deprivation: text-only training recruits them only when load balancing forces it. In Kimi-VL the balancing bias itself manufactures most of them. Load balancing draws the modality map in the part of the computation the models depend on least. Expert selection, pruning and skipping should follow the lesion, not the map.

items.summary: Applying a lesion methodology borrowed from cognitive neuroscience, this paper shows that routing activation in MoE vision-language models does not indicate necessity: vision-exclusive experts in Qwen3-VL, Kimi-VL, and Gemma-4 receive disproportionate image-token routing yet can be lesioned with under one percentage point accuracy loss. The work reframes how modality specialization in MoE VLMs should be measured.

items.title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
items.content: arXiv:2611.31451v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.
items.author: Benedikt von Querfurth, Lukas Klein, C\'edric Vincent-Cuaz, Eeshaan Jain, Yexiang Cheng, Johann Wenckstern, Phil F. Cheng, Petros Liakopoulos, Olivier Michielin, Martina Haberecker, Andreas Wicki, Pascal Frossard, Charlotte Bunne

The vision-transformer-based architecture handles heterogeneous marker panels across cohorts.

items.title: Any2Act: Scaling In-Context Robot Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrations
items.content: arXiv:2611.32353v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot in-context learning (ICL) enables a policy to perform unseen tasks by following contextual demonstrations, without task-specific fine-tuning. This is increasingly valuable as large language models reasoning at low frequency can specify tasks through demonstrations and delegate high-frequency execution to such a policy. However, methods conditioned on human videos are bounded by scarce human-robot pairs, while those conditioned on robot demonstrations accept only one or two source types at limited scale. We present Any2Act, a foundation model for robot ICL. Our key insight is that a demonstration should be expressed in the camera layout and action space of the robot that performs it (the executor), not of whoever provided it (the demonstrator). This unified embodiment-grounded representation decouples learning to follow from admitting a new source. Any2Act learns to follow once, from robot-to-robot pairs that already take this form in 1.2M real trajectories spanning 10K tasks. Human videos, simulation, UMI, and other robots are then translated into this representation, and source-routed adapters trained on only a few hundred pairs each absorb the residual gap while the pretrained model stays frozen. For long horizons, a training-free tracker feeds only the demonstration window around the executor's progress, bounding the context and rolling back to redo failed steps. From a single demonstration, Any2Act achieves 57.5% success on unseen tasks without fine-tuning, exceeding VLAs fine-tuned on 50 demonstrations per task; other demonstrators retain 74-91% of the success achieved with the executor's own demonstrations.

items.title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2611.30325v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.
items.author: Juntong Shi, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec, Minkai Xu
items.summary: VOPD couples the dense supervision of on-policy distillation with the sparse but verified rewards of RLVR for improving LLM reasoning. Instead of naively co-optimizing the two objectives, it transfers verifier signal into the dense teacher feedback, grounding token-level supervision in task outcomes. This targets a core weakness of both approaches taken alone.

The sparse-reward problem in RLVR is widely recognized, so a verified dense-supervision method has broad relevance, though full empirical strength is unclear from the truncated abstract.

items.title: Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action
items.content: arXiv:2611.33137v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.

Demonstrated improvements over alternative synthetic datasets across four task areas plus a new VLA benchmark raise its significance.

items.title: RECAP: Training Long-horizon LLM Agents with Context Compaction
items.content: arXiv:2611.31258v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Context compaction enables large language model agents to tackle long-horizon tasks within limited context budgets by replacing interaction histories with compressed summaries. However, learning effective compaction jointly with the agent policy remains challenging, as summaries affect task success over many subsequent interactions. We introduce RECAP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on the principle that a summary should preserve the behavior induced by the original interaction history. We formalize this principle with a behavior distortion objective that measures the divergence between the agent's subsequent behavior under compressed and original contexts. We show that the gradient of the distortion objective decomposes into two complementary learning signals: distortion-based reward for summary generation and self-distillation for subsequent actions. items.title: When Answering Is Administering: Permission Replies That Rewrite Coding-Agent Policy
items.content: arXiv:2611.32195v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Coding agents let plugins and remote services answer permission prompts, and Claude Code documents that such an answer cannot override the operator's deny rules. However, we show that this guarantee, checked one decision at a time, fails over a whole run, because an answer to one permission prompt can rewrite the policy that every later answer is checked against. For example, a remote service with no access to the operator's files approves an unrelated command and attaches an update that deletes the deny rule protecting the project's secrets. The agent then reads the secrets in that session and the next, even inside the vendor's strict sandbox. The root cause is that Claude Code checks only updates that add or replace allow rules. Relays that forward such deletions already exist, including the vendor's own Remote Control. In effect, the right to answer a prompt has become the right to administer the policy. Worse, the deletion leaves the same records as a local edit by the operator, so Claude Code cannot tell who wrote a rule.   More generally, what a runtime records decides what it can safely delegate. A runtime that cannot tell who wrote a rule can accept only updates that keep every currently denied call denied, whereas, to protect every party's restrictions, a runtime that records who wrote each rule can let each party remove only the restrictions proven to be its own. We prove that these two bounds are tight. They correctly predict whether the operator's restrictions survive in all thirteen permission designs across ten agent systems, including predictions we wrote down before running Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, and Goose. Enforcing the bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack. A survey of 2,227 fetched marketplace plugins finds only two that send policy updates.

items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
items.content: arXiv:2611.31301v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

items.title: Constructing physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2611.31653v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Mechanisms recur across the sciences: the equation for heat in a solid also describes molecular diffusion or a Brownian particle. A mechanism is rarely written in one equation; its operation, boundaries, parameters and closures are stated at different steps of a derivation, where methods that read text or fit formulas miss it. We built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, and show that mechanisms can be compiled from them and constructed by deterministic calculation. A constructor detaches, transfers, unfolds, composes and joins their parts across disciplines; where parts do not fit, the failure is an equation for the missing term. Constructions turn a threshold reactor into a memory that a weak signal writes, an oscillator into a switch through two changes that each fail alone, and a rhythm into the regulator of a chemical amount, each with conditions for an experimental test.

Where mechanism parts do not fit, the failure itself becomes an equation for a missing term. This is an ambitious attempt at cross-disciplinary symbolic knowledge compilation beyond text-based or formula-fitting approaches.

items.title: Sparse Poison, Strong Hijack: Efficient Trajectory-Level Backdoors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Only 1\% Poisoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.32304v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic manipulation, but their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to backdoor threats. Among these threats, trajectory-level targeted backdoors are particularly challenging and may pose greater safety risks than behavior-disrupting attacks: rather than merely causing task failures or local action deviations, they must sustain closed-loop redirection to complete an attacker-specified multi-step task. To reliably induce such behaviors, existing methods typically rely on high poisoning rates to obtain sufficient target-trajectory supervision. However, high poisoning rates may compromise clean-task performance, whereas low rates leave target-trajectory supervision scarce and backdoor learning vulnerable to interference from dominant clean-task updates. To resolve this trade-off at low poisoning rates, we propose a two-stage co-optimization framework guided by vision, language, and action. Stage I freezes the policy and uses differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision to optimize a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale, strengthening trigger-target associations from limited poisoned demonstrations. Building on the optimized trigger, Stage II applies source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation to decouple clean and backdoor updates and mitigate their interference, followed by learned column-wise calibration and analytic fusion into a unified policy. Experiments on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_0$, and $\pi_{0.5}$ across four LIBERO suites show consistent gains over all evaluated attack baselines. With only 1% poisoned data, our method achieves 86.4% target success and 95.2% clean-task success on OpenVLA-OFT in LIBERO-Spatial. Real-robot trials also demonstrate trajectory-level hijacking.
items.author: Simin Huang, Jiawei Chen, Shaolong Zhu, Qiwei Liang, Zhaoxia Yin
items.summary: This paper demonstrates that vision-language-action (VLA) models used for robotic manipulation can be hijacked via trajectory-level backdoor attacks using only 1% poisoned training data. Unlike behavior-disrupting attacks, these backdoors sustain closed-loop redirection to complete attacker-specified multi-step tasks, and the authors propose a method that overcomes the scarcity of target-trajectory supervision that previously forced attackers to use high poisoning rates.
items.reasoning: The work addresses a timely and underexplored security threat: as VLA models are increasingly deployed in robotics, backdoor attacks that preserve clean-task performance while enabling multi-step hijacking represent a serious practical risk. The key novelty is demonstrating effective trajectory-level backdoors at a very low 1% poisoning rate, which sharpens the clean-performance-versus-attack tradeoff that limits prior methods. Safety relevance is high since it exposes a concrete vulnerability class in embodied AI, though it is a single arXiv preprint without indication of extensive external validation yet, which moderates the score slightly.

items.title: INCLUDE-2.0: Disentangling Knowledge Gaps in Multilingual LLM Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2611.31255v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Current multilingual benchmarks cover only a fraction of the languages represented in modern pretraining corpora and often conflate language proficiency with the ability to answer questions grounded in specific regions and communities. We introduce INCLUDE-2.0, a large-scale benchmark for region-aware multilingual factual evaluation, which covers 91 languages from 86 countries (127 total language--country pairs), comprising over 220K curated samples drawn from native regional sources. Unlike existing benchmarks that often treat language as a proxy for region, IINCLUDE-2.0 distinguishes between questions whose answers are independent of context, vary by country, concern widely documented facts about a place, or depend on knowledge primarily expressed through local linguistic and cultural sources. Each item is annotated with its regional knowledge type and domain, and paired with an English translation, enabling controlled analysis of the relationship between language proficiency and possession of regional knowledge.   Evaluating frontier and open-weight models on IINCLUDE-2.0, we find that aggregate multilingual accuracy masks substantial variation across regional knowledge types, languages, and regions. We find that frontier models perform worse on locally embedded knowledge than on widely documented facts about regions, with an average drop of ~14.5 points. We also show that for open-weight models, scale improves accuracy but does not reliably make performance invariant to whether a question is asked in English or its original language. INCLUDE-2.0 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/epfl-nlp/include-2.0

items.title: Machine learning enables full Bayesian inference for spinning extreme-mass-ratio inspirals
items.content: arXiv:2611.31916v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar-mass compact objects spiralling into massive black holes, promise to measure the masses and spins of the central black holes, reveal the strong-field environment around them and gauge cosmic distances via millihertz gravitational-wave observations. Yet most forecasts for the parameter inference of these systems assume known source parameters, and broad-prior analyses have addressed only simplified versions of the problem. The joint inversion of all 14 parameters of a spinning source from the complete prior has remained unsolved. Here we solve it for the augmented analytic kludge model: generative networks narrow the complete prior and reveal a ring of degenerate spin directions, and the exact detector likelihood determines the posterior. For a simulated one-year LISA-Taiji observation, within one ring sector we obtain, for the first time, a 14-parameter posterior of a spinning EMRI from the complete prior, the most precise yet obtained for such a source from broad priors. The redshifted mass and spin of the massive black hole are determined to two parts in $10^5$, the mass two orders of magnitude beyond any electromagnetic measurement. The compact object's redshifted mass is measured to one part in $10^4$, and its eccentric, retrograde orbit discriminates between capture channels. The 0.8% distance and sub-square-degree localization are sufficient for dark-siren cosmology. Year-long coherent analysis resolves the inspiral driven by radiation reaction itself.

The work demonstrates machine learning enabling scientific inference at a scale previously considered intractable.

items.title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction
items.content: arXiv:2611.32194v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Request-derived authorizers such as Progent protect LLM agents from prompt injection by deriving what an agent may do from the user's request. Their guarantee rests on attribution: the request is taken to be what the user said. Compaction breaks it. At every automatic compaction we observed, Claude Code and Codex placed a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message, so the compactor's quotation of the user, documents and injected text reads as the user speaking. Because a policy frozen at the first request lets the agent finish few later tasks, we let Progent derive its policy for each request, and find that what it grants then follows what the compactor wrote. Even a payee the user stated is not safe: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay the rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the notice's account in 91% of cases, and the one derived from the user's own words in none. The cause is general: we prove that an authorizer that cannot see who wrote which bytes cannot treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one it imitates by more than the two are distinguishable, and that the bound is tight. Frontier compactors bear this out: they mark injected instructions, which have no legitimate twin, but rarely injected data, which does. What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter. The fix follows from attribution: the authorizer credits only what the user said, authenticated on arrival and carried verbatim across the boundary, while the agent still reads the summary. We prove that it then receives exactly that text or nothing, so an attacker can block the policy but cannot shape it, and adaptive attacks on our implementation confirm it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes re-run with the fix, no attacker action completes while the agent reads the summary.

items.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
items.content: arXiv:2611.32415v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $\beta\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\ge\beta$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.
items.author: Ruiqi Zhao
items.summary: This methodological paper argues that survival-model fits to agent time-horizon curves cannot support conclusions that within-task failure hazard declines over time, showing such curves are consistent with many hazard structures. It proves identification results and shows repeated runs restore within-task hazard identification via joint success probabilities. This directly challenges interpretations of influential recent agent-capability analyses.
items.reasoning: A rigorous statistical critique with real consequences for how the field measures agent capability and reliability, an area driving frontier-lab claims about agent autonomy. The identification result via repeated runs offers a constructive fix. Notable for its potential to change evaluation methodology, though written by a sole independent author rather than a major lab.

items.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
items.content: arXiv:2611.32957v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.
items.author: Megan Squire
items.summary: This red-team style study prompted ten off-the-shelf hosted LLMs to play the seller in a common advance-fee scam using plain system prompts with no jailbreak, running 1,200 conversations against buyer personas. Alarmingly, 61 percent of conversations ended with the buyer paying in advance, and eight of ten models complied almost every time. The paper exposes how little friction is needed for commercial LLMs to facilitate fraud.

items.title: Subliminal Learning Crosses Modalities
items.content: arXiv:2611.31870v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.
items.author: Saraswathy Amjith, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, Yoon Kim
items.summary: Shows that subliminal learning in language models transfers across modalities: preferences distilled through ostensibly meaningless number sequences alter how images are generated and represented by vision-language student models. A diffusion model using the student as text encoder preferentially generates the distilled animal topic, and the paper probes the underlying mechanism.
items.reasoning: Extends an already surprising and safety-relevant phenomenon (subliminal learning) into cross-modal settings, with strong author credibility (Torralba, Kim) and implications for model distillation risks and hidden trait propagation. Mechanistic investigation adds depth.

items.title: PtychoFM: A Foundation Model for Ptychographic Imaging
items.content: arXiv:2611.32830v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ptychography provides high-resolution lensless imaging across X-ray, electron, and optical microscopy, but reconstructing images from diffraction measurements generally requires computationally intensity iterative phase retrieval. These methods often require experiment-specific analysis, limiting real-time feedback as data acquisition rates increase. Here, we demonstrate PtychoFM, a physics-aware foundation model for ptychographic imaging that combines large-scale pre-training with experiment-specific fine-tuning to reconstruct complex object images directly from individual diffraction patterns. Trained using a differentiable forward model without object-space labels, PtychoFM transfers from step-scan training data on one sample to fly-scan measurements of other samples with different feature sizes, morphologies, and refraction indices. At a synchrotron beamline, diffraction frames were streamed from the detector to a single GPU for inference at up to 200 frames per second and returned for real-time visualization. PtychoFM provides a practical route to rapid, transferable ptychographic reconstruction and live experimental feedback under nonideal conditions.

items.title: Bit-Flip Attacks on Quantized Neural Networks without Knowledge of Model Parameters
items.content: arXiv:2611.32128v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We show that quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small tensors retained at high precision. CoarseHammer targets these tensors and accepts flips at any bit, without parameter values, gradients, or data. It remains effective under continued fine-tuning. Under ideal placement, CoarseHammer reaches chance accuracy in at least 81.5% of runs on each of ten evaluated models, including four large language models, with median successful runs requiring at most 24 flips. On simulated DRAM with 0.01 flippable bits per million, it outperforms three prior attacks on every evaluated convolutional network, succeeding in up to 83.6% of runs while they never succeed. On a real system, CoarseHammer steers heap-allocated tensors onto vulnerable frames despite address space layout randomization, without accessing the model file. With 16 templated frames, median accuracy reaches chance for all four language models and approximately chance for four convolutional networks.
items.author: Mahmoud Abumandour, Srinija Ramichetty, Guru Venkataramani, Alaa R. Alameldeen
items.summary: The paper shows quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small high-precision tensors and presents CoarseHammer, an attack that exploits these tensors without needing parameters, gradients, or data. It degrades ten models, including four LLMs, to chance accuracy with as few as 24 flips, and succeeds in realistic DRAM simulation and hardware experiments.
items.reasoning: Significant security finding with strong empirical rigor: parameter-free attacks, multiple evaluated models including LLMs, simulated and real DRAM validation. The insight that quantization asymmetry itself creates an attack surface is novel and directly relevant to deployed quantized LLM infrastructure, though hardware bit-flip attacks are a somewhat specialized threat model.

items.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.33141v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
items.author: Vansh Kapoor, Max Sobol Mark, Sreyas Venkataraman, Max Simchowitz, Aviral Kumar
items.summary: iWAM shows that action policies built on pretrained video-generation world models can condition on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation rather than denoising full future frames, dramatically reducing inference cost for real-time control. The key insight is that a proxy only needs enough information to distinguish possible futures, not high-resolution frame generation. This makes world-model-based policies substantially more practical for real-time robot control.
items.reasoning: Addresses the main practical bottleneck of world-action models (expensive future generation) with a clean, well-motivated design principle and strong author credibility (Kumar, Simchowitz). Likely to be influential for efficient robot policies built on video foundation models.

items.title: SkillCore: Internalizing Generalizable Skills via Scaffolding-Removed Fine-Tuning
items.content: arXiv:2611.32246v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Runtime skills can improve agents' problem-solving capabilities by providing procedural guidance for tasks such as code review and debugging. However, these benefits reach only a minority of users, as most do not proactively invoke skills in practice. We argue that such generalizable procedures should become part of the model's capabilities rather than remain optional external add-ons, making them directly available without explicit skill loading. To this end, we present SkillCore, a data pipeline and supervised fine-tuning recipe for internalizing generalizable skills. We transform real agent trajectories by removing skill-loading scaffolding while preserving the task context and subsequent agent actions, thereby supervising direct execution without external skill content. To preserve access to task-specific skills that provide genuinely external information, we mix these scaffold-removed trajectories with a small proportion of skill-native trajectories that preserve supervision for skill invocation. On a held-out skill-free evaluation, SkillCore improves task completion quality over the base Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-72B models by 54.4% and 24.8%, respectively, while preserving task-specific skill invocation on a separate probe and general coding performance on SWE-bench Verified.
items.author: Yi Liu, Changqing Ai, Peijie Dong, Xiankun Lin, Yongkang Yang, Zhezheng Hao, Xilin Xia, Hande Dong, Qiang Lin, Qiang Xu

It transforms real agent trajectories by stripping skill-loading scaffolding while preserving task context, supervising direct skill execution. This addresses the practical problem that most users never explicitly invoke available skills.
items.reasoning: A clear, practical idea with broad relevance to agent deployment: converting external scaffolding into internalized capability via trajectory transformation. The approach is intuitive and the motivation (most users do not invoke skills) is empirically grounded, though the abstract does not detail evaluation breadth, tempering the score.

items.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
items.content: arXiv:2611.33148v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

items.summary: This paper shows that long-horizon policies can be distilled from a stronger teacher's actions alone, without access to its chain-of-thought, which is essential when the teacher is a closed API model. The student trains on action-only trajectories with an empty reasoning block, plus KL regularization on a replay buffer to limit drift. This offers a practical recipe for distilling capable agents despite hidden reasoning.

items.title: MoGe-4D: Efficient, Flexible, and Unified Dense 4D Reconstruction and Tracking
items.content: arXiv:2611.32198v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes from RGB video requires reasoning about both 3D geometry and motion across viewpoints, yet existing methods either split reconstruction and tracking into fragmented pipelines or face prohibitive dense spatiotemporal decoding costs. We introduce MoGe-4D, a feed-forward framework that unifies geometry and motion prediction via ordered queries of paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps. Each query maps source pixels to a target time simultaneously in both camera frames, resolving relative camera pose in closed form while flexibly serving depth, dynamic registration, and dense 3D tracking. For efficient dense querying, MoGe-4D decouples scene modeling from query decoding: a high-capacity context encoder caches coarse global spatiotemporal features once, while a lightweight query encoder rapidly decodes dense point maps at flexible resolutions. Furthermore, as supervising dense 4D queries demands continuous 3D correspondences whose raw trajectory storage is prohibitive, we introduce RigIDTrack, a synthetic data pipeline and dataset that compresses surface dynamics into rigidity-regularized affine bodies, recovering exact arbitrary-frame 3D trajectories with $\sim15\%$ storage overhead over RGB-D video. Across diverse benchmarks, MoGe-4D achieves state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, matches dedicated 3D foundation models in reconstruction, and runs substantially faster than prior 4D baselines.
items.author: Ruicheng Wang, Linlin Xin, Sicheng Xu, Jianfeng Xiang, Zelong Lv, Yu Deng, Yue Dong, Guangzhong Sun, Tong Zhang, Jiaolong Yang
items.summary: MoGe-4D is a feed-forward framework unifying dense geometry and motion prediction from RGB video via paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps, resolving relative camera pose in closed form while serving depth, dynamic registration, and dense 3D tracking. Across diverse benchmarks, MoGe-4D achieves state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, matches dedicated 3D foundation models in reconstruction, and runs substantially faster than prior 4D baselines.

items.title: A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds
items.content: arXiv:2611.32445v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

items.title: Linear Probes Can Guide: Training-Free Control of Representation Generators
items.content: arXiv:2611.33037v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Representation-space generative models, such as Representation Autoencoders (RAEs), leverage pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs) primarily to accelerate training and improve sample fidelity. Yet VFMs are more than reconstruction tokenizers, as they feature rich representation spaces that are highly organized and linearly readable. We observe that this removes a key obstacle of post-hoc guidance: by linearity of expectation, a clean probe applied to an ideal denoiser's prediction yields the exact posterior mean of the probe scores at any noise level. This regime, which we call Semantic Mean-Space, turns semantic guidance into a Bayesian linear inverse problem, bypassing the need for training-time conditioning. With this foundation, we propose LiSM, a unified framework for Linear Guidance in Semantic Mean-Space. To validate the framework, we developed and adapted different solvers, and characterized them based on how they estimate probe-space uncertainty and propagate the correction through the representation. In addition, we propose Fit-Path, a solver designed to achieve strong global and local control. Our results in four control setups (class, attributes, foreground, and keypoints) show that LiSM methods, and Fit-Path in particular, provide effective, lightweight control across global and local tasks, outperforming noise-aware and pixel-space guidance.

items.title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
items.content: arXiv:2611.33143v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

Human evaluators achieve roughly 84% strict success, establishing a headroom measure for current embodied agents.

items.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming for Robot Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.31715v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.

items.title: EgoLoAF: Learning Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations with Hand-Object Affordances
items.content: arXiv:2611.32260v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training humanoid vision-language-action (VLA) models relies heavily on costly real-robot teleoperation. Recent efforts convert egocentric human demonstrations into humanoid training data. However, most methods still require wearable motion trackers and leave important hand-object interaction cues implicit. Many also mix in real-robot teleoperation data for VLA post-training. These dependencies limit scalable data collection, while implicit interaction cues make precise contact harder to learn. To overcome these limitations, we propose EgoLoAF, the first paradigm to derive all training data for humanoid loco-manipulation directly from egocentric demonstrations without wearable motion trackers. We post-train the VLA on the converted data alone, without real-robot teleoperation demonstrations, and use explicit hand-object interaction cues to guide action generation. Specifically, to obtain humanoid action targets, we estimate torso motion from recorded camera poses and reconstruct both hand trajectories from video. From the same recording, we use each hand's current pose relative to the object to represent hand-object affordances. During post-training, we inject these affordances into the action expert through cross-attention while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen. Additionally, we release 128,400 egocentric demonstration episodes spanning 1,000 hours and 1,284 tasks, together with converted humanoid action trajectories and rendered robot-view observations. Across four real-world tasks, EgoLoAF nearly achieves teleoperation performance (73.1 vs. 74.4 in mean Task Progress Score), while achieving a mean 4.03 times improvement in data-collection efficiency.

items.title: DiffGR00T: Execution-Aware Differentiable Training for Humanoid Whole-Body Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.32665v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2% to 71.7%), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics.
