The quantified demonstration of evaluation pitfalls, such as alignment procedures masking large errors, provides a genuinely useful service to the community and could shape how 3D/4D models are benchmarked going forward.

items.title: Lost on Campus: Evaluating Embodied Spatial Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in the Wild
items.content: arXiv:2611.33145v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.

items.title: The Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Undermines Black-Box Model Integrity Verification
items.content: arXiv:2611.31455v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Black-box integrity verification aims to detect unauthorized modifications to outsourced models using only prediction APIs. Existing frameworks seek to improve verification efficiency through sensitive fingerprints: queries whose predictions are more likely to change under tampering than those of genuine inputs. We show that this sensitivity can also help dishonest providers recognize verification queries and selectively conceal tampering. We prove that excess sensitivity relative to genuine inputs lower-bounds statistical distinguishability. We evaluate five integrity verification frameworks across three model architectures, three datasets, and three adversarial knowledge settings. When the deployed framework is known, our fingerprint detectors achieve AUCs at least 0.989, and selective filtering makes all five frameworks require significantly larger estimated query budgets than genuine inputs, reversing their intended efficiency advantage. A query-efficiency advantage remains marginally in a small subset of evaluated settings with poor detection transfer. We further design verification methods under stronger concealment constraints but find that reduced detectability comes with losses in sensitivity or fingerprint-generation success. Our results expose a sensitivity-detectability tension and show that sensitivity alone does not ensure efficient black-box verification against adaptive malicious providers.
items.author: Shahinul Hoque, Farhin Farhad Riya, Jinyuan Sun, Fnu Suya
items.summary: This paper identifies a fundamental flaw in black-box model integrity verification: sensitive fingerprints designed to detect tampering can themselves be exploited by dishonest providers to identify and evade verification queries. The authors prove a lower bound linking excess sensitivity to statistical distinguishability and empirically show fingerprint detection failures across five frameworks, three architectures, and multiple adversarial settings. It reframes model integrity verification as a harder adversarial problem than previously assumed.
items.reasoning: Strong conceptual contribution with both theoretical proof and broad empirical evaluation; reveals a structural weakness affecting a whole class of verification frameworks. Important for AI security and model auditing, though niche in immediate application scope.

items.title: Ego2Real: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Visuo-Tactile Demonstrations
items.content: arXiv:2611.32101v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations offers a scalable path toward robot skill acquisition. Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator's force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions. Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer. We present Ego2Real, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands. Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages: (1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry; and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards. By combining refined motion references with physical contact rewards during training, Ego2Real guides anthropomorphic robotic hands to emulate demonstrated contact behaviors while adapting to their own morphology and actuation. Experiments show that incorporating tactile supervision into both reconstruction and policy learning yields higher manipulation success rates, underscoring the importance of enriching egocentric demonstrations with tactile observations to improve their quality and transferability.

items.summary: Ego2Real transfers bimanual dexterous manipulation skills from human egocentric demonstrations augmented with tactile gloves to robotic hands. Tactile supervision is applied at two stages: tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction and subsequent policy learning, addressing ambiguities that vision alone cannot resolve about contact and force intent.
items.reasoning: Combining egocentric video with tactile gloves for bimanual dexterous transfer is a compelling scaling path for human-to-robot skill acquisition. The dual-stage tactile supervision is technically interesting, though practical dependence on tactile gloves may constrain data collection scale.

items.title: AI research agents crowd onto the same projects, and how to spread them out
items.content:
Summary: We may soon have autonomous AI researchers who choose their own research projects. We find that without careful design, current agents concentrate on a small number of projects. Two agents picked at random chose the same project about 1 time in 60, against about 1 in 530 for humans at AI safety hackathons. Agents from different labs mostly choose different projects, but agents from the same lab often choose the same ones, even with different models. Varying launch prompts helps only a little, varying harnesses not at all, and letting agents search the literature doubles the effective number of projects, but crowds agents onto one research area. Small interventions can spread them out. With a shared registry of what earlier agents had chosen, agents almost never duplicate each other. Without coordination, agents can take a weighted sample across all possible projects to spread themselves out. These interventions spread out the project selection, but we were not able to measure the impact this would have on the quality of the selection.

This is a compressed version of the results; the full paper and GitHub repo can be found here.

# Why

items.title: Who Gets the Dangerous Model First?
items.content:
Anthropic announced its new AI model Mythos alongside a restricted-access initiative called Project Glasswing, which was intended to help select organisations identify and patch vulnerabilities in major software and web browsers before the public had access to the models. But on June 12, the US Department of Commerce sent a private letter to Anthropic, causing the company to shut down access to both Mythos and Fable worldwide. When Mythos was restored, US organisations gained priority.

This unprecedented series of events set the stage for something new: the spectre of state control over powerful AI as it emerged from development. At first, Anthropic held the decision-making process on who gained access through Project Glasswing, but that control rapidly shifted to the US government, which in turn set the rules for international access. The theoretical concern was to protect against hostile states, but in practice, it affected allies across the globe in different ways. Japan managed to engage through direct diplomatic channels to get access. Korea engaged directly with Anthropic. The EU, arguably worst affected, suffered months of delays negotiating access, complicated by US restrictions. A new security dilemma made itself known to any country outside the exclusivity circle: powerful AI models may be controlled by a foreign state whose interests do not align with their own.

The answer is to make sure the process of who gets access and why is transparent, independently reviewable and predictable. Allies in particular need a formal mechanism to align their access and come to terms with the realisation that they cannot allow themselves to remain dependent, so must pursue domestic capabilities.

I hold shares in Anthropic and other companies discussed; full disclosures in the paper.

items.title: Spec-Test Coverage Gap: Detecting Overspecified Tests in SWE-Bench-Style Benchmarks
items.content: arXiv:2611.31839v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: SWE-bench-style benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified (Verified) and SWE-bench Pro (Pro), evaluate coding agents with tests taken from the change that originally fixed each issue. However, these tests can enforce details the task never states, causing correct alternative fixes to fail. Such overspecified tests have so far been found mainly through expensive expert review. To address this, we define the Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG), a 1-4 scale measuring overspecification, and score it with two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which are given the specification and the test patch. A task is flagged as overspecified when both judges score it 3 or higher. Our study has three parts. First, we validate the judges on 206 tasks that earlier human audits and agent results label as overspecified or fine. Second, we apply STCG to all 500 Verified and 731 public Pro tasks and compare the flags with the results of the top 30 Verified submissions. Third, we verify the flags by asking Claude Opus 5.5 to loosen the overspecified requirements of flagged tasks, and regrade 2,186 failed patches from those submissions. Our main findings are: (1) Overspecified tests are detectable: on the validation tasks, the judges correctly flag 89% of the tasks that human audits identify as overspecified and wrongly flag only 4% of the tasks known to be fine. (2) Overspecified tests are common: applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag 23% of Verified and 35% of Pro tasks. (3) Flagged tasks are much harder for agents: the top 30 Verified submissions resolve only 31% of the flagged tasks on average, against 88% of the other tasks. (4) Overspecified tests change the leaderboard: relaxing the tests lets 61% of the 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass. Counting these patches as resolved would add 33 to 60 tasks to each top-30 submission, raising resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.

Validated against 206 expert-reviewed tasks, it detects tests that enforce unstated details and cause correct alternative fixes to fail, replacing expensive expert review.

items.title: Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.32199v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Our goal is to build language models that are steerable by design. Today's language models are pretrained with next-token prediction, which relegates alignment and control to the final 1% of training tokens or inference-time interventions. These models repurpose a single input channel for both instructions and data, leading to common failure modes where the model mistakenly treats data as instructions such as intentional jailbreaks and unintentional in-context alignment drift. To correct this, we propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the very start, producing Mancelle-3B. An encoder processes high-level semantic features of upcoming text with cross-attention that prevents the token stream from writing back into this control channel. During pretraining, the model learns to rely on these features to predict the next token, turning the channel into an effective handle for steering the model. Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than prompt- and activation-based methods on comparable open models while maintaining fluency, and it withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines. We reproduce this against a more controlled baseline with Mancelle-400M. Our results show that robust control can be built into language models if we do so early and intentionally.

items.title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
items.content: arXiv:2611.33093v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.
items.author: Guangyuan Wang, Chengran Li, Minchen Luo, Jichen Feng, Mengdi Wang, Yifan Zhang

It captures hardware-specific failure modes like state corruption that passes output tests. This is a rigorous benchmark for agentic hardware design, an emerging frontier.

items.title: UniCon: Unified Framework for Efficient Contrastive Alignment via Kernels
items.content: arXiv:2604.16678v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Contrastive objectives power state-of-the-art multimodal models, but their training remains slow, relying on long stochastic optimization. We propose a Unified Framework for Efficient Contrastive Alignment via Kernels (UniCon), which spans linear and nonlinear encoders as well as one-to-one and many-to-many alignments. At its core, UniCon introduces the contrastive similarity weight matrix $S(\gamma)$, which enables closed-form global solutions that provably replace minibatch back-propagation with exact updates. Through the lens of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), UniCon provides a kernelized perspective that unifies contrastive alignment and reveals its connection to spectral methods. To validate the theory, we conduct experiments on synthetic, unimodal, multimodal, and zero-shot tasks, demonstrating that UniCon achieves substantial efficiency gains while preserving generality and strong empirical performance.

items.title: EmbodiSafety: Benchmarking Risk Understanding and Response in Embodied AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.33054v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Progress in embodied foundation models is largely measured by task success, while the physical safety of their decisions remains underexamined. Safety evaluations centered on rule following and binary judgments do not adequately assess whether embodied models understand environmental hazards and make safe decisions. We introduce EmbodiSafety, comprising 1,092 snapshot tasks and 540 trajectory tasks across 844 visual scenarios to assess safety over short and long horizons. Six response modes cover direct execution, refusal, clarification, constrained execution, autonomous recovery, and human escalation. Distinguishing recovery from human intervention makes the boundary of safe autonomy an explicit evaluation target. Our protocol assesses mode correctness, risk identification, and actionable handling, with complete decision accuracy requiring all applicable checks to pass. Claude-Opus-5.5 achieves the highest complete decision accuracy among reference models, reaching 56.1% on snapshots and 61.5% on trajectories. We further develop a data construction pipeline and curate 40k examples for safety alignment. Supervised training on this corpus raises the complete decision accuracy of Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B.

items.title: Lazy gas, hot gas, and a thousand robots
items.content: Amazon Robotics operates over a million robots across more than 300 warehouses worldwide. Inside a single warehouse, thousands of robots share the floor, moving inventory for order fulfillment and stock replenishment. Finding efficient, collision-free robot paths to their destinations is therefore essential for smooth operations. Let us formulate the underlying multiagent pathfinding (MAPF) problem a bit more precisely. Consider a typical warehouse layout as a W x H rectangular grid. At each time step, a robot can make one of five choices: move north, east, west, or south, or wait. These choices must be coordinated to avoid collisions. Over a planning horizon of T time steps, finding optimal robot paths involves approximately n = 5WHT binary decision variables, giving 2n possible combinations before accounting for feasibility constraints. Finding optimal paths that minimize the total move cost or arrival time without collisions is NP hard in general and can become computationally intractable even for moderate numbers of robots. In a paper we presented at this year’s International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), we show that physics offers a way around this intractability: plan trajectories as if the robots were particles of gas. Modeling the robots as a cold, lazy gas, whose particles spend only the minimum effort to reach their destinations, yields optimal, minimum-energy paths. This is equivalent to treating trajectory planning as an optimal-transport problem. It yields optimal paths, but computing them may take too long for real-time deployment. Modeling the fleet as a hot gas, whose particles jitter randomly along the way, yields trajectories that are computationally faster but potentially suboptimal. As the temperature drops to zero, however, the jittery hot-gas paths settle onto the lazy-gas ones. Our approach uses a Schrödinger bridge — a hot-gas model — to efficiently approximate the solution to an optimal-transport problem — the cold-gas model. Optimal transport To develop the formal connection, let us travel back to 1781 in France to meet Gaspard Monge, the father of differential geometry. Monge was looking for the most efficient way to transport excavated dirt to military fortifications. His studies gave rise to the optimal-transport problem, which asks how to transport resources from a set of sources to a set of destinations while minimizing cost, such as distance traveled or work done. Monge’s sources were the locations containing dirt. His formulation required all mass at each source location to be transported to one destination, producing a deterministic transport map. Although intuitive, Monge’s original formulation is a difficult nonlinear optimization problem with a potential combinatorial explosion in discrete settings. Finding an optimal map is therefore technically challenging and, in some settings, impossible. Roughly 150 years later, Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich relaxed this restriction by allowing mass from one source to be split among multiple destinations. His key insight was that this relaxation converts a difficult optimization over transport maps into a linear program, a class of problems for which highly efficient computer algorithms were subsequently developed. Kantorovich received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to the theory of optimum allocation of resources. Optimal transport connects two mass distributions, also known as marginals, through minimum-cost transport plans. This two-marginal formulation represents only the initial and final configurations and the cost of transporting between them, not the intermediate paths or collisions along those paths. Formulating MAPF as optimal transport therefore requires a multistage approach, because robots generally cannot move from their starting locations to their destinations in a single time step; their locations must also be represented at every intermediate time. We develop this connection in detail in our paper, using multimarginal optimal transport (MMOT), which extends optimal transport to a sequence of marginals. In other words, the additional marginals represent robot locations at intermediate times in MAPF, allowing motion to be modeled across both space and time. In the case of anonymous MAPF problems, where any robot can go to any destination, a key result we prove in the paper is the following: The MMOT formulation solves the combinatorial anonymous MAPF problem to optimality with a runtime of O(n1.68) seconds in practice and with a theoretical upper bound of roughly O(n3). Formally speaking, we achieve this by carefully preserving the total unimodularity of the underlying constraint matrices. We next provide a brief explanation of total unimodularity (TU). Consider the decision variables in a transport plan as a vector or a point in a high-dimensional space, with each coordinate specifying how much mass is transported from one grid cell to another in a single time step. The set of all feasible plans forms a geometric object called a polyhedron. Total unimodularity guarantees that every corner of this polyhedron has integer coordinates. Since a linear objective attains its optimum at a corner of the corresponding feasible polyhedron, a linear program (LP) provides optimal and integer solutions in polynomial time. Without total unimodularity, a linear program may return a fractional solution; for example, it may send half of a robot along one route and half along another. Going back to the scale of Amazon warehouses, a square 150 × 150 grid with 1,125 robots has 3.4 million decision variables over a planning horizon of T = 30. Our TU-preserving MMOT provides optimal robot trajectories from their starting locations to their destinations in 478 seconds. By contrast, the non-TU, NP-hard formulation often fails to find even a single feasible solution in 12 hours. Finding an optimal solution in 478 seconds, however, might still be impractical. A natural question is whether we can improve the solver’s runtime by accepting a slightly suboptimal solution. It is not generally clear how to formulate such a tradeoff in clean technical terms, which leads to our next contribution. Gases hot and cold The path to answering this question begins, unexpectedly, not with robots or linear programs but with Erwin Schrödinger and a cloud of hot gas in 1931 Germany. Schrödinger asked, Given the observed distributions of gas particles at two different times, what was the most likely evolution between them? The emphasis here is on most likely: hot gas particles diffuse randomly, through Brownian motion, rather than following deterministic paths. This “hot gas” characterization contrasts with classical optimal transport, which can be modeled as “lazy gas” diffusion, in which particles expend only the minimum work needed to reach their destinations. It turns out that the temperature of the gas provides the technical lever needed to traverse the spectrum from lazy gas (optimal but potentially longer runtimes) to hot gas (computationally faster but suboptimal trajectories). To relate Schrödinger's gases back to MAPF, we devised a probabilistic Schrödinger bridge between the initial and final robot configurations. Instead of selecting a deterministic set of paths, the bridge casts robot transport as a shadow, i.e., the most likely way for the robot mass to flow from one state to another. In our paper, we show that this is equivalent to an entropic relaxation of the MMOT problem. The amount of entropy added is analogous to the gas temperature and controls how much randomness is added to the robot trajectories. This allows us to extend a very fast method called Sinkhorn iterations to solve for the shadow. Because the shadows are probabilistic, they divide each robot’s mass across possible destinations in space and time. Since individual robots can’t split apart, we can’t execute this plan directly. The shadow, however, tells us where the optimal paths concentrate; that is, it reveals the important corridors. We can recover integrality by removing those decision variables where the mass is small or robot travel is less likely from the MMOT. Scalability: In practice, the Schrödinger pipeline (shadow plus integral projections) scales nearly linearly, O(n1.15), versus O(n1.68) for the direct MMOT solver. Looking ahead We’re developing extensions to labeled MAPF problems, where each robot has a fixed destination, and lifelong MAPF, where robots handle continuous streams of tasks. The connection between optimal transport and multirobot coordination opens a rich design space, offering opportunities to combine principled linear and integer programs with learning-based approaches like DeepFleet, imitation learning, and everything in between.

items.content_html: Amazon Robotics operates over a million robots across more than 300 warehouses worldwide. Inside a single warehouse, thousands of robots share the floor, moving inventory for order fulfillment and stock replenishment. Finding efficient, collision-free robot paths to their destinations is therefore essential for smooth operations. Let us formulate the underlying multiagent pathfinding (MAPF) problem a bit more precisely. Consider a typical warehouse layout as a W x H rectangular grid. At each time step, a robot can make one of five choices: move north, east, west, or south, or wait. These choices must be coordinated to avoid collisions. Over a planning horizon of T time steps, finding optimal robot paths involves approximately n = 5WHT binary decision variables, giving 2n possible combinations before accounting for feasibility constraints. Finding optimal paths that minimize the total move cost or arrival time without collisions is NP hard in general and can become computationally intractable even for moderate numbers of robots. In a paper we presented at this year’s International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), we show that physics offers a way around this intractability: plan trajectories as if the robots were particles of gas. Modeling the robots as a cold, lazy gas, whose particles spend only the minimum effort to reach their destinations, yields optimal, minimum-energy paths. This is equivalent to treating trajectory planning as an optimal-transport problem. It yields optimal paths, but computing them may take too long for real-time deployment. Modeling the fleet as a hot gas, whose particles jitter randomly along the way, yields trajectories that are computationally faster but potentially suboptimal. As the temperature drops to zero, however, the jittery hot-gas paths settle onto the lazy-gas ones. Our approach uses a Schrödinger bridge — a hot-gas model — to efficiently approximate the solution to an optimal-transport problem — the cold-gas model. Optimal transport To develop the formal connection, let us travel back to 1781 in France to meet Gaspard Monge, the father of differential geometry. Monge was looking for the most efficient way to transport excavated dirt to military fortifications. His studies gave rise to the optimal-transport problem, which asks how to transport resources from a set of sources to a set of destinations while minimizing cost, such as distance traveled or work done. Monge’s sources were the locations containing dirt. His formulation required all mass at each source location to be transported to one destination, producing a deterministic transport map. Although intuitive, Monge’s original formulation is a difficult nonlinear optimization problem with a potential combinatorial explosion in discrete settings. Finding an optimal map is therefore technically challenging and, in some settings, impossible. Roughly 150 years later, Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich relaxed this restriction by allowing mass from one source to be split among multiple destinations. His key insight was that this relaxation converts a difficult optimization over transport maps into a linear program, a class of problems for which highly efficient computer algorithms were subsequently developed. Kantorovich received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to the theory of optimum allocation of resources. Optimal transport connects two mass distributions, also known as marginals, through minimum-cost transport plans. This two-marginal formulation represents only the initial and final configurations and the cost of transporting between them, not the intermediate paths or collisions along those paths. Formulating MAPF as optimal transport therefore requires a multistage approach, because robots generally cannot move from their starting locations to their destinations in a single time step; their locations must also be represented at every intermediate time. We develop this connection in detail in our paper, using multimarginal optimal transport (MMOT), which extends optimal transport to a sequence of marginals. In other words, the additional marginals represent robot locations at intermediate times in MAPF, allowing motion to be modeled across both space and time. In the case of anonymous MAPF problems, where any robot can go to any destination, a key result we prove in the paper is the following: The MMOT formulation solves the combinatorial anonymous MAPF problem to optimality with a runtime of O(n1.68) seconds in practice and with a theoretical upper bound of roughly O(n3). Formally speaking, we achieve this by carefully preserving the total unimodularity of the underlying constraint matrices. We next provide a brief explanation of total unimodularity (TU). Consider the decision variables in a transport plan as a vector or a point in a high-dimensional space, with each coordinate specifying how much mass is transported from one grid cell to another in a single time step. The set of all feasible plans forms a geometric object called a polyhedron. Total unimodularity guarantees that every corner of this polyhedron has integer coordinates. Since a linear objective attains its optimum at a corner of the corresponding feasible polyhedron, a linear program (LP) provides optimal and integer solutions in polynomial time. Without total unimodularity, a linear program may return a fractional solution; for example, it may send half of a robot along one route and half along another. Going back to the scale of Amazon warehouses, a square 150 × 150 grid with 1,125 robots has 3.4 million decision variables over a planning horizon of T = 30. Our TU-preserving MMOT provides optimal robot trajectories from their starting locations to their destinations in 478 seconds. By contrast, the non-TU, NP-hard formulation often fails to find even a single feasible solution in 12 hours. Finding an optimal solution in 478 seconds, however, might still be impractical. A natural question is whether we can improve the solver’s runtime by accepting a slightly suboptimal solution. It is not generally clear how to formulate such a tradeoff in clean technical terms, which leads to our next contribution. Gases hot and cold The path to answering this question begins, unexpectedly, not with robots or linear programs but with Erwin Schrödinger and a cloud of hot gas in 1931 Germany. Schrödinger asked, Given the observed distributions of gas particles at two different times, what was the most likely evolution between them? The emphasis here is on most likely: hot gas particles diffuse randomly, through Brownian motion, rather than following deterministic paths. This “hot gas” characterization contrasts with classical optimal transport, which can be modeled as “lazy gas” diffusion, in which particles expend only the minimum work needed to reach their destinations. It turns out that the temperature of the gas provides the technical lever needed to traverse the spectrum from lazy gas (optimal but potentially longer runtimes) to hot gas (computationally faster but suboptimal trajectories). Instead of selecting a deterministic set of paths, the bridge casts robot transport as a shadow, i.e., the most likely way for the robot mass to flow from one state to another. In our paper, we show that this is equivalent to an entropic relaxation of the MMOT problem. The amount of entropy added is analogous to the gas temperature and controls how much randomness is added to the robot trajectories. This allows us to extend a very fast method called Sinkhorn iterations to solve for the shadow. Because the shadows are probabilistic, they divide each robot’s mass across possible destinations in space and time. Since individual robots can’t split apart, we can’t execute this plan directly. The shadow, however, tells us where the optimal paths concentrate; that is, it reveals the important corridors. We can recover integrality by removing those decision variables where the mass is small or robot travel is less likely from the MMOT. Scalability: In practice, the Schrödinger pipeline (shadow plus integral projections) scales nearly linearly, O(n1.15), versus O(n1.68) for the direct MMOT solver. items.title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
items.content: arXiv:2611.31427v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM agents operate through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, feedback loops, and resource constraints. A model may possess the knowledge needed to solve a task yet fail to express that knowledge through a particular harness. This raises a basic question: when a policy fails under a given harness, is it missing task knowledge or the competence to operate the interface? We distinguish two components of agentic competence: task competence, the knowledge and reasoning needed to solve a task, and interface competence, the ability to act on that knowledge through a given harness. Across four reasoning and agentic benchmarks, we show that harness-conditioned training yields vastly different outcomes depending on how these interact. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge from trajectories collected through different harnesses into a shared policy, but this knowledge is realised only when training preserves or improves competence on the inference-time interface. Otherwise, single-harness training can induce interference in interface competence, sometimes catastrophically collapsing performance on a held-out harness despite improvements in underlying task knowledge. To disentangle task and interface supervision, we introduce harness rehearsal: distillation on traces that carry minimal task knowledge while exercising the target interface. Cross-harness task supervision or rehearsal alone yields little gain, but their combination yields gains far larger than either: on BFCL V3 multi-turn with Qwen3-4B, they achieve 8.5% and 32.5% respectively, versus 58.8% together. Finally, on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is more robust than distillation to single-harness training: it does not substantially degrade performance on other harnesses, and interface competence acquired through multi-harness distillation persists through subsequent RL.
items.author: Chaeeun Lee, Hossein A. Rahmani, Aryo Pradipta Gema, Kexin Xu, Emine Yilmaz, Pasquale Minervini, T. Ian Simpson, Chen Jin, Amrutha Saseendran
items.summary: The paper distinguishes task competence (knowledge needed to solve a task) from interface competence (ability to express that knowledge through a given agent harness) and studies how harness-conditioned training affects each. Across four reasoning and agentic benchmarks, it shows training outcomes vary dramatically depending on how these competences interact, clarifying whether policy failures stem from missing knowledge or poor harness operation.
items.reasoning: A conceptually clean decomposition with direct practical relevance to how agent harnesses are built and how agentic training data should be conditioned. The multi-benchmark experimental design and strong author list (including Minervini and Gema) increase credibility, though the analysis-focused contribution is incremental rather than a new capability.

items.title: Self-Improving Long-Horizon Reasoning by Learning Summaries from Local Continuations
items.content: arXiv:2611.31621v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.
items.author: Haoqun Cao, Tengyang Xie
items.summary: The paper targets context-length degradation in reasoning models by training a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward derived from a frozen reasoning model's reliable short-context behavior, to compress long reasoning histories into compact states. This avoids relying on final-answer rewards or distillation from stronger models, preserving local behavior while extending effective reasoning horizons.
items.reasoning: Long-horizon reasoning degradation is a central limitation of current reasoning models, and the Delta-KL signal that measures the summary state's contribution alone is a clever, novel training objective. The approach is theoretically motivated and could influence how context compression and summarization are trained, though empirical scope appears to be controlled benchmark settings.

items.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.31756v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.
items.author: Ilia Hashemi Rad, Feijie Wu, Haoyu Wang, Jing Gao
items.summary: TACT-Bench is a stateful safety benchmark for tool-use agents featuring scenario-specific personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Adversarial tasks target actions explicitly prohibited by a hidden policy while requiring the agent to continue legitimate work in the same interaction. It fills a gap between benchmarks testing compromised tool channels and those testing only static multi-turn attacks.
items.reasoning: Timely and well-scoped safety benchmark addressing adaptive social-engineering attacks on agentic systems, an increasingly critical gap as agents gain autonomy. Score held back by unclear breadth of evaluated models.

items.title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
items.content: arXiv:2611.31795v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case, q has a unique form and we provide sufficient conditions for valid implementations to exist; in the nonlinear case, we provide an ODE-based algorithm for constructing implementations. We call this framework Constructive Causal Abstraction (CCA), and use CCA to formulate the difference between machine-learning model auditing and editing. With the Bias-in-Bios biographies dataset, we demonstrate that CCA allows practitioners to articulate assumptions when detecting the model's gender bias. Finally, CCA resolves a well-known paradox known as "interpretability illusion" which points to a mismatch between the subspace for editing and the one where the model implements a signal-to-output pathway.
items.author: Yuchen Zhu, Sergio Hernan Garrido Mejia, Dominik Janzing
items.summary: The paper's central insight is that causally consistent macro-level causal models can be constructed rather than merely verified: ill-defined macro interventions are interpreted as missing macro-level variables that can be repaired by introducing completion machinery. The authors apply this framework in a mechanistic interpretability case study. This addresses a foundational difficulty in causal abstraction, where macro relations are rarely well-defined.

items.title: Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation for LLM Unlearning
items.content: arXiv:2611.31932v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while preserving unrelated model capabilities. Existing likelihood-based methods commonly optimize against fixed forget sequences, providing only negative supervision on what the model should not generate and overlooking the states visited by the evolving unlearned policy. We introduce Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation (CPSD), a new unlearning framework that constructs an explicit knowledge-reduced target distribution and distills it along the model's own trajectories. Given a student rollout, a frozen reference model evaluates each token under a plain context and a privileged context containing the forget information. CPSD treats the resulting distributional shift as a knowledge-associated direction and reverses it to obtain a counterfactual unlearning target. The student is then trained to match this target at every rollout position while retaining its utility on unrelated data. We further introduce a privacy-enhanced variant that combines distributional unlearning with lightweight sequence-level suppression. Experiments under OpenUnlearning show that CPSD improves the forgetting-utility trade-off over NPO across TOFU forget-set sizes and Llama models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters. On MUSE-News, the privacy-enhanced variant improves all reported knowledge, memorization, privacy, and utility metrics over NPO.
items.author: Fangzhou Lin, Shuo Xing, Xin Li, Wenbin He, Zhengzhong Tu, Liu Ren
items.summary: CPSD is a new framework for LLM unlearning that constructs an explicit knowledge-reduced target distribution and distills it along the model's own sampled trajectories, rather than providing only negative supervision on fixed forget sequences. A frozen reference model evaluates each token under plain versus privileged contexts to produce contrastive signals, aiming to remove designated data influence while preserving unrelated capabilities.
items.reasoning: Unlearning is a high-value safety and privacy topic, and the on-policy trajectory-level formulation with privileged-context contrast is a meaningful methodological advance over likelihood-based baselines. Credibility is moderate as an academic group, but the problem framing and evaluation direction are strong.

items.title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
items.content: arXiv:2611.32384v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.
items.author: Songtao Jiang, Yuan Wang, Fucheng Niu, Hualiang Wang, Jian Wu, Zuozhu Liu
items.summary: This paper proposes a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop where LLM agents diagnose structured failure patterns in a frozen nnU-Net medical imaging pipeline, form falsifiable hypotheses, run counterfactual experiments, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves it derives two principles for 3D medical segmentation: shifting computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder to preserve thin-anatomy boundaries, and support-confined region contrast to fix inter-region errors. It matters because it moves beyond scalar-fitness NAS and LLM evolution by explicitly exploiting failure information for scientific architecture discovery.
items.reasoning: The failure-driven, hypothesis-testing framing is a genuinely interesting alternative to black-box architecture search, and the domain grounding in medical segmentation makes results concrete. However, impact is limited to a specialized domain and the loop depends on a frozen strong baseline pipeline; broad applicability remains to be demonstrated.

The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

items.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
items.content: arXiv:2611.32884v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

items.summary: This paper identifies agent laziness — committing to an answer before sufficient evidence even while the agent stated belief admits multiple candidates — and proposes RLVB (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs), which uses the simulator-computed posterior over the answer at each step to reward agents for continuing while multiple answers remain plausible and committing only when evidence suffices. Outcome-only rewards cannot teach this timing because lucky guesses earn the same reward as evidence-backed answers. The approach directly targets calibration between belief and action on long-horizon tasks.
items.reasoning: The laziness phenomenon is a crisp, relatable diagnosis of a real agent failure mode, and RLVB is a clean, well-motivated training solution leveraging privileged simulator posteriors during training. The requirement of a computable answer posterior limits applicability to simulated or verifiable settings, which holds back generality, but the core contribution is strong for the agent-training literature.

items.title: The Date You Didn't Set: The System-Prompt Date as a Hidden Variable in LLM Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2611.31254v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The system prompt of many instruction-tuned models carries a date, usually today's, filled in automatically for conversational and agentic requests alike, so an unchanged evaluation can send a different prompt each day. In this paper, we explore how much this hidden input changes evaluation outcomes. Across six instruction-tuned models and four benchmarks, with prompts, decoding, and configuration fixed, every model is affected: two plausible dates (2024--2026) switch a median $6.6\%$ of test items between correct and incorrect. Even rerunning the evaluation one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size, although nothing in the setup was changed. In addition, using a grammar-constrained variant of Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to search dates of any year, we find dates that cost the Llama-3.x models up to $36.5$ points of held-out accuracy. Beyond accuracy, switching to another plausible date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes $15$--$32\%$ of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. Yet none of the eleven evaluation stacks we audit pins the date. With the date and the rest of the setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte; we therefore recommend pinning, logging, and reporting the date.

items.title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
items.content: arXiv:2611.31286v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts.   The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.

items.summary: DeMillo and Lipton revisit their nearly fifty-year-old thesis that mathematical proofs are social artifacts, applying the DLP framework to OpenAI's October 2026 release of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts claiming solutions to 372 open problems. They argue that mass-produced, unreadable machine-generated proofs constitute a form of pollution of the mathematical ecosystem rather than genuine progress.
items.reasoning: A substantive position paper by highly credible veterans of the field engaging directly with a major current event in AI-assisted mathematics. It is argumentative rather than empirical, but its framing of proof industrialization as an ecosystem-level risk is timely and likely to influence debate on automated mathematical discovery.

items.title: FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.31705v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/
items.author: Jiaqi Yin, Baoyue Zhang, Jiyuan Zhang, Wenxuan Liu, Zhaofei Yu, Yue Deng, Tiejun Huang
items.summary: FoveaWAM is a native 4D world-action model for manipulating moving objects that allocates predictive precision by role: millimeter-accurate SE(3) trajectory prediction for the manipulation target, while modeling surroundings only through clearance and imparted motion. This decoupling addresses the latency-accuracy tension where every millisecond of scene forecasting delays action execution.
items.reasoning: Strong robotics contribution with a clear insight about role-decoupled prediction, targeting the real-time closed-loop manipulation problem that current world models handle poorly. From a credible author group, though empirical results cannot be fully assessed from the abstract.

items.title: Exploring Multi-Player Social Games as Verifiable Training Grounds for Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.31821v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The training of socially intelligent language models often relies on large language model (LLM) judges, which are expensive, noisy, and vulnerable to reward hacking. Multi-player social games offer a natural alternative: they require open-ended communication to coordinate with teammates and infer hidden roles, while their rules provide an objective outcome which can serve as a verifiable reward for training. Using three social games, we explore how much social intelligence Qwen3 models can acquire through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Results show that against a much stronger Gemma-3-27B model, SFT and RLVR raise the win rate of Qwen3-4B from 33% to 81% on the three trained games, and from 39% to 54% on three additional held-out games. In contrast, in-context strategies such as prompting improve the win rate of Qwen3-4B by only about 6 pp across the same games we train and evaluate on. Furthermore, we show that the gains from SFT and RLVR hold across the model sizes 1.7B, 4B, and 32B. Qualitative analyses of agent behavior show signs of stronger social intelligence; for example, trained agents tend to share information more openly, check each other's claims against public evidence, and coordinate their votes. More broadly, our results demonstrate that training LLMs on verifiable outcomes in social games can cultivate generalizable social behaviors, which offers a scalable path for building socially intelligent agents.
items.author: Keyu He, Michael Li, Jiarui Liu, Mingqian Zheng, Koichi Onoue, Tongshuang Wu, Maarten Sap
items.summary: This work uses multi-player social games as verifiable-reward environments for training socially intelligent LLMs, avoiding noisy and hackable LLM judges. Applying SFT and RLVR to Qwen3-4B (an existing model family) across three social games raises win rate against a stronger Gemma-3-27B opponent from 33% to 81%, showing that rule-based outcomes can serve as objective social rewards.
items.reasoning: Well-designed RLVR study addressing a real problem (reward hacking in social-skill training) with strong empirical gains and cross-model evaluation, from a credible academic team. The generalization of learned social intelligence to untrained settings remains the key question, tempering the score slightly.

items.title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT
items.content: arXiv:2611.31849v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.
items.author: Hanbin Ko, Hong-Jun Choi, Jihun Kim, Young-Gon Kim, Dongheon Lee, Chang Min Park
items.summary: This paper identifies a context shortcut in joint-embedding predictive architectures for chest CT, where clinically important findings like small nodules are unpredictable from surrounding anatomy and thus become invisible to the prediction loss. The proposed JECT method gives radiology reports a dual role as both a predictor condition and a learning signal via masked section-text prediction. This matters because it exposes a fundamental flaw in how self-supervised medical pretraining can systematically fail to encode the rare findings that matter most for diagnosis.
items.reasoning: A clear conceptual contribution (naming and analyzing the context shortcut) grounded in a clinically important domain, with a practical dual-use solution for report supervision. Medical AI pretraining research is impactful, though the authors are academic rather than a major lab and the scope is specific to chest CT.

items.title: HuluOPD: Unifying Heterogeneous Medical Specialists into One Lightweight Model with Unlabeled Prompts
items.content: arXiv:2611.32021v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.

A continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss enables supervision across differing architectures and tokenizers. This could substantially cut deployment costs for medical AI by consolidating many specialist models.

items.title: Integral DeltaNet: Improved Linear Attention with Adaptive Memory Integration
items.content: arXiv:2611.32063v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
items.author: Junsoo Oh, Jihun Yun, Junhyuck Kim, Hanbaek Lyu
items.summary: Integral DeltaNet improves linear attention for long-context language modeling by maintaining two complementary recurrent states, combining delta-rule updates with an integral-style adaptive memory integration to reduce memory collisions and avoid discarding information relevant to future predictions. It builds on DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet, which compress history into a fixed-size state. This contributes to the active architecture research direction of linear-time alternatives to softmax attention.
items.reasoning: Timely contribution to the competitive linear attention / subquadratic architecture space with a clear technical mechanism addressing known DeltaNet limitations. Novelty is architectural and incremental relative to the fast-moving DeltaNet family, hence not top-tier scoring.

At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.

items.title: Making Evaluation Explicit Is Not Enough: Supervising the Evaluation Process in Generative Reward Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.32161v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generative reward models (GRMs) make language-model evaluation more explicit by generating critiques, rubrics, or intermediate analyses before predicting a final preference. However, explicit evaluation does not necessarily imply a reliable evaluation process: under outcome-only supervision, a model may reach the correct final preference while producing weak or unsupported intermediate judgments, turning the evaluation into a post-hoc rationalization. We introduce STEP-GRM, a framework that directly supervises the intermediate evaluation process of rubric-based GRMs. In addition to conventional preference supervision, STEP-GRM provides structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments, encouraging the model to learn not only the correct final preference but also a more reliable process for reaching it. Extensive experiments show that STEP-GRM achieves strong performance on standard reward-modeling benchmarks while improving the consistency and correctness of intermediate evaluations. Moreover, reward signals produced by STEP-GRM lead to better downstream policy optimization, demonstrating that more reliable evaluation processes can translate into practical gains beyond reward-model accuracy.

items.reasoning: Directly targets a core reliability problem in reward models used for LLM alignment: unfaithful chain-of-evaluation under outcome-only training. The process-level supervision idea is significant for RLAIF and reward-model faithfulness, a high-leverage research direction, though results details are limited in the abstract.

items.title: DAiSy: Online Data Selection by Adaptive Utility Estimation for LLM Pretraining
items.content: arXiv:2611.32294v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Model-aware online data selection prioritizes the training documents that contribute the most given the model's current state. Existing online selectors rank candidates upon gradient-based data utility scores, which requires the full forward-backward pass of the main model on every candidate document. Scoring each document therefore pays as much as training on it, yet only a small fraction is used for the real model update. We introduce DAiSy, a lightweight linear auxiliary model that learns to predict data utility scores from frozen document embeddings, which eliminates the computation overhead and infrastructure burdens. The linear estimator is updated alongside the main language model, fitting to the exact gradient-based utility scores obtained from the backward pass of regular training steps. Consequently, scoring a candidate requires only a linear transformation, bypassing the costly gradient-alignment computation. We demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency for LLM pretraining in English and multilingual scenarios, with various steering target designs. The improvements from DAiSy can consistently survive the instruction-tuning phase.

The linear-surrogate idea is simple but well-placed; impact depends on empirical quality of the approximation, which the abstract suggests is solid.

items.title: MXFP4 for LLM Inference: Complementary Post-Training Quantization Techniques and Their Interactions
items.content: arXiv:2611.32873v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization. By sharing a scale factor across groups of 16 or 32 elements, these formats enable aggressive low-precision quantization with minimal accuracy degradation, particularly when combined with modern PTQ algorithms. Their accuracy depends on how the numerical format interacts with rotation, PTQ, and scale selection. We study the composability of PTQ configurations across six LLMs and three microscaling formats: MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4, systematically varying Hadamard rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale-selection strategy. Our central finding is that effective quantization recipes are format dependent: both MXFP4 and NVFP4 support accurate 4-bit inference, but techniques that benefit one do not necessarily transfer to the other. MXFP4 benefits substantially from rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation, consistent with its finer-grained scales capturing more within-block variation. Building on these findings, we introduce Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that mitigates clipping error in power-of-two block scales and improves accuracy across a majority of the evaluated MXFP4 configurations. We show that pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most of the accuracy lost at 4-bit and, on Llama-3.1-8B, matches or exceeds our in-house BF16 baseline. An additional study finds that augmenting MXFP4 with a per-tensor macroscale, a mechanism intrinsic to NVFP4, does not improve average accuracy, suggesting that global rescaling alone does not address the limitations of E8M0 block scales for MXFP4 quantization. Together, these results provide practical guidance for combining numerical formats, rotation, PTQ, and scale selection for accurate low-precision LLM inference.

This is directly relevant to efficient low-precision LLM deployment on emerging hardware.

items.title: How to build and train your recurrent-depth model: A fixed-point perspective
items.content: arXiv:2611.31513v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation, yet it remains unclear why this works. We show that input injection, commonly used in recurrent-depth models, is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth. The guarantees require a Lipschitz operator, which for SwiGLU leads to a weight constraint in both row and spectral norm, while only a row norm constraint for gates. Based on these constraints, we develop an optimizer tailored to each parameter group, Sparrow, which provides a drop-in replacement of Muon/MuonH with no overhead, that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.
items.author: Thomas Pethick
items.summary: The paper explains why truncated backpropagation works for recurrent-depth models by showing that input injection is exactly Halpern iteration, which provably converges with backpropagation windows polylogarithmic in depth under Lipschitz constraints. It derives norm constraints for SwiGLU and gated operators and introduces Sparrow, a drop-in Muon-style optimizer that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.
items.reasoning: Combines clean fixed-point theory with a practical new optimizer (Sparrow) claiming general training speedups. The theoretical grounding of truncated backprop for recurrent-depth models is a meaningful contribution to an architecture class gaining attention, though the work appears single-author and needs independent validation.

items.title: Meta-Amortized Cognitive Modeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.31914v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cognitive modeling is highly iterative. Researchers repeatedly revise model structures, parameterizations, covariates, and experimental designs as theories evolve and data accumulates. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks provides rapid estimation for individual models, but every revision requires new simulations and training. Here, we introduce CogFormerV2, a meta-amortized framework that enables researchers to specify, revise, and fit cognitive models with a single network, carrying amortization across an entire space of models all at once. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it delivers accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across more than 14.6 billion model configurations spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions, with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. It can fit empirical data from distinct behavioral tasks and extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer. Released as an open-source interactive application, CogFormerV2 provides a reusable infrastructure for meta-amortized inference in cognitive modeling, while carrying the potential to accelerate computational modeling workflows at large.
