items.title: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing
items.content: arXiv:2611.32617v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight ($\sim$67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

items.title: Simultaneously Boosting Efficiency and Capability for Linear Attention via Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification
items.content: arXiv:2611.32877v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Self-attention's quadratic complexity constitutes a core bottleneck for Vision Transformers (ViTs). Existing efficiency-oriented optimizations, including softmax-based and linear attention (LA) variants, generally compromise model representational capacity, leading to inevitable performance degradation. We propose a novel linear attention which alleviates this efficiency-capability dilemma. For the first time, we embed an Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification (ACCAP) mechanism into the QKV projection of linear attention, which enables the model to retain high-dimensional feature information while performing computations with reduced channels. We further fuse a focused kernel function and a self-gating module into ACCAP to construct a lightweight linear attention module (ACCAP-LA). Our theoretical analysis shows that, compared to standard linear attention, ACCAP-LA reduces the attention module's parameter count by 79.17% and FLOPs by 77.5%. Extensive experiments demonstrate ACCAP-LA's effectiveness: when applied to ViT, it achieves 79.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with only 5.8M parameters, and more notably, it boasts strong cross-architecture compatibility, boosting EfficientViT-b1 and PVT-T by 3.3% and 3.4% respectively.

items.title: PointX: Multi-View Consistent Intrinsics by Querying Surface Points
items.content: arXiv:2611.33157v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/
items.author: Miguel Farinha, Sam Sartor, Iliyan Georgiev, Giuseppe Vecchio, Ronald Clark, Michael Fischer
items.summary: PointX is a feed-forward multi-view transformer that predicts intrinsic scene properties (albedo, roughness, metallicity, normals, irradiance) per 3D surface point rather than per pixel, pooling a point's tokens across the views in which it appears. This yields a single, multi-view consistent decomposition per surface point, resolving ambiguity in per-pixel approaches.
items.reasoning: Reframing intrinsic decomposition as point-based querying across unposed images is a clean architectural contribution to inverse rendering, with practical relevance to 3D reconstruction pipelines. items.content_html: arXiv:2611.33157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/

items.title: CRAB-H: Task-Centric Certification for Healthcare Autonomous Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.31470v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper introduces CRAB H as a task-centric certification methodology for healthcare autonomous systems. CRAB H extends the ARC governance architecture by introducing the task as a first-class governance object, represented through Task Requirement Profiles TRP H. Each profile defines the cognitive capabilities, governance constraints, evidentiary requirements, and operational assumptions necessary for the safe execution of a specific healthcare activity. Rather than asking whether a robot achieves a sufficiently high benchmark score, CRAB H asks whether demonstrated capabilities satisfy the requirements of the task. Certification becomes a comparison between demonstrated capability and required capability. A reliability-gated assurance allocation mechanism routes cognitive dimensions that cannot be reproducibly evaluated to LEA operational requirements rather than discarding them. Governance integrity is preserved: unreliable dimensions are governed, not ignored. The Capability Margin is defined as the threshold-based conjunction of per-dimension compliance determinations, not as a subtracted scalar preserving non compensatory governance logic appropriate for safety-critical healthcare deployment

items.title: Exteroceptive Sensor Faults in Autonomous Vehicles: A Cross-Modal Taxonomy and Fault Injection Toolkit
items.content: arXiv:2611.31667v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autonomous vehicles rely on cameras, LiDAR, and radar to perceive their surroundings, yet these exteroceptive sensors can be degraded by hardware aging, environmental interference, miscalibration, embedded software errors, and combinations of these causes, with direct consequences for perception quality and safety. Existing surveys and benchmarks mostly address individual sensors, isolated conditions, or vehicle-level consequences, and no common vocabulary relates fault origins across the three modalities. This paper reviews the literature on exteroceptive sensor faults and proposes a cross-modal, origin-driven taxonomy that organizes them into five categories, namely hardware, environmental, calibration, software, and synergistic faults, mapping each entry to its physical or logical mechanism, observable manifestation, and affected subsystem, and relating the categories to the safety analyses of ISO 26262 and ISO 21448. To make the taxonomy operational, we release an open-source fault injection toolkit with 94 symptom-level routines (41 camera, 27 LiDAR, and 26 radar), four graded severity levels, reproducible burst scheduling, and per-frame labels recording the fault category, affected subsystem, and severity. Examples on the Boreas dataset illustrate how each category alters camera images, LiDAR point clouds, and radar scans. Together, the taxonomy and the toolkit provide a shared reference and a controlled testbed for studying sensor reliability, developing and benchmarking fault detection and diagnosis methods, and building fault-annotated datasets for the safety validation of perception systems. The toolkit is publicly available at https://github.com/davidepossenti/AV-SensorFault-Toolkit.

items.title: PreWAM: Exploring the Design of Latent Future Prediction for World-Action Modeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.31901v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.

This matters because world-action models tie action generation to visual future prediction, and the choice of prediction space directly affects policy learning quality for robotic manipulation.

items.title: Learning When a Robot Should Ask For Help: Adaptive Intervention Requests in Human-Robot Teaming
items.content: arXiv:2611.31925v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robots operating in complex environments occasionally encounter situations where autonomous navigation fails. Requesting and receiving a timely intervention from their human supervisor can be critical for failure prevention or recovery. However, requesting help too frequently or at inappropriate times can increase operator workload and reduce team efficiency, while delayed requests may lead to prolonged downtime or unrecoverable failures. In addition to alert timing, the human, robot and task context also influences the intervention outcomes. This paper proposes an algorithm for learning to generate adaptive human intervention requests during human-robot teaming. A help-seeking policy is trained via offline reinforcement learning based on past intervention helpfulness and autonomous progress. This learned alert policy enables a robot to selectively request human help when the intervention outcome is likely to be beneficial. We evaluate the proposed policy in different task environments and user expertise levels in simulation, followed by evaluation in a physical user study. Our findings demonstrate that the learned policy improves exploration efficiency, reduces unnecessary alerts, and enhances novice user support without compromising expert performance in real-time human-robot teaming missions.

items.summary: This paper trains a help-seeking policy via offline reinforcement learning so robots request human intervention at appropriate moments, balancing failure prevention against operator workload. The approach incorporates human, robot, and task context when deciding when to alert a supervisor.
items.reasoning: Addresses an underexplored and practically important problem in human-robot teaming with a principled offline RL formulation. Novelty is moderate since help-seeking via RL has precedent, but the context-aware framing and intervention-outcome analysis add value.

items.title: DeCoNav-Act: Benchmarking Collective Physical Capability in Multi-Robot Mobile Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32683v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot teams can split workloads or combine complementary bodies, but only if each robot leaves the shared world in a state its teammate can use. Existing multi-robot benchmarks emphasize task allocation and skill sequencing, rarely testing whether the resulting physical states are usable. To evaluate collective physical capability, we introduce DeCoNav-Act, a benchmark for language-guided multi-robot mobile manipulation in a shared physics simulation. Its 350 homogeneous and 150 heterogeneous tasks, each verified by joint reference execution, span two coordination mechanisms: parallel workloads in shared space and physical dependencies in which one robot establishes a condition for a teammate to use. Beyond team success, DeCoNav-Act measures path efficiency and handoff coverage and success, and adds a diagnostic from verified pre-handoff states. Evaluating sensor-grounded adaptations of ASPIRE and RAX and our agent CoMoMa, we find that with GPT-5.6-luna no method completes a task, at most 8.8% of dependencies are reached, and even from pre-handoff states no handoff is completed; with GPT-6.1-sol, CoMoMa establishes the condition in 26.5% of trials, but only 4.1% succeed.

items.title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.33144v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

items.title: Can forced refusals make models "snap out" of a jailbreak?
items.content:
TL;DR: Getting a single refusal into the context of a jailbroken model partially negates the jailbreak on Llama (compliance with harmful tasks falls from 93% to 58%) but not Qwen (52% to 51%) and this is not notably affected by the details of the refusal e.g. on policy or off policy. Telling the models the prior turns were forged works even better on Llama, but not Qwen.

## Why ask this

Many-shot jailbreaking (MSJ) attacks were first publicized in 2024 (Anil et al. 2024), and work by filling the context with fake turns where "the assistant" complies with requests that should trigger refusals. This typically results in the model continuing to comply with inappropriate requests.

Labs stopped publishing MSJ numbers separately from other pre-fill attacks but the latest report from a then frontier model, the Claude Opus 4 system card (May 2025), still showed ~25% compliance with harmful requests on one MSJ evaluation, "almost exactly the same" as Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Opus 3.

Several papers have published partial defenses, but all of them have practically significant limitations (Anil et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2026). In particular, all published defenses[1] only test what happens on the very next turn.

We wanted to know what happens after the model refuses: does it stay aligned, or  go back to being jailbroken?

## Setup

We used Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for the main results, we also piloted Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.3, but its baseline compliance rate was too high for us to reliably detect jailbreak effects. All runs were done using bf16, T = 1.0, max 1,024 new tokens....

items.summary: An empirical test of whether injecting a single refusal into the context of a many-shot-jailbroken model cancels the attack. Compliance with harmful tasks dropped from 93% to 58% on Llama but not on Qwen (52% to 51%), and telling the model prior turns were forged helped only Llama; refusal phrasing details did not matter. This probes a simple potential defense against a persistent jailbreak class that has remained at roughly 25% compliance even on frontier systems.
items.reasoning: Simple, well-designed experiments on an important attack class with a clear, practically relevant finding (strong model dependence, partial mitigation). Limitations are the two-model scope and unknown robustness to adaptive attacks, but it advances the sparse defenses literature for many-shot jailbreaking.

items.title: ExpGuard: Guarding Long-Horizon LLM Agents against Corrupted Experience
items.content: arXiv:2611.32085v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.

It models provenance and execution dependencies, learns task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and repairs risky experiences at inference time.
items.reasoning: Agent memory poisoning is an emerging and important threat surface, and the framework covers the full lifecycle from provenance modeling to online repair, which is more complete than detection-only work. The contribution is timely and relevant to agent security, though evaluation breadth in the abstract is not fully clear.

items.title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions
items.content: arXiv:2611.32776v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.
items.author: Hayeong Lee, Youngjun Suh. Byung-Jun Lee
items.summary: This paper proposes Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), an auxiliary objective for latent world models that identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal, rather than regressing actions with squared error as in standard inverse dynamics. The authors show theoretically that under exact behavior matching CIA can reward action information that leaves the optimal inverse-regression objective unchanged, and that targeting plausible in-context action alternatives preserves information supplied by the next latent beyond history. This sharpens what world model representations should encode for planning.
items.reasoning: A theoretically grounded improvement to a widely used technique (inverse dynamics auxiliary loss for world models), with a clear analysis of why squared-error regression under-trains action-relevant representations. The idea is elegant and likely broadly applicable to offline RL and model-based planning, though empirical scope in the abstract appears limited.

CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.

items.title: SD-Cache: Learnable Memory Consolidation with State-Guided Dynamic Caching
items.content: arXiv:2611.31265v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as persistent services that must reason over large volumes of external knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds model responses in relevant documents, but the retrieved content must still be encoded and stored in the key-value (KV) cache. As this content accumulates, the cache grows linearly, increasing memory consumption and inference cost. Existing memory-compression methods address this problem either by retaining a subset of cached states or by learning context compressors that map documents to compact latent representations. Despite these advances, consolidating information under tight memory budgets while preserving its usefulness for future queries remains challenging. We investigate how the model's native KV states can be selectively consolidated into a fixed-size working memory without access to future queries. To this end, we introduce SD-Cache (State-guided and Dynamically updated Cache), a query-agnostic KV-memory consolidation framework that operates alongside a frozen generator LLM. SD-Cache learns to consolidate layer-wise KV states into fixed-size memory through selective anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement, processing new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimisation. Experiments on retrieval-augmented question answering and synthetic long-context benchmarks show that SD-Cache maintains competitive downstream performance under constrained memory budgets.

items.title: NRG-Twins: Pixel-Level Ground Truth for Rigidity Violations in Generated Videos
items.content: arXiv:2611.32431v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.

items.summary: NRG-Twins creates per-pixel ground-truth labels of 3D-consistency violations in generated video by pairing real clips with keyframe-conditioned re-creations from a video generator, computing where and how much rigidity breaks. These labels can be used to train rewards or guidance that push video generators toward 3D consistency. This addresses a subtle, previously unlabeled failure mode of generated video used as 3D content.
items.reasoning: A creative data-generation trick that makes an otherwise unlabeled failure mode measurable at pixel level, relevant to the fast-moving video generation field. The real-generated twin construction is clever and reusable, though the pipeline depends on current generator quality and application is specialized.

items.title: Scaling Laws of Ensemble Uncertainty in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.32801v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Many use cases for large language models (LLMs)---from AI safety to exploration and human interaction---can benefit from epistemic uncertainty estimates. We argue that existing Bayesian Deep Learning solutions, which are often restricted to a fixed model family, fail to capture the full epistemic uncertainty at practical LLM scales. This is because the error due to the bounded capacity of the model family remains invisible to disagreement among models supported by the prior. We relate this error to the well-known power-law scaling of LLM loss with model size. We then show that a second power law quantifies the shrinking disagreement within ensembles as model size increases. Its slower decay relative to the capacity law above suggests that ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and become more competitive as an axis for scaling, compared to a single larger model. Finally, a third power law quantifies the loss of ensemble diversity as members share a larger fraction of training before branching, and therefore identifies a further limitation, beyond the capacity error, for LoRA ensembles and optimization-based or second-order methods that approximate uncertainty around a single training solution. At a high level, these findings suggest diverse ensembles can be a promising axis, both for scaling and uncertainty quantification at larger scales.

items.title: Transformers with Signatures: Towards Universal In-Context Learning in Path Space
items.content: arXiv:2611.31439v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general, and elusive in particular when target responses depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Building on the universal linear approximation property of signatures, we construct explicitly a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query.   Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.

items.title: Latent Merger: Latent-Space Composition of Hypernetwork-Generated LoRAs
items.content: arXiv:2611.33048v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.

items.title: Agentic Systems Need Multi-Run Evaluation: A Study of Retrieval and Response Variability in a Deployed Enterprise RAG System
items.content: arXiv:2611.31266v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Previous RAG systems have mostly been evaluated in a single-run setting, and with the advent of agentic RAG, systems are still often evaluated the same way. However, agentic RAG systems introduce a source of run-to-run variability, since several of their components make decisions non-deterministically. Such systems typically comprise a retrieval stage followed by a generation stage, and the retrieval stage in particular can behave differently across runs. For example, the agent might issue a different number of parallel searches from one run to the next, which alters the retrieved documents and therefore the final answer. In this paper we study this behavior in a deployed agentic RAG system for product-documentation questions, running each of 739 questions ten times and analyzing the execution traces to find where different runs first diverge. We find a substantial gap between success in any run and success in every run: the retrieval hit rate is 69.4% when the correct page is found in at least one run, but 50.9% when it must be found in all ten. Responses also stay similar in meaning while varying in wording, with an average BERTScore of 0.90 and a BLEU of 0.49. Trace-level analysis shows that retrieval is the largest source of divergence (43.9%), and the number of parallel searches at the first retrieval step alone accounts for 20.1% of divergent pairs. Taken together, these results show that single-run evaluation can hide reliability and consistency issues in agentic RAG systems, and that multi-run evaluation is necessary to reveal them.

items.summary: This study of a deployed agentic RAG system for product-documentation questions shows that run-to-run variability in non-deterministic components, particularly the retrieval stage, materially changes retrieved documents and final answers. The authors argue that single-run evaluation is inadequate for agentic systems and present multi-run analysis from a production deployment. The findings have direct implications for how agentic AI reliability should be measured in practice.

items.title: Dreamcatcher: Remembering What Surprises a World Model in Video Streams
items.content: arXiv:2611.31765v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As live video streams grow longer, repeatedly encoding and processing their full histories becomes increasingly costly. Answering questions as they arrive therefore calls for visual memory built in one pass before future questions are known. Existing methods mainly keep tokens that differ from earlier ones or match surrogate queries fixed in advance. Without modeling world dynamics, these criteria struggle to tell subtle surprising details from expected change. We introduce Dreamcatcher, a training-free framework and, to our knowledge, the first to use predictive signals from an independently pretrained, frozen video world model for online memory formation in streaming video question answering. Conditioned on recent history, the world model predicts incoming features using learned world priors. Its normalized prediction errors yield temporal and spatial surprisal signals that guide online segmentation and the retention of a frozen Video-LLM's native visual tokens, balancing surprising details with broad visual coverage under budgets that decay with segment age. At query time, an evidence gate admits a segment from a similarity-based shortlist only when the Video-LLM judges that it adds evidence for the question beyond the current view. We evaluate Dreamcatcher on three streaming and three offline long-video benchmarks. On OVO-Bench, Dreamcatcher achieves the highest overall accuracy among the compared training-free methods for each of four frozen Video-LLMs, reaching 78.9% with Qwen3.8-27B. With the three Qwen Video-LLMs, it also reduces average input tokens for answer generation by more than 80% relative to their base models at 1 fps.

items.summary: Dreamcatcher is a training-free framework for streaming video question answering that uses predictive signals from a frozen pretrained video world model to decide what to store in memory online. By modeling expected dynamics, it distinguishes genuinely surprising details from expected change, outperforming token-difference and fixed-query heuristics.

items.title: DraftKV: Protecting Persistent Worlds through Hierarchical Streaming Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2611.31944v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Interactive video world models enable action- and camera-controlled exploration, yet struggle to maintain consistent spatial geometry and appearance when revisiting previously explored locations. Historical KV caches help auto-regressive video diffusion models maintain long-term consistency, but their retrieval and attention computation introduce substantial latency as history grows. We propose DraftKV, a training-free framework that retrieves historical KV caches based on geometric grounding and query-conditioned relevance, while combining CPU offloading with tile-wise streaming attention to reduce GPU memory usage and inference latency. Theoretically, we show that draft relevance reproduces the mean branch of full-resolution block relevance exactly, so its deviation is confined to the $\beta$-weighted max branch, and we bound retrieval utility loss in terms of the measured Top-K selection overlap. We further show that draft relevance cannot distinguish blocks with similar pooled descriptors regardless of camera pose, motivating geometric grounding before refinement. Then, we introduce streaming CG-Attention, which overlaps CPU-to-GPU KV transfers with attention computation through tile-wise streaming, hiding transfer latency while maintaining bounded GPU memory usage. Experiments across diverse model families show that DraftKV achieves superior generation quality and consistency while achieving $3.27\times$ end-to-end speedup and 42.2% peak GPU memory reduction over other CPU-offloaded KV cache retrieval methods. Notably, DraftKV enables high-quality interactive world generation with historical KV retrieval on a single H100 GPU using SolarWM-33B.

items.title: Let The Pixels Through: Rethinking Long Skip Connections for Scalable Pixel Diffusion
items.content: arXiv:2611.32151v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training pixel diffusion models remains less straightforward, owing to the ad hoc training recipes and architecture designs, along with the sensitivity to hyper-parameter choices. We show that strong denoisers can be built by refining existing pixel-native designs from the literature. Specifically, we revisit the long skip connection in U-Net and find that the optimization benefit commonly attributed to it is not necessary for its denoising benefit. We further find that the conventional linear combination of features from the skip and main backbone is inadequate for regimes of various noise levels. Motivated by these observations, we introduce two core modifications. First, we adopt asymmetric long skips, which propagate fine-grained information from input embeddings to decoder layers. Second, we introduce adaGLU, a SwiGLU-like MLP block, in decoder layers to adaptively filter information from the embeddings before being added to main-branch features. The above designs give a simple pixel diffusion transformer architecture. When trained from scratch, it scales smoothly from small-scale baselines up to 1.6B parameters, achieving 1.62 and 1.70 FID on ImageNet-256 and -512, respectively. Besides, it natively supports multimodal inputs, such as text and images, yielding competitive performance in text-to-image generation. We release our codes at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/PiT
items.author: Jiachen Lei, Jiahong Wu, XiangXiang Chu
items.summary: The paper revisits long skip connections in U-Net-based pixel diffusion models, finding that their optimization benefit is separate from their denoising benefit and that linear skip-main feature combinations are inadequate across noise levels. It introduces asymmetric long skips and a nonlinear combination scheme that improve training stability and quality of pixel-native diffusion models. This helps make pixel diffusion more competitive with latent approaches.

We show that strong denoisers can be built by refining existing pixel-native designs from the literature. Specifically, we revisit the long skip connection in U-Net and find that the optimization benefit commonly attributed to it is not necessary for its denoising benefit. We further find that the conventional linear combination of features from the skip and main backbone is inadequate for regimes of various noise levels. Motivated by these observations, we introduce two core modifications. First, we adopt asymmetric long skips, which propagate fine-grained information from input embeddings to decoder layers. Second, we introduce adaGLU, a SwiGLU-like MLP block, in decoder layers to adaptively filter information from the embeddings before being added to main-branch features. The above designs give a simple pixel diffusion transformer architecture. When trained from scratch, it scales smoothly from small-scale baselines up to 1.6B parameters, achieving 1.62 and 1.70 FID on ImageNet-256 and -512, respectively. items.title: First-Hit Photoconsistency for Neural Surface Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.32998v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent neural implicit and Gaussian splatting approaches have achieved impressive results in multi-view surface reconstruction. However, jointly optimizing geometry and appearance introduces ambiguities. A parametric appearance model can compensate for geometric errors, reproducing the input images accurately without an accurate surface. We demonstrate accurate neural implicit surface reconstruction using only multi-view patch photoconsistency with geometry-based visibility, without volumetric rendering or parametric appearance models. For each reference ray, sphere tracing computes the first surface intersection. Its position and normal define a local patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across visible neighboring views using colors sampled directly from the input images. For efficient sphere tracing, we use a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron. We use a single photoconsistency loss, without foreground masks or auxiliary geometric regularization. Experiments show that our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BlendedMVS (BMVS) among compared methods and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU.

items.title: DynaMimic: A Physics-Informed World Model for Humanoid Motion Tracking
items.content: arXiv:2611.32944v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Whole-body motion tracking enables humanoid robots to reproduce diverse skills from human demonstrations. Existing model-free reinforcement learning methods either distill motion specialists into a single policy at the cost of performance or train a generalist policy directly using cluster-scale computation. SuperMimic reduces this computational cost through a differentiable world model that implicitly learns the physics shared across motions by predicting the next state from the current state and action. However, this implicit formulation may not fully capture the underlying physical processes. Errors around changes of support can accumulate over imagined rollouts used to train the tracking policy. To address this challenge, we introduce DynaMimic, a differentiable world model that explicitly incorporates shared physics into state prediction. Specifically, its network predicts a contact wrench at each candidate support link and a residual generalized force. DynaMimic then uses these predictions to compute the next state through closed-form Lagrangian forward dynamics. Across 60 full LAFAN1 motions, DynaMimic reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 18.6% relative to SuperMimic. For terrain tracking, we give both methods the same local height maps. Relative to terrain-conditioned SuperMimic, DynaMimic reduces MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour (66.15 to 56.28~mm) and by 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips (141.88 to 126.57~mm). On a real A3 humanoid, the learned policies can perform diverse skills, such as floor recovery, cartwheel and a box vault.

items.title: ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection
items.content: arXiv:2611.31424v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, agents can perform more complex tasks with tools and maintain longer interactions with users. These benign conversations contain evidence on task results, user concerns, and operational constraints. The risk is that attackers who can observe benign conversations (evidence) may construct stronger indirect prompt injections without increasing the attackers' control over prior turns or the later injection. However, we still lack a clear study of how effectively attackers can select and use this evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ContextLure, a red-teaming framework in which an attacker silently observes an existing benign conversation, extracts evidence, and constructs an injection. The challenges are twofold: (a) selecting useful evidence and (b) presenting it as reasons for an unauthorized action, without changing the prior benign conversation. To efficiently exploit (a) the effect of evidence on attack success, our framework selects evidence across 2 dimensions: User/System Preferences with 3 selection policies. And to enhance (b) the process of turning the selected information into the malicious request, we introduce an Urgency/Priority matrix with 4 rewriting strategies. Across the evaluated conditions, we reach 67.4% ASR on AgentDojo and 87.3% on InjecAgent. These results show that attackers can use benign interaction evidence in later attacks without first poisoning the benign conversation.

As an attack framework rather than a defense, its impact depends on whether mitigations emerge, but it should inform agent security design.

items.title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
items.content: arXiv:2611.31736v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs.   On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.

items.summary: The paper argues that LLM-generated simulation programs that faithfully reproduce historical data can still answer what-if questions incorrectly when policy changes are applied. The proposed Vouch library judges whether each individual answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the specific change requested, replacing whole-program pass/fail verdicts with intervention-level assurance. This is a novel reliability angle on agentic simulation workflows.

items.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
items.content: arXiv:2611.31833v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

items.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
items.content: arXiv:2611.31974v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.
items.author: Shifang Zhao, Haoyu Wang, Yuyang Yin, Dong Chen, Xingyilang Yin, Yunkang Tao, Honghao Chen, Guangzhi Wang, Yiran Wang, Junfu Pu, Cheng Cheng, Xiaodong Cun, Ying Shan

With a credible author list, the benchmark could become a useful reference point, though benchmark value depends on community uptake.

items.title: Economic World Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.32663v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Can artificial intelligence reproduce the economic dynamics that emerge as households, firms and governments interact and adapt through markets and institutions? To answer this question, we define an economic world model (EWM) as an agent's internal representation of how an economic system works, enabling counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. We then propose a general framework for studying EWMs that links three tasks: simulating agent behaviour, learning economic transitions and systematically evaluating the dynamics. As an initial implementation, we learn household policies from microeconomic data and calibrate a structural economic transition model using macroeconomic data, linking individual decisions to aggregate dynamics. Our micro-to-macro evaluation framework compares simulated individual actions and group distributions with observed microdata and assesses macroeconomic dynamics through forecasting and counterfactual experiments. Results show that simulated and observed household consumption distributions overlap by 94.9%, while EWM forecasts closely track real GDP and several other aggregate levels. In government-borrowing counterfactuals, the EWM reproduces the benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission from borrowing to consumption. For ex ante planning, the EWM enables an LLM agent to achieve 10.29% higher simulated GDP under the epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions. This initial EWM is only a starting point. We invite economists and AI researchers to build a stronger EWM together. Economists can contribute richer economic models and knowledge, while AI researchers can develop stronger data-driven methods for simulating agent behaviour and learning economic transitions. Together, we aim not only to reproduce real economic dynamics, but also to discover and test new mechanisms that support better decisions and benefit society.

items.title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.33012v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As clinical AI agents begin to interact with electronic health records (EHRs), large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate their actions. But how reliably can these judges recognize clinically dangerous mistakes, especially when an agent appears to have completed its task successfully? We investigate this question using MedAgentBench by introducing controlled clinical errors into verified agent trajectories. The experiments include 416 faulty trajectories, eight error categories, and six open-weight LLM judges. By comparing each faulty trajectory with its correct counterpart, we measure whether judges genuinely recognize errors rather than simply flagging more actions as unsafe. The findings show that access to clinical evidence significantly improves judge reliability. When shown only the final answer, judges cannot distinguish errors that leave it unchanged, while flagging 56% of correct trajectories. With full trajectory information, the ability to distinguish unsafe actions from correct ones reaches a score of 0.75, and providing actual EHR responses improves discrimination by 0.39. Surprisingly, including the agent's reasoning does not improve overall performance and reduces detection of incorrectly reported clinical values by 0.18, which remain the hardest errors to detect. MedGemma performed worse than the general-purpose model and was the only judge to miss potentially dangerous medication overdoses. We also find that the benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with an intentionally skipped laboratory check, while combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults.

By comparing each faulty trajectory with its correct counterpart, the design separates true error detection from over-flagging. Findings indicate access to clinical evidence shapes judge reliability, with implications for using LLM judges in medical agent safety pipelines.
items.reasoning: A well-designed controlled study on an important safety question — whether LLM judges can detect clinically dangerous agent errors — with a clean paired fault-injection methodology. Single benchmark (MedAgentBench) and open-weight-only judge pool limit scope, but the safety implications for clinical AI are significant.

MedGemma performed worse than the general-purpose model and was the only judge to miss potentially dangerous medication overdoses. We also find that the benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with an intentionally skipped laboratory check, while combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults.

items.title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
items.content: arXiv:2611.29120v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). The transforms, audits and raw records are available from the authors.

items.title: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication
items.content: arXiv:2611.31801v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.

items.title: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion
items.content: arXiv:2611.31962v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.

items.title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes
items.content: arXiv:2611.32032v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement.   Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.

The core insight that LLM consensus is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure is a valuable safety principle.

items.title: RetraQ: Manifold-Constrained Critic Guidance for Flow Policies in RL
items.content: arXiv:2611.32148v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A learned critic can improve a pretrained flow-matching policy by steering sampled actions toward higher predicted value. However, even a critic that fits the behavior data well can provide misleading action gradients. Gradient components pointing away from the data-supported region are weakly constrained by behavior data and can lead guidance to exploit critic extrapolation errors. We introduce RetraQ (Retraction-based Q-guidance), which uses geometry encoded by the pretrained flow to constrain both the direction and the destination of critic guidance. A single velocity evaluation of the frozen flow defines a denoising map. RetraQ filters the critic gradient with the map's Jacobian and applies the map itself to correct the updated action. Our analysis characterizes when these operations approximate tangent filtering and retraction onto the behavior manifold. The same update guides actions at test time and provides targets for policy distillation and online reinforcement learning. In controlled studies, RetraQ improves true return while keeping refined actions close to the data-supported region, and its distillation targets remain more stable than those of raw critic ascent. In offline-to-online training on LIBERO and OGBench, RetraQ achieves higher mean final success than the evaluated critic-guidance baselines. On a real-world plug-insertion task, test-time RetraQ improves the success rate of a behavior-cloned $\pi_{0.5}$ policy from 55.0% to 76.7%. Online training further increases success to 98.3% in only 30 minutes and 100% within one hour. Project page: https://2027ICLR.github.io/retraq/

items.reasoning: A principled geometric solution to a real failure mode in RL fine-tuning of flow policies, relevant to the active area of post-training robotic and diffusion policies. The theoretical grounding and efficiency (one velocity evaluation) are strengths; empirical breadth is not yet clear from the abstract.

items.title: DiCT: Teaching X-ray Vision-Language Models to Reason via Imagining CT
items.content: arXiv:2611.32344v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Diagnosing with X-rays often requires reasoning about the 3D locations of abnormalities and their spatial relationships to surrounding anatomical structures, yet such reasoning remains challenging due to the loss of spatial information in 2D projections. To address this challenge, we propose Dreaming in CT (DiCT), a three-stage progressive CT-to-X-ray reasoning transfer framework that leverages a CT vision-language model (VLM) to guide an X-ray VLM. Through this CT-guided transfer, the student acquires CT-informed 3D reasoning capabilities, enabling it to reason directly from 2D X-rays without explicit CT reconstruction at inference time. The framework begins with instruct the dreamer, which equips the X-ray student with initial CT-oriented reasoning capabilities and establishes a structured interface that distinguishes X-ray observations from CT imagination. Building on this structure, visualize the dream introduces CT-guided on-policy distillation (OPD), where the CT teacher selectively guides the X-ray student's reasoning trajectories to transfer 3D anatomical knowledge. Finally, manifest the dream adapts the acquired reasoning capabilities from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to real clinical X-rays. Experiments across two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA demonstrate DiCT's effectiveness across radiological reasoning tasks, achieving a 1.66 percentage point improvement over a CT reconstruction-based baseline on 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification with 12.77$\times$ lower inference computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongYep/DiCT.

This targets a real clinical limitation where 2D projections lose spatial information needed for diagnosis.

items.title: REBEAL: Human References Are No Longer the Best Translation, and Metrics Do Not Notice
items.content: arXiv:2611.32623v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reference-based MT evaluation assumes the human reference is correct and better than the systems it scores. Both assumptions now fail, since the human reference ranks first in none of the 2024 WMT MQM campaigns and carries annotated errors in 19% to 87% of its segments. What a metric does with a flawed reference is a question about the metric, and it would have been worth asking before reference quality came into doubt. We introduce REBEAL (Reference Bias EvALuation), a benchmark that probes how MT metrics respond to seven types of controlled reference contamination, drawn from the error categories those campaigns record. Across eight widely used metrics and three language pairs, recent learned metrics (xCOMET, MetricX) prove more robust than their predecessors, but each family fails in its own way. Surface metrics show no length sensitivity, so contamination hides in longer segments, while learned metrics accept references in unrelated languages as nearly correct. The failure they share is named-entity contamination, which no metric detects and which flips up to 8 of 36 system pairs when ranking nine MT systems.

items.title: Sample-Efficient In-Context Adaptation via Sleep
items.content: arXiv:2611.32802v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The ability to learn and generalize from limited experience, or sample efficiency, is a cornerstone of intelligence. How can we build language models that turn a few user interactions, a few snippets of unfamiliar code, or a handful of experimental results provided in context into knowledge that generalizes? Prior work has found that sleep, a process where the model performs $N$ recurrent forward passes to refine its representations of a chunk of context, can improve long-context reasoning (specifically, within SSM-attention hybrid models). We study whether this method also improves in-context adaptation on general, non-synthetic tasks for transformer language models. To this end, we pre-train language models up to 1.2B-parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Notably, longer sleep (i.e., using a larger number of recurrent forward passes $N$) enables the model to learn faster in-context on multiple few-shot algorithmic, question-answering tasks, while also achieving lower next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with $N=2$ and $N=4$ match the no-sleep baseline's loss using $2.10\times$ and $2.39\times$ fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.

The authors pretrain language models up to 1.2B parameters and up to 100B tokens to test sample efficiency from limited in-context experience.
items.reasoning: An intriguing inference-time mechanism with biologically inspired framing, evaluated at reasonable pretraining scale (1.2B) and on general tasks rather than synthetic ones. The Microsoft-affiliated author list adds credibility; significance depends on how broadly the adaptation gains hold, which the abstract only partially establishes.

items.title: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
items.content: arXiv:2611.32851v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.

items.title: CaLA: Causal Latent Adjustment for World Models under Adaptive Policies
items.content: arXiv:2611.31431v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World models is answering ``imagine" answers to ``what-if'' questions via imagined rollouts. But rollouts collected by adaptive policies induce treatment-outcome confounding in imagined rollouts. We study this problem in Match-3 difficulty adjustment, where latent player skill influences both assigned difficulty and churn. We build a fully specified Match-3 SCM with sequential mechanics, adaptive assignment, and paired ground-truth interventions, on which unadjusted models fit to the logged trajectories select difficulty settings that raise churn. We then introduce Causal Latent Adjustment (CaLA), a DAG-constrained world model that infers a variational player representation from pretreatment history. Across our evaluations, CaLA provides the most reliable population-level intervention estimates and competitive individualized decisions, although rich handcrafted histories can remain advantageous for individual-level adjustment. We further find that residual correction can degrade causal decision quality despite improving predictive fit, highlighting the need to distinguish predictive accuracy, confounding adjustment and the behavior of downstream causal estimators.

It proposes CaLA, a DAG-constrained world model with a variational player representation inferred from pretreatment history, which avoids selecting settings that inadvertently raise churn.

items.title: ReJEPA: Bounded Predictive Regulation for Latent World Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.31910v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Latent world models learn representations by predicting future states in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels. When training across multi-frame sequences, however, not all frames and spatial regions are equally informative or predictable. We argue that forcing a world model to minimize every prediction error may be unnecessary and harmful. Under standard $L_2$ loss, unbounded gradients force the encoder and predictor to overfit noisy or transient frames at the expense of core physical structure, while amplifying gradient conflict with representation regularizers. Conversely, $L_1$ loss bounds large gradients, but its constant gradient magnitude near zero disrupts the local smoothness required for planning. We resolve this tension with \textbf{ReJEPA}, a bounded predictive regulation principle that combines bounded gradients for large errors with smooth quadratic behavior near zero, instantiated simply via the element-wise $\log\cosh$ loss.   As a drop-in training replacement across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA~2.1, $\log\cosh$ consistently outperforms $L_2$, a curvature-matched quadratic control, $L_1$, and Smooth-$L_1$ baselines without altering architectures or inference procedures. Notably, the gains grow with environmental complexity, scaling from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world autonomous driving on NAVSIM. Probing and geometric analyses confirm that relaxing the penalty on extreme errors yields representations that better capture physical states and align with the true planning cost landscape.

items.title: Contrastive Proxy Forests: Completeness-Preserving Proxy Learning from Multimodal Records
items.content: arXiv:2611.32708v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Proximal causal inference removes unmeasured confounding using two proxies of the confounder, an outcome-side W and a treatment-side Z. The proxies must satisfy exclusion restrictions and be complete, meaning that they reflect every aspect of the confounder. In practice, they are a few variables hand-picked from a structured table, even though clinical notes and physiological waveforms carry rich information about the confounder. Such records are too high-dimensional for a proximal estimator, and generic compression such as PCA may keep modality-specific variation (style) instead of the confounder, destroying completeness. Our key observation is that, under the proximal condition, the confounder is the only link between a treatment-side and an outcome-side modality beyond the covariates. Learning what they share therefore captures the confounder and filters out modality-specific style. Contrastive Proxy Forests (CPF) learns both proxies by contrasting the two modalities, given the covariates, on a separate unlabeled sample, and passes them to a proximal causal forest. This contrastive objective has an exact closed-form solution, ridge canonical correlation analysis. We prove that CPF preserves the exclusion restrictions exactly and that its proxies inherit the completeness of the raw records under conditions we characterize. Where style is strong, CPF lowers the error of conditional effects by 10-22% relative to PCA proxies, and on MIMIC-IV it is the only method whose point estimate of warfarin's effect on stroke falls inside the range of randomized trials.

items.summary: This work learns proxies for proximal causal inference from high-dimensional multimodal data such as clinical notes and physiological waveforms, preserving the completeness condition that hand-picked table variables often violate. The key insight is that under the proximal condition the confounder is the only link between treatment-side and outcome-side views, enabling contrastive extraction of confounder-relevant information.
