items.content_html: arXiv:2611.32407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.

items.title: HS-OVSeg: Multi-Granularity Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation in Remote Sensing via Heterogeneous Supervision
items.content: arXiv:2611.32518v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) enables flexible, text-driven mapping of remote sensing (RS) imagery beyond predefined categories. Despite advances in segmentation foundation models, RS-OVSS remains constrained by the scarcity of large-scale, semantically diverse datasets with accurate pixel-level annotations. Meanwhile, existing RS datasets contain abundant scene- and object-level annotations that offer valuable semantic information but lack precise pixel-wise supervision. To exploit these complementary sources, we propose HS-OVSeg, a unified training framework that integrates heterogeneous scene-, object-, and pixel-level supervision for RS-OVSS. Specifically, we generate pixel-wise pseudo-labels using SAM3, conditioned on scene-level class names and object-level class names with bounding boxes. Combined with ground-truth semantic masks, these pseudo-labels enable joint training across all three annotation granularities through LoRA-based fine-tuning of SAM3. Our unified training spans 20 RS datasets, including 3 scene classification, 4 object detection, and 13 semantic segmentation datasets, with 1,000 images from the 7 classification and detection datasets manually annotated for pixel-level evaluation. HS-OVSeg substantially outperforms existing RS-OVSS models across both the 20 training-source and 5 held-out datasets, demonstrating strong multi-granularity segmentation capabilities under heterogeneous supervision. The code will be publicly available upon publication.

items.title: ShapeQuest: Towards Granularity-Controlled Edit-Conditioned 3D Asset Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2611.32621v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Given a reference asset and an instruction such as "remove one armrest," a retriever must find variants that make the edit and preserve the other parts. This search is well established for images but remains underexplored for individual 3D assets. To study this problem, we introduce ShapeQuest and ShapeQuester, a new benchmark and model for edit-conditioned 3D asset retrieval. ShapeQuest's open-source pipeline edits textured meshes through part additions, removals, and material and colour changes. It controls edit granularity across five levels, defined by the fraction of the object's surface area each edit affects. It constructs multiple valid targets when an instruction leaves the choice of part open. A vision-language model judges each edit from views chosen to expose the edited parts, and human raters audit its judgments. ShapeQuest has 87,824 queries in 50 categories and a 50,919-shape gallery with competing edits. To distinguish these variants, ShapeQuester learns retrieval alongside reconstruction of the edited point cloud, with part masks supervising changed and preserved regions. With a frozen pretrained point encoder, ShapeQuester reaches 50.4 operation-macro mAP@10 on the test split, against 47.2 for the fusion baseline with the same inputs and 48.6 for the strongest baseline. Reconstruction adds 6.5 points on the validation split when the point encoder is trained from scratch, including 3.3 from part masks.
items.author: Faris Abu-Ali, Sankalp Sinha, Didier Stricker, Muhammad Zeshan Afzal
items.summary: The authors introduce ShapeQuest, a benchmark and pipeline for edit-conditioned retrieval of 3D assets: given a reference mesh and an instruction such as removing an armrest, find variants that apply exactly the edit. The benchmark controls edit granularity across five surface-area levels and uses a VLM judge to validate edits, with ShapeQuerster as the accompanying model.
items.reasoning: A genuinely novel problem formulation extending compositional image retrieval to textured 3D assets, with a thoughtfully designed open-source benchmark including granularity control and multiple valid targets. However, the task is niche and adoption will depend on community uptake of the benchmark.

items.title: SAVERA: Bridging Frozen Vision and Language Models via Sparse Alignment and Visual Evidence Reuse
items.content: arXiv:2611.32828v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Independently pretrained vision and language models may learn shared structures of the same underlying world, providing a foundation for combining them to build multimodal capabilities. However, a key challenge remains in aligning cross-modal feature representations while preserving access to visual information before and after language adaptation. To this end, we propose sparse alignment with visual evidence-guided residual adaptation (SAVERA), a framework that combines frozen vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space and prompt-guided residual fusion. Specifically, we first present shared-space projection, activation reconstruction and encoding (SPARE), which represents original visual, adapted visual, and textual features through shared soft-gated sparse encoding, with branch-specific reconstruction to preserve their respective information. Second, we devise bridge--text embedding and activation matching (BEAM), a bidirectional cross-modal alignment module that aligns adapted visual and textual features at both the sample and neuron levels, establishing fine-grained cross-modal correspondence. Finally, we introduce prompt-conditioned residual integration of vision and adapted features (PRIVA), a prompt-guided residual fusion module that models vision--language interactions through gating and attention and integrates complementary information from original and adapted representations through residual fusion. Extensive experiments show that SAVERA achieves competitive performance on image captioning and visual question answering while reducing object hallucination.
items.author: Jiajun Shen, Chuancheng Shi, Jiayi Lyu, Yanpeng Sun, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
items.summary: SAVERA connects independently pretrained vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space plus prompt-guided residual fusion, preserving access to original visual evidence before and after language adaptation. Its SPARE component represents original and adapted visual information for evidence reuse during multimodal fusion.
items.reasoning: The goal of aligning frozen unimodal models without erasing visual evidence is worthwhile, and the sparse shared-space design is plausible for parameter-efficient multimodal construction. However, the approach assembles several known techniques (sparse projection, residual adaptation, prompt fusion) and the abstract does not indicate a decisive advance or large-scale validation.

items.title: NEST: Uncovering and Nesting Unknown Objects in Open-World Object Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.32981v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Open-world object detectors aim to localize objects of classes not covered by their training annotations, but most label them only as "unknown". This label tells a system that an object is present but not what it is, while its broader category would allow a more informed decision. We therefore address both uncovering unknown objects and assigning them to the broader categories of a given class taxonomy. For uncovering, we find that most unknown objects are already localized and labeled "unknown" in our base detector, but are discarded during final top-k selection because background receives higher scores. To mitigate this, we propose a class-agnostic ranker that estimates how well each predicted box fits an object and uses these scores to select the final predictions. Across three benchmarks, our detector improves unknown recall by 3.8% to 195.1% relative to the strongest baseline in each task, while maintaining competitive known-class detection. For categorizing, we draw on Euler diagrams, in which the region of a category contains the regions of its members. Our categorizer builds each category's region from the known classes and learns how much room to leave for members it has never seen. On the same detections, it categorizes unknown objects more accurately than existing hierarchical methods. Code is available at https://github.com/TUM-AVS/NEST.
items.author: Yuchen Zhang, Yuan Gao, Sebastian Schmidt, Johannes Betz
items.summary: Addresses open-world detection beyond the generic unknown label by assigning uncovered objects to broader categories of a given taxonomy, with a class-agnostic ranker that scores how object-like each predicted box is to prevent discarding unknowns during top-k selection. Combines uncovering with taxonomy nesting for more informed downstream decisions.
items.reasoning: A useful refinement of open-world detection moving from unknown labeling to coarse taxonomy assignment, with a clear diagnostic insight about score-based discarding; novelty and broader impact appear moderate.

items.title: ROVO: Robust Rotation-Only Visual Odometry for UAVs at Low and Moderate Altitudes
items.content: arXiv:2611.32475v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Image noise can confound rotation and translation estimates in monocular visual navigation for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at low and moderate altitudes, where even small perturbations may cause large errors in translation direction. Inspired by angular cues in long-range visual perception, we propose rotation-only visual odometry (ROVO) for monocular aerial imagery. ROVO estimates pairwise rotations from matched images, robustly averages them over overlapping windows, and aligns consecutive windows through shared frames. By retaining only orientation in the trajectory state, it prevents uncertain landmark depth from propagating to later estimates. In trajectory simulation, sliding-window ROVO achieved a mean orientation error just 10.7% as large as that of the conventional SLAM baseline. On real flight data, ROVO achieved rotation accuracy comparable to ORB-SLAM3 and DPVO under the original Bell412 settings. With a narrower FoV or at higher flight altitude, ROVO reduced relative rotation RMSE by 19.7--69.4% compared with the next-best method in each comparison. Code and simulation tools are available at https://github.com/sssxxxkkkk/ROVO.

Simulation shows orientation error reduced to roughly a tenth of comparable approaches.
items.reasoning: The rotation-only formulation is a clever way to avoid error propagation from landmark depth at low altitudes, with clear quantitative gains. Still, evaluation appears simulation-heavy and the scope is a focused perception component rather than a broad advance.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2611.33086v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.

Demonstrated on cyber threat intelligence, it argues brittle ER systems fail unpredictably when upstream ambiguity is discarded. The design points toward more robust NLP pipelines for adversarial, high-stakes text.

Pipeline-level uncertainty management is a valuable direction, yet demonstrated impact and generalization remain limited at this stage.

items.title: Faithful Persona Steering under Incongruity via Dual-Stream Refinement
items.content: arXiv:2611.31848v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Standard LLM personalization typically frames identity as a static retrieval task, overlooking the inherent incongruity of human personas, where stable traits coexist with atypical, context-specific stances. Existing methods struggle to reconcile these dimensions: prompting succumbs to context drift over long sequences, while fine-tuning often suppresses idiosyncratic "quirks" in favor of generic distributional patterns. To bridge this gap, we present QuirkyMind, a framework that disentangles identity definition from its expression. First, Traits Anchoring constructs a dual-stream latent state, fusing a sentence-level summary for semantic stability with a token-level sequence for generative control. This state is stabilized via In-Context Narrative Refinement using an alternating objective: a discriminative InfoNCE loss anchors the persona in representation space to prevent drift, while a generative cross-entropy loss ensures faithful verbalization. Finally, Persona Steered Generalization transfers the refined state to downstream tasks via parameter-efficient adapters. Empirical evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference demonstrate that QuirkyMind mitigates drift, consolidating persona knowledge without erasing authentic incongruities.

It constructs a dual-stream latent state fusing sentence-level semantic stability with token-level generative control, stabilized via in-context anchoring, addressing context drift in prompting and quirk-suppression in fine-tuning.

However, personalization is a competitive area with many concurrent approaches and the long-term generalization of the method is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Who gets the information? An $\alpha$-fair label-coverage framework for multi-label feature selection
items.content: arXiv:2611.32200v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent information-theoretic filters for multi-label feature selection disagree on how to distribute relevance over labels: some amplify features that inform a few labels, others balance what every label receives. We show these choices are implicit social welfare functions. Treating labels as agents whose utility is the information they receive, we propose FLIC, which greedily maximises the $\alpha$-fair welfare of per-label information coverage. A single parameter $\alpha$ moves from utilitarian ($\alpha=0$) through proportionally fair ($\alpha=1$) to max-min selection ($\alpha\to\infty$), and a dozen published relevance terms lie on this axis, most as special cases, first-order approximations or limits. The objective is monotone submodular for every $\alpha\ge0$ whenever each label's information is, so greedy selection is a $(1-1/e)$-approximation; this fails for $\alpha<0$, and the max-min limit is inapproximable. Fano's and the Hellman-Raviv inequalities tie raw coverage to the Bayes Hamming loss and normalised coverage to per-label relative error. FLIC uses bias-corrected, label-wise conditional information and has no relevance-redundancy trade-off parameter. On 22 data sets, FLIC is the best of 14 information-theoretic filters on seven of nine metrics, winning 86 of 117 pairwise comparisons significantly and losing none significantly. Among 17 methods it ranks first on ranking loss, coverage and macro-AUC with two classifiers and has the best mean rank (narrowly with ML-kNN), while three embedded methods lead on Hamming loss, one-error and micro-F1.

items.summary: FLIC reframes multi-label feature selection as an alpha-fair social welfare problem, treating labels as agents and greedily maximizing the alpha-fair welfare of per-label information coverage; a single alpha parameter interpolates between utilitarian, proportionally fair, and max-min selection, subsuming many published relevance terms as special cases. The objective is monotone submodular, enabling efficient optimization.
items.reasoning: Elegant theoretical unification connecting feature selection to fairness/welfare economics with provable submodularity, but the problem area is mature and the practical gain over existing filters is likely modest. Good methodological craft, niche impact.

items.title: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32474v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation (B$^2$-UniDA) aims to adapt a target model to an unlabeled target domain under arbitrary label-space relationships, while neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible during adaptation. Under such restrictive information access, reliable target supervision is unavailable, while predictions from the black-box source model can be unreliable due to source bias and domain shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Progressive Reliable Supervision (PReS), which progressively establishes and refines reliable target supervision by coordinating complementary knowledge from the black-box source model, foundation models, and the evolving target model. PReS first identifies reliable known samples by exploiting semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and cross-model consensus between the black-box source model and CLIP. It then estimates the sample-wise reliability of the two predictors and adaptively integrates their complementary predictions to construct reliable pseudo labels. The resulting supervision is exploited asymmetrically to encourage confident and discriminative predictions for reliable known samples while maintaining uncertain yet locally consistent predictions for potential unknown samples. As adaptation proceeds, the emerging target-domain knowledge is further leveraged to refine both the pseudo labels and the known/unknown sample partition, forming a closed-loop process in which supervision construction and target adaptation mutually reinforce each other. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under diverse label-space relationships demonstrate that PReS achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance under the restrictive B$^2$-UniDA setting.
items.author: Jing Li, Zhe Zhang, Huateng Sun, Yuhui Yang, Wanli Xue, Xu Cheng, Fan Shi, Jianhua Zhang, Qinghua Hu, Shengyong Chen
items.summary: PReS progressively establishes reliable target supervision for black-box universal domain adaptation, where neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible and label-space relationships are arbitrary. It coordinates knowledge from the black-box source model, foundation models, and the evolving target model to identify reliable known samples and handle unknown classes. This addresses an increasingly realistic restrictive setting for adaptation.
items.reasoning: Tackles a genuinely hard and practically relevant setting, and leveraging foundation models alongside black-box source predictions is a sensible modern twist. However, domain adaptation is a mature field and the contribution reads as a competent combination of existing components rather than a conceptual breakthrough.

items.title: One, No One and One Hundred Thousand CTs: Testing Anatomical Control in Text-to-CT Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.33003v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent advances in deep learning and the public availability of computed tomography (CT) datasets with paired reports have enabled many Text-to-CT generators. However, their evaluations almost always differ in preprocessing and metrics, which hinders comparison. Moreover, their protocols almost never test how editing the report changes the CT, not even at the same seed, so the report is often assumed to control the anatomy without evidence of how much and how consistently it does. We therefore propose CtrlCT, a toolkit that tests two properties of a generator, Credibility and Control. Credibility tests compare generated CTs, as a population, with real CTs and reports; Control tests are metamorphic and need no reference CT: at a fixed seed, editing one finding should change it as requested, keep negated findings absent and shift distant anatomy no more than a new seed, and the change should hold across seeds. A Report Card summarises all measures and insights for each generator. We benchmark five public generators on 940 chest CTs and 687 edits of pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, holding out a sixth to test the toolkit. Among them, the most credible generators barely respond to an added effusion, while the most responsive produce less realistic and less diverse CTs. The analyses proposed in the literature do not reveal this. We release CtrlCT, its edits, seeds and 30,525 synthetic CTs after acceptance.
items.author: Francesca Pia Panaccione, Eugenio Lomurno, Matteo Matteucci
items.summary: CtrlCT is a toolkit that standardizes evaluation of text-to-CT generative models along two axes: Credibility (population-level comparison with real scans) and Control (metamorphic tests checking whether editing the report changes anatomy at a fixed seed). It highlights that existing evaluations rarely test whether reports actually control anatomy. This improves rigor in medical image generation evaluation.
items.reasoning: A useful methodological contribution addressing real evaluation gaps in medical generative models, with an elegant metamorphic testing design. However, it is an evaluation toolkit for a relatively specialized subfield.

items.title: Predict Backbone, Graft Dynamics: A Decoupled Paradigm for Time Series Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2611.31970v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Modern long-term forecasters are typically optimized for point-wise accuracy, which rewards dominant low-frequency backbones but often suppresses high-utility local dynamics such as abrupt variations, transient surges, and turning points. We propose Predict Backbone, Graft Dynamics, a decoupled forecasting paradigm that separates stable structural prediction from grounded dynamic restoration. We instantiate it as GRAFT, where a base forecaster predicts the reliable trajectory backbone, and a dedicated grafting path restores historically recurrent dynamics through retrieval-based evidence, phase-aware release, channel-wise control, and restoration-cooperative optimization. Unlike generic post-hoc revision methods that correct residual errors, GRAFT formulates the second stage as grounded dynamic grafting, where historical response evidence is calibrated into transferable dynamics and selectively grafted onto the backbone under phase-, channel-, and confidence-aware constraints. Across the full evaluation grid of seven benchmarks, two metrics, four horizons, and six backbones, GRAFT improves over the corresponding backbone in 87% of all comparisons, with average MSE/MAE reductions of 4.6%/3.9%. Dynamic-window analyses show that GRAFT restores local dynamics while preserving the stable backbone structure. These results suggest a new principle for high-utility forecasting: predict the backbone, then graft the dynamics.

Unlike post-hoc residual correction, it targets abrupt variations, surges, and turning points directly.
items.reasoning: The decoupled backbone-plus-dynamics design is a sensible idea for improving forecasting of high-utility events that point-wise losses suppress, but retrieval-augmented forecasting components are well-trodden and novelty is moderate.

items.title: Beyond Robust Algorithmic Recourse: Sharing the Burden of Validity through Model Multiplicity
items.content: arXiv:2611.32543v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Algorithmic recourse provides actionable recommendations that enable individuals to achieve favourable outcomes. Implementing recourse for individuals requires significant time and effort, thus emphasizing robust recourse: recommendations that remain valid even under future model updates. While robustness preserves validity, we show it introduces systematic harms by constraining feasible recommendations to regions that disproportionately reflect majority behavior, reducing individual flexibility and amplifying disparities. Thus, non-robust recourse risks invalidation, whereas robust recourse creates a preference for high-density regions in the data that induces unfairness. However, this trade-off is driven by an implicit assumption that individuals alone should bear the burden of validity. We challenge this narrative and show that strategic model selection can help maintain validity while relaxing robustness requirements for individuals. By leveraging multiplicity, the existence of equally good yet competing models, system owners can share this burden with individuals, thus resolving the tension between validity and unfairness.
items.author: Prakhar Ganesh, Afaf Ta\"ik, Golnoosh Farnadi
items.summary: The paper shows that robust algorithmic recourse, while keeping recommendations valid under model updates, systematically harms individuals by constraining recommendations to majority-density regions, reducing flexibility and amplifying disparities. It proposes sharing the validity burden through model multiplicity so that individual recommendations need not each be robust in isolation.
items.reasoning: A substantive fairness critique of a growing recourse literature with a constructive alternative mechanism; conceptually strong work in trustworthy ML, though recourse methods have limited industrial deployment so far.

items.title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
items.content: arXiv:2611.31613v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias. We investigate decision models (System One architectures) for silicon sampling. Using choice training, we update KEV model weights on historical respondent-level choice microdata by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without target-study data. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies from new domains (vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights, and AI) and new response formats. A small choice-trained model outperforms a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies. Although training on single studies lowers cross-entropy, it can exacerbate treatment-effect error. Choice training thus complements post-inference calibration by providing a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences.
items.author: Davood Wadi, Yu Ma
items.summary: The paper examines using LLMs as synthetic respondents in market research and conjoint analysis, showing that off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference regardless of model size or reasoning effort. Training smaller decision models via choice-based maximum likelihood on historical respondent microdata reduces treatment-effect error by 22-89% on held-out studies.
items.reasoning: Empirically valuable finding that purpose-trained decision models beat frontier LLM prompting for silicon sampling, with strong cross-study validation across scales. Niche application area but methodologically relevant to the broader synthetic-data debate.

items.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32718v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
items.author: Itai Mizlish, Boaz Ben-Moshe
items.summary: The authors distill Depth Anything V2-Large into an attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net that runs at 27.1 FPS in int8 on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-8L accelerator for robot navigation. They diagnose why direct quantization fails (91% of softmax weights below one int8 step at 449 tokens) and show the distilled student matches its float teacher closely.
items.reasoning: A well-executed and well-diagnosed edge-deployment result: the quantization failure analysis of attention is concrete, and the attention-free distillation with near-identical outputs is practically useful for cheap robot perception. Scope is a single model and platform, capping broader significance.

items.title: Change the Base, Change the Game: Rethinking Pan-sharpening
items.content: arXiv:2611.32002v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Many pan-sharpening (PS) networks reconstruct high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) images by adding learned residuals to 4$\times$-interpolated low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) inputs, incorporating panchromatic (PAN) detail only through these residual corrections. This raises a simple question: Why start with a blurry base when sharp spatial detail is already available? We propose PanBase, a sharper multispectral starting point designed for more effective residual learning. Guided by physical sensor characteristics, PanBase combines PAN spatial detail with LRMS spectral information while enforcing consistency with the LRMS observations under sensor-specific blur. We construct this base without neural network training, estimating only nine coefficients per spectral band through closed-form calibration. Our PanBase can be easily integrated into existing backbones with a global residual skip through two simple changes: (i) replacing the skip base with PanBase and (ii) concatenating it as an additional input. Using each backbone's original training recipe and matched training budgets, PanBase improves most reduced- and full-resolution metrics on WorldView-3, QuickBird, and GaoFen-2, while achieving 4.4$\times$ faster training convergence on average. In zero-shot evaluation on WorldView-2, standalone PanBase achieves competitive reconstruction without target-sensor fitting or neural refinement.
items.author: Jeonghyeok Do, Geunhyuk Youk, Munchurl Kim
items.summary: Questions the common pan-sharpening practice of adding learned residuals to blurry upsampled multispectral inputs, proposing PanBase, a training-free sharper starting point that fuses panchromatic spatial detail with multispectral spectra under sensor-specific blur constraints. Only nine parameters are estimated, and the improved base is shown to benefit downstream residual learning.
items.reasoning: A simple, physically grounded reframing of an established task with a training-free base construction; the insight is neat but pan-sharpening is a specialized remote-sensing niche.

items.title: FlashSegmentator: High-Throughput TotalSegmentator Inference without Loss of Accuracy
items.content: arXiv:2611.32208v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Purpose: To develop, evaluate, and publicly release FlashSegmentator, an open-source inference pipeline that increases the throughput of TotalSegmentator without retraining or loss of segmentation accuracy. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study used public datasets: 73 CT examinations from the TotalSegmentator test split (median age, 65 years; 37 male, 35 female, one unknown), 30 abdominal CT examinations from the Beyond the Cranial Vault (BTCV) dataset, 512 training-split CT examinations for concurrent-process analysis, and 55 MRI examinations. FlashSegmentator adds static-shape compilation, pipelining, batched sliding-window inference, and GPU postprocessing. Throughput was compared with the reference implementation (including its lower-resolution modes) and FastSegmentator on GH200, A100, and T4 GPUs. Dice agreement was tested with two one-sided tests (margin, +/-0.01). Results: FlashSegmentator processed 3782, 1810, and 270 examinations per hour on the GH200, A100, and T4 (57.7, 33.9, and 6.4 times the reference implementation and 3.20, 2.50, and 1.22 times compiled FastSegmentator). Dice scores were equivalent for all 117 structures on every GPU (mean difference <= 1.2 x 10^-5; P < .001) and at the examination level on BTCV. In contrast, the lower-resolution modes of the reference implementation processed 181 and 213 examinations per hour on the A100 but reduced mean Dice by 0.116 and 0.241. On MRI, throughput increased 94-fold with all 50 structures equivalent. Estimated A100 cloud cost per 10,000 examinations decreased from 997 to 29 US dollars. Conclusion: FlashSegmentator increased the throughput of TotalSegmentator on data center and entry-level GPUs without loss of segmentation accuracy compared with the reference implementation.
items.author: Yosuke Yamagishi, Tomohiro Kikuchi, Shouhei Hanaoka, Takeharu Yoshikawa, Osamu Abe
items.summary: FlashSegmentator is an open-source inference pipeline that increases TotalSegmentator CT/MRI segmentation throughput via static-shape compilation, pipelining, batched sliding-window inference, and GPU postprocessing, with no retraining and no accuracy loss. It was evaluated on public datasets including the TotalSegmentator test split, BTCV, and MRI exams. This has immediate clinical deployment value.
items.reasoning: Engineering-focused but highly practical: large throughput gains for a widely used medical segmentation tool with preserved accuracy and open release. Limited research novelty but real deployment impact.

items.title: Sub-Riemannian structure for Oriented Point Clouds
items.content: arXiv:2611.32361v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Many frameworks dealing with 3D (oriented) point clouds define locality in the ambient Euclidean space: $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs and radius balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are critical to define which points are "close to one another" and should exchange information. This can unintentionally merge sampled surfaces that are close in space but geometrically distinct such as the two faces of a thin leaf. Then, features are more prone to leak across boundaries which hinder performance. To address this, we propose to define a sub-Riemannian contact metric on position-orientation space $\mathbb{M}=\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{S}^2$: points are lifted to $(x,n)$ with $n$ a surface normal, and "motion" is constrained to a non-holonomic horizontal distribution in which spatial velocity must stay in the plane orthogonal to the normal which can reorient at a cost. From this, we derive an explicit score, which locally approximate the distance, to compare oriented points for downstream tasks. We report improved segmentation and correspondence accuracy near contact when using the score as a drop-in change inside PointNet++ aggregation mechanism as well as reduced leakage when using it to simulate heat diffusion on oriented points.
items.author: Thomas Besnier, Stefan Sommer
items.summary: This paper defines locality for oriented point clouds using a sub-Riemannian contact metric on position-orientation space rather than Euclidean k-nearest-neighbor graphs, preventing feature leakage between geometrically distinct surfaces that are spatially close, such as the two faces of a thin leaf. Points are lifted to position-normal pairs with motion constrained to a non-holonomic horizontal distribution.
items.reasoning: Mathematically principled and novel geometric reformulation with clear motivation from a known failure mode of Euclidean locality in point cloud processing; impact depends on demonstrated gains across point cloud architectures, which the abstract only implies.

To address this, we propose to define a sub-Riemannian contact metric on position-orientation space $\mathbb{M}=\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{S}^2$: points are lifted to $(x,n)$ with $n$ a surface normal, and "motion" is constrained to a non-holonomic horizontal distribution in which spatial velocity must stay in the plane orthogonal to the normal which can reorient at a cost. From this, we derive an explicit score, which locally approximate the distance, to compare oriented points for downstream tasks. We report improved segmentation and correspondence accuracy near contact when using the score as a drop-in change inside PointNet++ aggregation mechanism as well as reduced leakage when using it to simulate heat diffusion on oriented points.

items.title: DiffAnchor: Anchor-Space Diffusion for Monocular 3D Hand Pose Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32513v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate and efficient monocular 3D hand pose estimation is an important perception capability for embodied human interaction and dexterous manipulation. Recent diffusion-based methods model pose uncertainty by iteratively denoising 3D joint coordinates. However, directly diffusing the final joints requires the generative process to simultaneously explore plausible poses and recover precise coordinates, often relying on additional denoising steps or multiple hypotheses and consequently increasing inference cost. In this work, we propose DiffAnchor, a few-step anchor-space diffusion framework that diffuses anchors rather than joints. Our key insight is that stochastic exploration does not need to operate directly on the final output. Instead, diffusion searches for informative intermediate anchors that serve as local 3D regressors, while anchor-to-joint offset prediction and weighted aggregation complete precise joint localization. Specifically, fixed context anchors provide stable global references, whereas noisy dynamic anchors are iteratively refined toward informative joint regions. An importance-guided anchor selection and replenishment mechanism further retains useful anchors, removes ineffective ones, and explores insufficiently covered regions. This design reduces the precision burden of the diffusion process and enables accurate prediction using only a few denoising steps and a single hypothesis. Extensive experiments on HO-3D V2, NYU, ICVL, and InterHand2.6M demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the first three benchmarks and competitive performance on challenging interacting-hand estimation, while maintaining inference efficiency comparable to deterministic regression baselines.

This enables few-step inference without multiple hypotheses, reducing the cost typical of coordinate-space diffusion pose models.
items.reasoning: A clever reformulation that reduces inference cost for diffusion-based pose estimation and could inspire similar anchor-space designs elsewhere, but the task domain is specific and gains are incremental relative to state of the art.

items.title: Beyond Image-Text Pairs: Aligning Semantic Changes for Fine-Grained Visual Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.32817v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Image-text alignment serves as a foundation for modern vision-language models (VLMs), yet prevailing training paradigms provide limited supervision for learning how semantic changes correspond across modalities. To address this limitation, we propose a post-training method that learns cross-modal semantic change correspondences through controlled visual and textual variations. Specifically, we introduce a Semantic Difference Alignment (SDA) loss which can align the directions of corresponding visual and textual representation changes. We combine our proposed SDA with pairwise sigmoid matching to jointly learn image-text correspondences and cross-modal semantic changes, encouraging more fine-grained and discriminative visual representations. To support this learning, we construct VarFamily-40K, a dataset of image-text pairs with controlled cross-modal semantic variations. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in compositional understanding and downstream classification performance, alongside further gains on multimodal tasks when the adapted visual encoder is integrated into VLMs.

Impact depends on whether the improvement transfers across model scales and downstream tasks, and the abstract suggests a focused post-training contribution rather than a foundational one.

items.title: Sampling at Scale: Distributed Multi-Agent Trajectory Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.31561v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-agent trajectory optimization poses two coupled challenges: effectively exploring non-convex landscapes and scaling favorably to large teams of agents. Sampling-based methods are natural candidates for the exploration challenge but scale poorly with problem dimension. Moreover, their off-the-shelf integration into distributed optimization introduces a fundamental trade-off: sampling either fails to address the constraint-induced non-convexity or its search space grows with neighborhood size. We address this gap by introducing a $\underline{D}\text{istributed}$ $\underline{S}\text{ampling-based}$ $\underline{T}\text{rajectory}$ $\underline{O}\text{ptimization} \ \text{(DS-TO)}$ architecture built on a splitting mechanism tailored to sampling. Under this splitting, each agent samples only in its own control space, independent of neighborhood size, while still remaining exposed to both the constraint-induced non-convexity and the decisions of other agents. The resulting algorithm is fully decentralized, requiring only neighborhood communication, with all local updates executed in parallel across agents. Efficient variations, including parallel Jacobi updates within each agent's subproblem and single-step constraint linearization, further reduce computation. Experiments on 2D and 3D tasks with up to 1024 agents demonstrate improved exploration and constraint satisfaction over state-of-the-art derivative-based distributed optimization, and superior scalability to existing distributed sampling methods.

items.reasoning: A solid technical contribution to multi-agent motion planning, combining sampling-based exploration with distributed optimization. The approach is methodologically sound but sits within an established planning literature with incremental positioning.

items.title: Risk-Informed Path Planning: Collision and Grounding Avoidance Application for Autonomous Surface Vessels
items.content: arXiv:2611.32760v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) must demonstrate safety before and during operations, necessitating online risk assessment to guide decision-making at sea. This paper presents a risk-informed Rapidly Exploring Random Tree Star (RRT*) path planner that integrates a Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) as an online risk model. The BBN evaluates the probability and severity distribution of hazardous events, which are aggregated into a bounded scalar risk index. During the search, this risk index is evaluated at sample points along candidate edges. The planner optimizes a composite cost function comprising path distance, heading change penalties, and accumulated risk, subject to a hard constraint enforcing a risk acceptance limit. Each search tree vertex stores the BBN posterior at its state, enabling the tree to function as an explainable risk map for individual hazards. We define design requirements for the BBN to serve as the risk model in this context and introduce a runtime model that translates replanning deadlines into strict limits on single risk calculation times. The planner is demonstrated in a simulated harbor entry scenario involving collision and grounding hazards. Measured run times validate that the planner operates within the computational bounds predicted by the runtime model for a single replanning cycle.

items.summary: The paper integrates a Bayesian Belief Network as an online risk model into an RRT* path planner for autonomous surface vessels, aggregating hazard probability and severity into a bounded scalar risk index evaluated along candidate path edges. The planner optimizes distance, heading change, and accumulated risk under a hard risk-acceptance constraint.

items.title: A detective on demand: the Automated Auditor
items.content:
TL;DR: An automated auditor can make it possible to audit compute for frontier AI models. This is done by giving confidential information to an automated auditor in a safe environment that will be wiped after giving its report.[1]

It can be hard to send a credible signal. If a datacentre says "We are not running any training of frontier models", how do you know that they are telling the truth? Or if an employee that has signed an NDA says "According to what I see, this company is being reckless, but I can't reveal my reasons why I think this"?

In cases such as these, there is insider information that can lead to conclusions that the insider wants to show publicly. The problem is that they do not want to leak any of the insider information.

If only we could have a trusted auditor look at this insider information and assess it. They could then share the outcome of their assessment without leaking any of the insider information. In a lot of cases there is a legal framework for these auditors.[2] In the case of datacentre verification, this legal framework does not exist yet.  This is because there is no international agreement to enforce legal audits.

This means there is a need for an automated auditor, which allows organizations to show the trustworthy result of an audit in places where it is not possible for a legal audit to take place. An automated auditor also has the advantage that it can be given more access because it is wiped after a run.

The expected outsiders interested in this activity will be AI safety researchers and regulators. The general public can also benefit from the extra trust that can come from these reports.

This auditor needs to be trusted by both the insiders hosting it and the outsiders that want to understand where the report from the auditor comes from. So we want to satisfy both of their worries.

### Worries from the insider...
items.author: Jasper Blank
items.summary: A governance proposal for an automated auditor that receives confidential insider information in a secure, wiped environment and publishes only its conclusions, enabling credible signals like verifying that a datacenter is not training frontier models. It motivates the design via the absence of legal audit frameworks for compute verification. The post sketches how AI could substitute for trusted human auditors where no legal regime exists.
items.reasoning: A creative and timely idea connecting AI systems to the compute verification problem, with a clear threat model and mechanism. It remains a proposal without implementation or adversarial analysis of what the auditor itself could leak, but it contributes concretely to the verification literature.

items.title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations
items.content: arXiv:2611.31346v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in MLLMs have improved social understanding, enabling models to recognize emotions and distinguish truthful from deceptive behaviors. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on coarse-grained emotion recognition or binary truth-deception detection, overlooking the diverse ways people manipulate information in conversations, such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. Understanding these behaviors requires reasoning about underlying facts, participant knowledge, and conversational context, making them difficult to evaluate reliably. To address this gap, we introduce InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained information manipulation in conversations. InfoCon identifies six fine-grained strategies and derives a coarse consistency label from their factual and interactional relations. We develop an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to construct and verify reliable labels from rich contextual evidence. We benchmark representative multimodal models and systematically analyze their fine-grained information manipulation understanding, providing a testbed beyond binary truth-deception judgments.

items.summary: InfoCon is a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained information manipulation in conversations, going beyond binary deception detection to cover behaviors such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim across six categories. Reliable evaluation requires reasoning about facts, participant knowledge, and conversational context.
items.reasoning: The fine-grained taxonomy of conversational manipulation is a valuable step beyond coarse truth/deception labels and is relevant to trust and safety in social AI. Benchmark-only contribution with evaluation reliability challenges acknowledged by the authors; shares an author group and overlap with the ChartInt submission, suggesting a benchmark-series effort.

items.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.31559v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

The theoretical grounding and intervenability demonstrations are strengths, but the paper's practical impact depends on validation breadth, which appears limited in this initial work.

items.title: SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures
items.content: arXiv:2611.31787v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.

items.summary: SciFig2Data is an automated workflow for extracting structured experimental data from scientific PDFs, integrating figure localization, compound-figure panel decomposition, two-stage OCR semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal LLM reconstruction. It enables literature-scale recovery of measurements that are otherwise locked in figures. This supports meta-science, dataset construction, and knowledge extraction at scale.

items.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.31990v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
items.author: Dovud Asadov, Rustambek Urokov, Qobiljon Toshnazarov, Abduaziz Kayumov, Mardon Hazratov, Husanboy Mansuraliyev
items.summary: This analytical paper quantifies how much token dependency marginal-based set selection misses in masked diffusion language model parallel decoding, measured as conditional total correlation. Across four masked diffusion LMs, the best marginal-only predictor of this loss is off by roughly one bit, with most of its accuracy derived from the bound alone.
items.reasoning: A careful theoretical-empirical analysis of a specific limitation of parallel decoding in diffusion LMs, providing useful diagnostic tools. The contribution is rigorous and informative but narrow; it clarifies limits rather than delivering a new method with immediate wide impact.

items.title: Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification
items.content: arXiv:2611.32931v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A developer checking an assistant's report may need only an alarm that a claim is unsupported. A generative verifier, however, can continue decoding to quote and classify the errors. We study how much of that output is needed to recover its decision. In a frozen 2B span verifier, the choice between an empty error list and its first object precedes all localization. Native8 stops generation at this branch. The preceding seven syntax tokens are fixed, so Prefill1 supplies them as input and generates only the unrestricted branch token, using the same native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 reduces eager resident service by 84.84% relative to full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It saves 31.98% over Native8 even though their logical token totals are identical. Under default compiled execution, the extra saving is 6.74-26.73% on the complete workload, with small decision changes. Controlled evidence interventions and first-location decoding establish what these shorter readouts retain and what requires further generation.

However, it is a narrow optimization applicable to a specific verifier format, so novelty and general impact are modest even if engineering execution is solid.

items.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
items.content: arXiv:2611.33106v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.

items.title: LLM Genetic Feature Engineering
items.content: arXiv:2611.31277v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Feature Engineering is the (traditionally manual) process of constructing derived variables from an existing dataset by combining, transforming, or otherwise manipulating the original data fields to reduce statistical noise and extract meaningful, domain-specific quantities of interest from the raw dataset. Recent work demonstrates promising progress toward the au tomation of this process through the integration of large language models (LLMs) and various metaheuristics to guide the search for useful features. We build on this approach by introducing a novel genetic algorithm that implements selection, crossover, and mutation at the individual feature level, rather than at the level of the entire engineered feature set. In doing so, we enable in-process statistical analysis of newly-generated features, thereby enabling the genetic algorithm to simultaneously integrate individual and group-level feature metrics into its selec tion process. We demonstrate this capability using state-of-the-art feature importance metrics, and show that this approach yields superior predictive performance while driving meaningful improvements in feature relevance, algorithm robustness, and overall model interpretability.
items.author: Jonathan Thompson, Razvan Stefanescu, Manoj Varma Namburi, Liuxia Wang
items.summary: The authors introduce a genetic algorithm for LLM-driven automated feature engineering that applies selection, crossover, and mutation at the individual feature level rather than across entire engineered feature sets. This finer-grained search aims to reduce statistical noise and extract meaningful domain-specific quantities from raw datasets.
items.reasoning: A reasonable incremental improvement to LLM-guided feature engineering with a sensible algorithmic change, but the area is crowded and broad impact is limited by modest evaluation depth in the abstract.

items.title: Scoring Recovery-Time Agent Security: Proposals, Effects, and Retry Instructions
items.content: arXiv:2611.31318v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A timed-out tool write may be absent, committed, or still in flight. Evaluating an agent only on whether its goal exists can hide harmful recovery actions: auditing 12 supplied traces changes apparent completion from 10/12 to 8/12. We introduce an executable evaluation that separately records tool proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects. In 3,456 model episodes, the original task wording produces only 39/576 valid recoveries when the initial write is absent; a combined clarification produces 576/576. A further 1,584 episodes test stronger attacks and separate the effect definition from the recovery recipe with three rollouts per absent-state cell. Definition alone yields 276/288 valid recoveries; recipe alone yields 288/288. For Luna, malicious text is associated with 11.1 percentage points fewer valid recoveries under both original and definition-only wording, an availability signal limited by shared tasks and templates. The stronger attacks produce no attempted unauthorized or changed-key action and no unsafe effect. A trajectory audit finds six original-key retries after observing pending status: five denied and one deduplicated. Bounded checks distinguish atomic key enforcement from a delayed-commit race; stale negative reads also invalidate the evidence gate. A separate Claude Code program adds 720 successful episodes: 288 under the original attacks and 432 stronger-attack calibration episodes across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 5.5, with no observed proposal or effect deviations. The contribution is a measurement design and a diagnosis of availability, specification, and contract sensitivity, with no demonstrated general defense efficacy.
items.author: Paul Deepakraj Retinraj
items.summary: The paper introduces an executable evaluation that scores agent recovery from timed-out tool writes by separately recording proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects, showing that goal-based scoring hides harmful recovery actions. Across thousands of episodes, it quantifies how clarification wording and separating effect definitions from recovery recipes dramatically change valid-recovery rates.
items.reasoning: A careful, measurement-driven contribution to agent reliability evaluation, with the useful insight that apparent task completion can mask unsafe recovery behavior. The scale is respectable but the scope is narrow and centered on one failure mode.

items.title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits
items.content: arXiv:2611.31541v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A coding agent may need to upload a report while its sandbox blocks network access. A host mediator can restore delivery, but an injected instruction may add a secret to the approved request. We study this interaction using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs. Two prospective frozen-input cohorts comprise 110 and 300 runs on previously explored authored tasks. Restrictive sandboxing produces no observed attack harm but reduces benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24. Mediation restores uploads and admits disclosure; complete-line matching retains full benign utility but misses two value-only disclosures in the expanded cohort. A separate 72-run boundary study identifies encoded disclosure, observer misses, and formatting checks that obscure benign refusals. An 80-run SafeAgents/OpenShell follow-up shows that containment stops the tested guard misses among valid observations, while mediation restores benign uploads and delivers both encoded-attestation attacks. Twelve judge-error rows remain unscored. A separate response-capture diagnostic reproduces their failures at the native token budget. A 12-run exact-publication-contract experiment blocks both attacks but also rejects both benign formatting variants; a 4-run normalized follow-up restores both benign uploads while still rejecting both attacks. These small, single-model studies identify delivery-path and measurement limits; they do not establish general attack resistance.
items.author: Kunwar Singh Sangram, Krishna Mohan Guda Nagavenkata Srinivasa
items.summary: Using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs, this case study examines how sandboxing and host mediation compose in coding agents, showing that restrictive sandboxing eliminates observed attack harm but degrades benign utility, while mediation restores uploads but admits disclosure. A boundary study identifies encoded disclosure and observer misses that evade complete-line policy matching.
items.reasoning: A careful empirical study of the utility-security tradeoff in real agent defense compositions, with a sound measurement methodology. The findings are valuable for defense designers but confined to a case-study scope with limited generality.

items.title: LatentLens: Rethinking Latent Interface in Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.31582v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system communicate through continuous representations rather than decoded text. Prior work reports performance and efficiency gains, but neither separates latent communication from the agent harness nor examines its internal components, leaving its actual contribution unclear. We propose LatentLens, a framework that decouples the latent interface at two levels: externally from the agent harness, to measure its contribution to overall performance (RQ1), and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics, to identify the benefits and limitations of each (RQ2). Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve and can even substantially degrade accuracy. Internally, latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment can substantially degrade performance, and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures. Thus, while latent representations may preserve information, they do not necessarily ensure effective communication, which also requires compatible realignment, information accessibility, and stable propagation.
items.author: Ziqing Yang, Kewei Cheng, Mingjie Li, Yang Zhang
items.summary: LatentLens is a framework that decouples latent (continuous, non-textual) communication in multi-agent systems both externally from the agent harness and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics. Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, it clarifies how much of previously reported latent-communication gains actually stem from the interface versus the harness.
items.reasoning: A useful scientific contribution bringing experimental rigor to a trendy but under-examined technique, properly attributing where gains come from. The analysis is valuable but the finding is largely a corrective rather than a new capability.

items.title: RePT: 3D Geometry Emerges from 2D Relational Pretraining
items.content: arXiv:2611.31601v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.

items.reasoning: An intriguing finding about emergent geometric structure in representations learned without 3D supervision, with a clean held-out evaluation. The scope is modest and the metrics moderate, but the conceptual question, how physical geometry organizes in learned representations, is scientifically interesting.

items.title: GRUN: Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network for Image Restoration
items.content: arXiv:2611.31690v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Image restoration remains a fundamental challenge in low-level vision, requiring methods that handle diverse degradations while preserving scene structures and details. We revisit classical Retinex theory and propose a Generalized Retinex formulation that extends the illumination-reflectance decomposition into a Retinex-inspired content-environment factorization prior for image restoration. The key idea is to restore images using two learned factors: a content-dominant response (generalized reflectance) capturing scene properties and an environment-side response (generalized illumination) encoding task-dependent variations associated with the observed degradations. Based on this formulation, we develop GRUN (Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network), a MAP-guided deep unfolding framework that alternates reflectance restoration, illumination estimation, and progressive degradation inference across K stages with degradation-conditioned proximal operators. We further introduce a Degradation-aware Coupling Regularizer (DCR) that combines mutual information minimization, gradient decorrelation, and scale anchoring to promote complementary content-environment factor representations. Experiments on seven image restoration tasks, including denoising, dehazing, deraining, low-light enhancement, deblurring, underwater enhancement, and backlit enhancement, demonstrate competitive results on multiple benchmarks using the same architecture with task-specific weights. Moreover, the proposed Generalized Retinex design can be integrated into existing restoration methods, demonstrating its cross-architecture applicability. Code will be released.
items.author: Rihan Zhang, Fengyang Xiao, Yuhan Chen, Chunming He, Sina Farsiu
items.summary: GRUN revisits classical Retinex theory, generalizing illumination-reflectance decomposition into a content-environment factorization prior, and unfolds it into an optimization-inspired network for image restoration. It restores images via two learned factors capturing scene properties and degradation-dependent environmental variation.
items.reasoning: Solid low-level vision contribution with a principled reinterpretation of a classical prior and an unfolding architecture, but image restoration is a crowded field and the incremental gain over prior deep restoration methods appears modest from the abstract.

items.title: Beyond Rigid Hands: Deforming Skin into Contact-Consistent Hand Meshes
items.content: arXiv:2611.31950v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Hands grasp objects with soft skin. A fingertip flattens against a mug, and a palm curves around a bottle. Yet hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates the object where skin would press against it. Existing refiners keep the mesh rigid and adjust only the pose, trading pose accuracy for physical plausibility. We ask whether a rigid hand can instead touch the object as skin does while staying close to its original pose. We lift annotated or estimated rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes through an optimization that (i) slightly adjusts the joints and wrist to bring the fingers onto the object, (ii) deforms the skin so that penetrating regions settle onto the surface, and (iii) keeps this deformation consistent over time. Since deformation reaches only skin already near the object, we further train a lightweight head on the lifted annotations to predict where an estimated hand should touch and steer the deformation there. Unlike existing refiners, the lift more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability by closing contact gaps that the estimate leaves open. Existing hand-object datasets and estimators can thus adopt contact-consistent hands without changing the hand model or retraining the estimators.
items.author: Seonghwan Park, Min-Gyu Park
items.summary: The paper addresses the gap between rigid articulated hand meshes and realistic soft-tissue contact, where existing datasets and estimators produce hands that hover above or penetrate objects. The proposed optimization adjusts joints slightly and deforms skin so contact regions settle onto object surfaces, producing contact-consistent hand meshes that stay close to original poses. This improves physical plausibility for hand-object interaction modeling relevant to robotics, AR, and motion capture.
items.reasoning: A focused, well-motivated computer vision/graphics contribution addressing a genuine representational limitation in hand-object datasets. Impact is bounded to a specific subdomain, and the approach is an optimization-based refinement rather than a new foundational method.
