items.title: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers
items.content: arXiv:2611.33068v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Error-correcting output coding (ECOC) builds a multi-class classifier from binary classifiers. We study the excess error rate of ECOC over the Bayes (MAP) classifier when each binary classifier outputs a posterior estimate whose log-odds is corrupted by Gaussian noise. Recasting decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel, we derive an upper bound from the union and Chernoff bounds and a lower bound from the nearest competing category and the Mills ratio. The bounds show that a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate. The excess error rate stays bounded away from zero, by a constant that depends on the two largest posteriors and the noise level but not on the number of categories $M$, whenever the distance between the code words of the two most probable categories is bounded; for equidistant codes this distance is $d_{\min}$. Conversely, it is at most $M-1$ times a factor that is exponentially small in the minimum distance $d_{\min}$, and it vanishes whenever $\kappa\,d_{\min}-\ln(M-1)\to\infty$ for an explicit $\kappa$ (for general codes, under a posterior condition). For $n$-vs-rest codes with $n\geq2$, the upper and lower exponents coincide asymptotically, which determines the reliability function of ECOC in closed form. The results extend to correlated Gaussian noise with the Hamming distance replaced by an effective distance; when noise is shared at the level of categories, the effective distance stays bounded and the excess error rate does not vanish for any code. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. In a semi-synthetic setting, the measured decay agrees with the predicted exponent. On ResNet-50 features of CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k, the excess error over a log-likelihood decoding reference decreases with $d_{\min}$ and, for larger $M$, levels off at a moderate distance, while codes with $d_{\min}=1$ degrade as $M$ grows.
items.author: Gendo Kumoi, Hideki Yagi, Manabu Kobayashi, Shigeichi Hirasawa
items.summary: This theoretical paper derives upper and lower bounds on the excess error rate of error-correcting output codes over the Bayes classifier when binary classifiers produce posterior estimates corrupted by Gaussian noise. Recasting decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel, the analysis shows large Hamming distance is necessary and sufficient for reducing excess error, and characterizes when the error floor becomes independent of the number of classes. It provides clean information-theoretic insight into a classical multi-class classification technique.
items.reasoning: Rigorous and clean theory connecting coding theory and classification, but ECOC is a mature, less-active area, limiting contemporary impact. The bounds themselves are a solid but incremental theoretical advance.

items.title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.32303v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.

We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.

items.title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
items.content: arXiv:2611.32455v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant.   The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not.   Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.

items.title: WaveSR: Physics-Inspired Wave Evolution Attention for Efficient Image Super-Resolution
items.content: arXiv:2611.31984v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recently, physics-inspired neural networks have gained widespread attention due to their interpretability. The closed-form, frequency-time decoupled solution of the wave equation offers linear complexity and allows different frequency components to evolve independently, making it a potential alternative solution for efficient image super-resolution. Therefore, a physics-inspired wave evolution attention framework is proposed, namely WaveSR. The WaveSR framework involves two key modules, i.e., wave evolution attention (WEA) and Frequency-Adaptive Feed-Forward Network (FA-FFN). The WEA module achieves feature interactions through the analytical solution of the 2D wave equation in the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) domain, enabling independent evolution of different frequency components with learnable wave speed \(c\) and damping coefficient \(\alpha\). The FA-FFN module realizes adaptive frequency feature selection through learnable spectral modulation, effectively enhancing feature representation capability. Subsequently, we employ a two-stage training strategy with a hybrid objective that combines a spatial-domain pixel loss and a frequency-domain loss to improve reconstruction quality. Our method provides a preliminary exploration of physics-inspired neural networks for efficient image super-resolution.

items.title: EditText: Structure-Aware Generation and Selective Visual Transport for Fine-Grained Text Editing
items.content: arXiv:2611.32134v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fine-grained text editing aims to accurately replace text in a specified region while preserving the source text's font, color, and texture, as well as visual consistency in unedited regions. We present EditText, a unified framework for fine-grained text editing that combines target character generation with visual transport from the source image. The model uses dual-condition Fill inputs: a masked image and a source text style reference, both sharing a spatial reference with the target image. The masked image hides the original text and retains unedited content as a source canvas; the style reference supplies appearance cues that guide new character generation together with the target text. We introduce an Attention Transport framework in which Source Weight describes the attention allocated to a condition and the Spatial Aggregation Kernel describes its internal spatial attention distribution. Accurate transfer of source details depends on attention strength, the retention of details in condition features, and spatially accurate aggregation. For selected non-edit queries, we therefore preserve the total attention weight assigned to the masked image while redistributing its attention toward spatially corresponding neighborhoods, enabling selective visual transport. Multi-stage training, combined with a Glyph-aware Structural Loss on local target character structure, teaches the model to generate accurate text, preserve source text appearance, and retain unedited details. We also introduce TBench, a fine-grained text editing benchmark covering Alphabetic, Logographic, and Arabic numerals, to evaluate character updates, appearance preservation, and the preservation of unedited details. On TBench, EditText achieves state-of-the-art non-edit-region SSIM (0.9769) and full-image LPIPS (0.0460).

The work matters because precise text editing is a common requirement in design, document, and advertising workflows where generative models often distort style or surrounding content.

However, it addresses a fairly niche task (scene text editing), is from authors without noted major-lab affiliation, and the truncated content does not show benchmark comparisons or SOTA claims. items.title: CREDIT: Compositional Reliability Learning for Noisy Composed Image Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2611.32310v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image that satisfies user intent based on a multimodal query consisting of a reference image and a modification text. However, real-world training data are often corrupted by Noisy Triplet Correspondence (NTC), where the semantic correspondence among the reference image, modification text, and target image becomes unreliable. Existing methods implicitly assume that the correctness of triplet correspondence can be determined by fixed decision rules. However, under NTC, the authenticity of semantic correspondence is difficult to determine accurately, and different triplets exhibit varying degrees of semantic reliability rather than binary correctness. Consequently, deterministic confidence is insufficient to faithfully characterize correspondence reliability, often leading to overconfident supervision for unreliable triplets and progressively reinforcing noisy semantics during compositional representation learning. To address this challenge, we propose a Compositional Reliability learning framework with Evidential uncertainty and DiffusIon-guided refinemenT (CREDIT), which explicitly quantifies the uncertainty of triplet correspondence to estimate its reliability and suppress the propagation of noisy supervision. CREDIT consists of two complementary components: The Evidential Compositional Uncertainty Learning (ECUL) module explicitly models correspondence uncertainty via evidential learning, enabling uncertaintyaware reliability estimation to suppress noisy supervision. Building upon the reliable supervision provided by ECUL, the Diffusion-enhanced Reference Refinement (DRR) module further refines reference representations through textconditioned diffusion, producing more robust compositional query features. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CREDIT consistently outperforms existing methods under various settings.

It replaces fixed decision rules with compositional reliability learning that models varying degrees of semantic trustworthiness rather than binary correctness.

items.title: One Subspace Is Not Enough: LocalSubspaceAD for Training-Free Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.32424v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Defect-free industrial samples can vary considerably in appearance, texture, and geometry. In few-shot anomaly detection, this variability has to be modeled from only a handful of images. SubspaceAD showed that a single principal subspace of foundation-model patch features is a strong training-free model of nominal appearance. However, a single subspace has to cover all of the nominal data's variability, so a deviation that is anomalous for one semantic region can be within the nominal variability of another. We propose LocalSubspaceAD, which extends SubspaceAD from a single subspace to a mixture of subspaces, assigning each group of patches with similar features its own subspace. The set of patch-features is partitioned using k-means, one subspace is fit per cluster, and each patch is scored by the minimum of re-projection residuals over all subspaces. The proposed method requires no training and no EM refinement. On MVTec AD, VisA and Real-IAD with 1, 2 and 4 shots, it improves over a single subspace (SubspaceAD) on both evaluated backbones: by 1.2 to 1.8 points image AUROC on DINOv2, and by 1.4 to 4.4 points in image AUROC, pixel AUPR and AUPRO on DINOv3. The gains are most pronounced on objects with heterogeneous nominal appearance, such as multi-instance categories and PCBs. Ablations show that the gains stem from a finer-grained model of variability through locally oriented subspaces, rather than from the subspace offsets (cluster means). We further show that the gains do not stem from added capacity alone: the local subspaces appear to capture the structure of coherent clusters in feature space, and the model does not merely act as a compressed memory bank.

items.title: TDD: Target-Discrepancy Distillation for Underwater Image Enhancement
items.content: arXiv:2611.32467v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Underwater degradation changes image appearance and can compromise the semantic cues used to guide enhancement. Identifying scene content alone does not explicitly specify the appearance to recover or the input-dependent changes associated with that target. We propose target-discrepancy knowledge distillation (TDD) for underwater image enhancement, which organizes guidance around these two aspects of the same restoration problem. For each degraded-reference training pair, reference features from an underwater vision-language teacher provide target-appearance supervision, while paired feature residuals describe the observation's discrepancy relative to the same target. Both representations are jointly distilled into a lightweight guidance network that predicts them from the degraded image alone; neither the teacher nor reference images are required at inference. To align their use with their supervisory roles, we introduce progressive knowledge fusion within a multi-scale enhancement network. The estimated discrepancy first conditions spatial feature updates, after which target-appearance guidance refines the updated features and channel interactions consolidate their responses. This correction-before-refinement design lets target-guided refinement build on discrepancy-conditioned features. Experiments on six underwater benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance across full-reference and no-reference metrics. Ablations and feature visualizations analyze the contributions of the knowledge source, joint distillation, and progressive fusion.

This explicitly structures the enhancement problem around what to recover and how the input differs from it.

items.title: On the Capabilities and Limitations of Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Cloud Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32625v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in vision-language foundation models have enabled open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) without task-specific training, offering new opportunities for Earth Observation (EO) applications. However, their capabilities for cloud detection remain insufficiently explored. In this work, we evaluate twelve OVSS approaches across six publicly available EO datasets in a zero-shot setting, i.e., without fine-tuning or adaptation to the target data. We investigate both binary cloud detection and multiclass segmentation, distinguishing between thick clouds, thin clouds, cloud shadows, and background. Our results show differences in performance across models and datasets, with SegEarth-OV3 achieving the highest binary cloud detection performance on four of the six datasets. While several approaches demonstrate promising performance in binary cloud detection, multiclass segmentation remains more challenging, particularly when distinguishing between fine-grained cloud categories. Furthermore, our controlled prompt sensitivity analysis reveals model-dependent responses to alternative textual descriptions, with appearance-oriented prompts benefiting certain approaches while degrading the performance of others. Overall, our findings demonstrate both the potential and current limitations of zero-shot OVSS for cloud detection, establishing a comparative benchmark for future research on generalisable cloud segmentation. Code will be available at: https://github.com/josesosajs/zero-shot-cloudovss.

items.title: CityRecast: Suppressing Persistent Artifacts in Generative Satellite 3D Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.32863v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Satellite-based 3D reconstruction is limited by sparse observations and changes across acquisition dates. Existing methods use generative priors to recover missing visual detail, but ghosting, streaking, and blur persist in their Gaussian scenes. These artifacts become particularly apparent in low-elevation renderings. We introduce CityRecast to suppress these artifacts through Gaussian scene repair and supervision calibration. To correct the Gaussian distributions that produce these artifacts, we first use multi-angle warm-up to constrain their spatial extent. This reduces the initial ghosting carried into progressive refinement. Surface-guided replacement then continues to repair the Gaussian distribution while preserving existing appearance. To provide more reliable supervision for this process, observation calibration mitigates interference from multi-temporal observations. Joint refinement further reduces conflicts among generated views. Experiments on DFC2019 and IARPA demonstrate reduced artifacts in low-elevation renderings while maintaining satellite-view fidelity. Compared with Skyfall-GS, CityRecast reduces FID-CLIP by 25.3% on DFC2019 and 51.8% on IARPA. MUSIQ increases by 14.54 and 24.95 points, respectively.

Targets robust reconstruction under sparse observations and cross-date scene changes.

items.title: Cif-query bridging for audio-native asr transfer to visual speech recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.32697v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Audio-native automatic speech recognition (ASR) models provide strong speech-language priors, but their compact acoustic interfaces are mismatched with long, frame-level visual features. We propose CIF-Query Bridge, a lightweight connection from a Paraformer visual speech recognition (VSR) encoder to Qwen3-ASR. The existing visual continuous integrate-and-fire (CIF) predictor produces an input-dependent number of token-rate queries; a two-layer cross-attention bridge refines them against the complete frame sequence, and a linear adapter feeds the pretrained ASR projector and decoder. This design preserves access to uncompressed visual context while avoiding direct autoregressive processing of hundreds of video frames. items.title: A Self-Organizing Swarm Control Model for Underwater Robots Based on Turing-Type Reaction-Diffusion Principles
items.content: arXiv:2611.31637v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In underwater environments, Global Positioning System (GPS) signals and high-speed radio communication are unavailable, and severe constraints exist on communication bandwidth and visibility; consequently, applying conventional swarm formation methods, such as the Boids model, which require the relative positions and velocity vectors of neighboring vehicles, is difficult. This study proposes a decentralized swarm control model that operates without a leader or absolute coordinates, relying solely on the number of received signals from two communication channels with different transmission ranges (inner and outer neighborhoods). The proposed model extends a cellular automaton model based on Turing pattern formation principles to continuous space and is grounded in the fundamental concept that swarms form as robots move toward regions of higher potential calculated from the difference in received signal counts. Specifically, stable behavior is determined through temporal averaging of potential values, hysteresis-based state evaluation, stepwise turning based on temporal differences, and vector composition with an external directional command. Two-dimensional simulation results demonstrated that autonomous swarm formation and control of swarm spatial dispersion via a morphological parameter are achievable, confirming robustness in maintaining swarms and high polarization even under communication dropouts where the communication success rate decreases to approximately 0.7.

items.title: A Face Robot which Imitates Human Musculoskeletal Skin System and Its Evaluation on Basic Movement of Facial Expression
items.content: arXiv:2611.32413v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Facial robots require many coordinated, smallamplitude motions, but accommodating these motions in a compact face remains difficult. This paper presents an anatomically inspired facial-robot platform that reproduces the layered organization of the human facial musculoskeletal system. The platform comprises bone, muscle, and skin components whose geometry, shape, and attachment locations are derived from three-dimensional anatomical data. Wire-driven, compliant muscle components are routed through PTFE tubes, allowing actuation to be placed away from the face. We describe the selection and fabrication of 65 muscles (34 muscle types) required to reproduce the 47 target action units (AUs) in the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). We then evaluate the reproducibility of individual AUs in two stages: muscle actuation without skin and actuation after the silicone skin is attached. Forty of the 47 target AUs were reproduced with the muscle components, and 30 were reproduced after skin attachment. These results demonstrate the feasibility of reproducing a broad range of FACS facial expressions using an anatomically inspired musculoskeletal structure. The proposed platform provides a foundation for the systematic development and evaluation of future anatomically inspired facial robots
items.author: Shun Kaneko, Shunnosuke Yoshimura, Akihiro Miki, Kento Kawaharazuka, Kei Okada
items.summary: The authors build an anatomically inspired facial robot that reproduces the layered bone-muscle-skin organization of the human face using 3D anatomical data, wire-driven compliant muscles routed through PTFE tubes, and 65 muscles covering 47 Facial Action Coding System action units. They evaluate the platform on basic facial-expression movements. This matters for human-robot interaction, since lifelike expressive faces are central to social robots, and reproducing FACS action units provides a standardized basis for evaluating facial expressivity.
items.reasoning: Impressive hardware engineering with clear grounding in human anatomy and standard evaluation via FACS, continuing a recognized line of musculoskeletal robotics work. However, the contribution is primarily a niche platform design rather than an algorithmic advance with broad AI impact, and the significance is mostly within social/humanoid robotics and hardware communities.

items.title: Self-supervised quality evaluation of grid maps without ground truth
items.content: arXiv:2611.32550v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Maps are widely used in the robotics community for localization and path planning and the ability to identify incorrect or inaccurate regions of a map is an area of active research interest. For large environments, manual edits of the map can be very time consuming and a tool which can assist a map editor is needed. With this paper, we contribute to robot introspection through self-assessment of map quality, using only a given map as input to be independent of the underlying mapping algorithm. Current methods for map quality assessment rely on ground-truth or labelled information for training classifiers, both of which can be difficult to obtain. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised learning approach to map quality assessment of 2D occupancy grid maps which identifies regions of a map that require further investigation. We leverage an autoencoder for patches extracted from the map to capture the dominant structure of the map. By evaluating the reconstruction loss of a patch reconstructed with the learned model, we can evaluate whether it contains an unusual structure, which indicates the need of further investigation. We evaluate our method on the outcome of state-of-the-art grid mapping methods using benchmark datasets as well as maps from warehouse environments, highlighting the application to more complex environments. We show that the method identifies regions with sparse data, clutter, and misregistrations.

It targets robot introspection and assistance for human map editors in large environments.

items.title: I still don't believe in superintelligence
items.content:
I see versions of this statement quite frequently. A recent example came from Aella, saying that “The gap between you and the less intelligent people around you is miniscule [sic] compared to the gap between you and superintelligence.”

A few months ago, I would have more or less believed this. At least for games like Go and chess, in which we’ve had superhuman AIs for a decade or more, I thought the gap between the AI and the top human was much larger than the gap between the top human and me. Many seem to derive their intuition about superintelligence the same way:

In my post last month “Human vs AI in Go in 2026”[1], I explained that I’m really intrigued by the situation of human vs. AI in Go because it seems to be where so many derive their intuitions about superintelligence. In that post, I quoted Noam Brown saying on the Dwarkesh Podcast that Go AIs are “unimaginably, orders of magnitude stronger than any human alive.”

But I now think this is false in Go and chess! In both of these games, one way to measure the relative strength of players is the amount of handicap the stronger player must give for the weaker player to win. This gives a natural measure of the skill gap in these games. As I discussed in the previous post, modulo some caveats, the distance between the best Go AI and the best human player in 2026, Shin Jin-seo, seems to be around just 2 stones. And even before the age of Go AIs, the distance between the top pro players and God—perfect play—was considered to be about 4 stones....
items.author: Haoxing Du
items.summary: An argument against the intuition that superhuman AI is vastly beyond the best humans, using handicap-based skill-gap measurements in Go and chess to claim the human-AI gap is smaller than commonly assumed. The author challenges quotes like Noam Brown's characterization of Go AIs as orders of magnitude stronger than humans. This pushes back on a common intuition pump used in AI risk discussions.
items.reasoning: A concrete, quantitative critique of an influential intuition about superintelligence, with a reasonable metric (handicap gaps). The inference from narrow games to general superintelligence is contested and the argument may overcorrect, but it usefully grounds an abstract debate in measurable data.

items.title: Gated Concept Adapters: Layer-Wise Concept Bottlenecks for Auditable Text Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.32600v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Human-facing text understanding systems are used to infer affect, moderate harmful content, and support socially sensitive decisions. However, Transformer predictions are difficult to audit because they are produced from high-dimensional hidden states that do not provide a compact, inspectable interface for human analysis or intervention. We introduce Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers. Token representations are mapped into concept activations, filtered by learned gates, pooled into layer-level summaries, and exposed to the prediction head as a concept-mediated interface. The dimensions can be inspected through usage statistics, signature n-grams, post-hoc concept names, and targeted concept interventions. We evaluate GCA on fine-grained emotion classification, toxicity detection, topic classification, and a controlled verb-cloze stress test. In the affective and safety-relevant classification settings, GCA learns comparatively low-redundancy and intervention-sensitive concept representations while retaining useful predictive performance. On toxicity detection, it remains close to an unconstrained ModernBERT baseline while enabling concept-level inspection, targeted intervention, and lightweight post-hoc control. On GoEmotions, the end-to-end concept model incurs a macro-F1 cost relative to unconstrained RoBERTa, while a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduces this gap. On AG News, GCA remains competitive with recent concept-based baselines, and the Qwen verb-cloze experiment clarifies the limits of concept-mediated full-vocabulary prediction. Overall, GCA provides a neural concept interface for auditable text understanding, prioritizing transparency, diagnosis, and intervention over unconstrained accuracy maximization.
items.author: Niloofar Ranjbar, Saeedeh Momtazi, Mohammad Mehdi Homayounpoor
items.summary: Gated Concept Adapters attach gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected layers of pretrained Transformers, creating a concept-mediated interface for predictions in text understanding tasks. The approach aims to make predictions auditable and intervenable for sensitive applications like affect inference and content moderation.
items.reasoning: Concept bottleneck methods for interpretability are established, but the layer-wise gated adapter design applied to pretrained Transformers is a reasonable refinement. Relevant to AI transparency, though from a relatively unknown group and the auditable-benefits claims would need strong validation.

items.title: Evaluating Frontier-Model Agent Skills with Open-Weight Models in a Science Gateway
items.content: arXiv:2611.31480v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Scientific analyses that span many jobs and computing sites depend on workflow management systems to run reliably, but writing a production workflow requires expertise in such a system, which many domain scientists do not have. Coding agents can supply this expertise when they are guided by skills and packaged procedures for recurring tasks. We wrote skills and specialist agents for the Pegasus workflow management system with a frontier model, and the PegasusAI Studio science gateway offers them to scientists through a chat interface. New users without frontier-model credits need an open-weight model, served at no cost on research cyberinfrastructure, but skills written for a frontier model may not work with an open-weight solution. This paper presents a method for adapting such skills. An evaluation harness drives the real gateway as a user would, scores the workflows the agent builds, and feeds recurring failures back to the frontier model that maintains the skills. We evaluated 21 open-weight models on 17 tasks. The five highest-scoring models are close in quality after one trial per task, and their median response times differ twelvefold. In repeated trials with the best of the three open-weight models, we repeated scores of 0.76 on workflow building against 0.82 for Claude. The harness led to five changes to the initial skills. We also identify challenges in evaluating agents within operational systems: evaluation failures can be mistaken for model failures, and agents can circumvent experimental controls within their privilege domain. In a controlled ablation, an initially significant effect disappeared when the restrictions were properly enforced.
items.author: Komal Thareja, Mats Rynge, Anirban Mandal, Ewa Deelman
items.summary: The authors packaged Pegasus workflow-management expertise as skills and specialist agents built with a frontier model, offered to scientists through the PegasusAI Studio gateway, then tested whether those skills transfer to open-weight models served free on research cyberinfrastructure. The paper evaluates how well agent skills written for a frontier model work when users lack frontier-model access.
items.reasoning: A useful applied case study on skill portability between frontier and open-weight models in scientific workflow automation, with practical value for research infrastructure. It is domain-specific and evaluation-oriented rather than methodologically novel, and the abstract suggests a focused, incremental contribution.

items.title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
items.content: arXiv:2611.31823v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

It further estimates realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering rather than relying on prompted difficulty targets. This improves controllability of educational problem generation beyond surface-level specifications.

items.title: Conformalized Tree-Based Gradient Ensembles for Out-of-Distribution Detection and Plausible Recourse
items.content: arXiv:2611.31319v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Counterfactual recourse provides actionable feature adjustments that reverse unfavourable predictions made by automated decision models. However, when recourse search optimizes purely against classifier confidence or narrow proxy scores over gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT), search procedures can exploit boundary artifacts and low-density regions---an instance of Goodhart's law---yielding out-of-distribution (OOD) recommendations that appear favourable nominally while lacking manifold plausibility. In this paper, we study conformalized OOD gating coupled with actionability-constrained counterfactual search across two tabular benchmarks: Adult and Give Me Some Credit (GMSC). Calibrating finite-sample anomaly gates (gate_IF, gate_LOF, and the conjunctive gate_ALL) at significance level delta = 0.05 over isolation forest, local outlier factor, and k-nearest-neighbor signals, we audit generated counterfactuals against held-out GMM and OCSVM detectors alongside ablation studies (gen10, gen100, and relax). Across matched recourse pairs where both constrained and unconstrained searches succeed, gate_ALL significantly reduces held-out OCSVM flags on Adult (N=541, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0296, p_Holm = 4.0e-4) and lowers both held-out flags on GMSC (N=540, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0346, p = 1.0751e-4; Delta flag_GMM = -0.1663, p = 3.5679e-16) while increasing matched recourse cost (Delta cost = +0.3035, p = 1.3365e-5) and narrowing overall feasibility. Our findings formalize the cost--feasibility--plausibility trade-off and demonstrate how conformal OOD gating audits recourse reliability on tabular ensembles.
items.author: Mariam Zakaria Moussa Ali
items.summary: This work addresses Goodhart-style exploitation in counterfactual recourse for gradient-boosted decision trees, where search against confidence proxies yields implausible out-of-distribution recommendations. It combines conformalized OOD gating using anomaly detectors with actionability-constrained counterfactual search, validated on the Adult and Give Me Some Credit tabular benchmarks.
items.reasoning: A methodologically sound combination of conformal calibration and constrained recourse addressing a real robustness problem in deployed tabular decision systems. Solid but incremental within an established line of work, and limited to two benchmarks.

Our findings formalize the cost--feasibility--plausibility trade-off and demonstrate how conformal OOD gating audits recourse reliability on tabular ensembles.

items.title: Does Research-Paper Context Improve LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation? An Exploratory Simulation Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.32381v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.

items.summary: The authors test whether supplying specific research papers as context improves navigation code that Claude Opus 5, an LLM released in mid-2026, writes for a Go2 quadruped with the locomotion policy frozen. items.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.32372v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.
items.author: Jan Rohleff, Johannes Schropp
items.summary: This paper provides convergence guarantees for the VAE-NLME algorithm, which applies variational autoencoders to nonlinear mixed-effects models used in pharmacometrics for dosing and regulatory decisions. It proves almost-sure convergence of the ELBO objective to stationary points without requiring exact encoder training, and connects the ELBO solution to maximum likelihood.
items.reasoning: Rigorous theoretical work that strengthens the statistical foundations for applying VAEs in a high-stakes domain (drug development), but the niche application area and theory-focused contribution limit broad ML impact.

items.title: On the Effectiveness of Resampling for Supervised Graph Anomaly Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.32598v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Class imbalance and scarce anomaly labels motivate oversampling in supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD), but its benefits across detectors and benchmarks remain unclear. In the low-label setting of GADBench, with 20 labelled anomalies and 80 labelled normal nodes, we compare class weighting and up to six oversampling strategies in ten detector configurations from three families: graph neural networks (GNNs), tree ensembles on neighbourhood-aggregated features, and tabular foundation models, on 17 datasets. On the eight datasets with organic anomalies, no strategy has a statistically resolved average gain in any configuration, and which nodes are labelled matters as much as the strategy. On the nine datasets with injected anomalies, Gaussian-noise oversampling (ROSE) gains up to 5.2 AUPRC points in four of the six tree and tabular foundation model configurations, and in all six only on attribute-swap anomalies; in four GNNs its gain is not distinguishable from zero. This gain depends on the injection recipe, which gives swapped nodes an atypical feature norm: it is no longer distinguishable from zero when the swap uses a single random donor or preserves the norm, although most detectors then also stop detecting the swaps. Over the 17 datasets, tuning the tree detectors adds about three points, as much as ROSE, and cuts ROSE's gain by about half or more. With the same source nodes and class weight, sampled graph views are not distinguishable from plain copies of those nodes. We recommend tuning baselines, repeating labelled splits, reporting organic and injected anomalies separately, and checking label-free degree and feature-norm baselines.
items.author: Cyril Perosino (GOAL), Rino Di Chiara (Polito), Hamida Seba (GOAL)
items.summary: The paper systematically compares class weighting and six oversampling strategies across ten detector configurations (GNNs, tree ensembles, tabular foundation models) on 17 GADBench datasets in the low-label regime. It finds no statistically resolved gains on datasets with organic anomalies, while which nodes are labelled matters as much as the strategy, with Gaussian oversampling helping only on injected-anomaly datasets.
items.reasoning: A useful negative-result-heavy empirical study that tempers expectations for a popular technique family in graph anomaly detection; rigorous but unlikely to shift mainstream research priorities.

items.title: When Is Product Decoding of ECOC MAP-Consistent? Pair Structure and the n-vs-Rest Codes
items.content: arXiv:2611.33044v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Error-Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) combine binary classifiers by the sum decoder, which totals probabilities, or the product decoder, which totals log-likelihoods. In the noiseless setting, where the binary classifiers output the true posteriors, we ask on which code matrices each decoder always agrees with the Bayes-optimal (MAP) class. For the sum decoder the answer is known: the code must be equidistant (James and Hastie, 1998). We answer the question for the product decoder. Two classes are compared through the votes of the columns on which they differ: the sum decoder decides by their sample mean, the product decoder by an M-estimator with influence function artanh, and each vote is the MAP margin plus a bias determined by the other classes alone. Our main theorem states that the product decoder is MAP-consistent if and only if, for every class pair, the columns on which the two classes differ are matched with the columns obtained by swapping the two classes (or their complements), and equivalently if and only if the code is a union of n-vs-Rest codes. Efficient equidistant codes are therefore excluded: Hadamard codes ($M\ge 8$), which meet the Plotkin bound with $M-1$ columns, have no such pairs, and for the Sylvester type the reversal margin can be at least a constant 0.0182 independent of $M$. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. On six real datasets with estimated probabilities, the product decoder is slightly more accurate when each column is calibrated, and the sum decoder is better when the calibration error differs across columns; in either case the decoders disagree only near ties.
items.author: Gendo Kumoi
items.summary: The paper characterizes code matrices for which the product decoder of error-correcting output codes agrees with the Bayes-optimal class in the noiseless setting, complementing the known equidistance condition for the sum decoder. It analyzes comparisons via an M-estimator with artanh influence function and specializes to pairwise and one-vs-rest structures.
items.reasoning: A precise but narrow theoretical answer to a classical question about ECOC decoding; relevance has declined as ECOC methods are less central to modern deep learning practice.

items.title: Exact Volume-Preserving Diffeomorphic Shear Splitting: Continuous-Discrete Geometric Bounds, Reversible Memory Backpropagation, and Expressivity Frontiers in Volumetric Mapping
items.content: arXiv:2611.31343v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(D\Phi) = 1) without topological folding (det(D\Phi) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox).   We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(\Omega) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(\Omega). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations).   We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(D\Phi)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.

items.summary: The paper formulates an exact structure-preserving framework for incompressible 3D image registration using cascaded coordinate shears whose convective nonlinearities vanish, enabling closed-form integration and eliminating numerical volume drift seen in SVF/LDDMM methods. It also provides geometric bounds, reversible memory-efficient backpropagation, and expressivity analysis.
items.reasoning: Technically deep contribution with exact guarantees where prior methods only approximate incompressibility, plus a memory-efficient reversible backprop scheme. Single-author mathematical work with strong rigor but adoption depends on integration into standard medical imaging pipelines.

items.title: Measuring Counterfactual Credit in a Replayable Wildfire-Suppression Benchmark
items.content: arXiv:2611.31499v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, learned critics are usually evaluated by how well they predict the team's return. Yet predicting a team's return and assigning credit to individual actions are distinct tasks. To test credit directly, we introduce FLARE (Fireline Learning Agents in a Replayable Environment), a stochastic wildfire suppression benchmark in which any moment of a fire can be replayed with different actions under the same random events. Replaying one step measures the immediate effect of each agent's suppression, which we call simulator credit and use for training. Replaying to the end of the episode measures the effect of each action, which we use for grading critics. In a comparison over eight seeds with multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO), simulator credit reduces the interquartile mean burn score (each cell's burning time, capped and averaged over the map; lower is better) from 26.6% with shared reward to 20.9%. Learned credit from a centralized COMA-style critic does no better than the shared reward. Four trained critics predict the team's return well, yet the credit they assign is 9 to 42 times larger than the credit measured by replay. The critics also give heterogeneous agents nearly identical action rankings. These results show that a good fit to the team's return is a weak test of a critic's credit.

items.reasoning: A creative benchmark design enabling true counterfactual credit measurement, addressing a real evaluation gap in multi-agent RL. Impact depends on community uptake and the generality of findings beyond the wildfire domain.

items.title: A General Framework for E-process Stopping Rules in Best-Arm Identification
items.content: arXiv:2611.31898v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We propose an e-process stopping rule in the best-arm identification problem. The e-process stopping rule is different from the Chernoff stopping rule by its hypothesis structure on the stopping decision. The major benefit of an e-process stopping rule is the flexibility in stopping rule design and in fact, it recovers previously suggested Chernoff stopping rule on several bandit problems. Moreover, we analyze the asymptotic optimality of the $\delta$-PAC algorithm with the decomposition of e-processes. The decomposition separates optimality conditions into three parts; the sampling policy allocation convergence, the efficiency of e-process design, and the bandit problem's inherent stochastic behavior. Subsequently, we prove a sufficient condition for asymptotic optimality in bandit algorithms. For the application of an e-process stopping rule, we derived an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the generalized linear bandit problem.
items.author: Donghyun Park, Seohwa Hwang, Junyong Park
items.summary: The paper proposes e-process-based stopping rules for best-arm identification, offering flexible design that recovers the classical Chernoff rule as a special case. It analyzes asymptotic optimality of delta-PAC algorithms, decomposing conditions into sampling-policy convergence, e-process efficiency, and inherent stochastic behavior, and proves a sufficient condition.

items.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
items.content: arXiv:2611.32595v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We prove that the following problem is \textbf{NEXPTIME}-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.
items.author: Marco S\"alzer
items.summary: The paper proves that deciding whether there exists a bounded-degree graph (even degree 3) accepted by a message-passing neural network with sum aggregation and ReLU activations is NEXPTIME-hard. This is a tight computational complexity result for verification of MPNNs on local graph classes.
items.reasoning: A crisp, provable complexity-theoretic result with implications for the feasibility of formal verification of GNNs, which is conceptually important. However, it is a single hardness theorem in a specialized theory area with no algorithmic or empirical component, limiting breadth of impact.

items.title: Generating Schema-Aligned Synthetic Dialogues and Measuring Their Diversity
items.content: arXiv:2611.32631v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to obtain at all. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. Naively prompting a language model for such dialogues yields small variations of a single conversation, so we add a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan that orders the fields of the record as explicit mechanisms for variation. We measure the variation that reaches the output through embedding space, where the embedding variance spreads over about two and a half times as many independent directions with our full configuration compared to without (participation ratio 23.3 against 9.2). Two corpora of medical dialogue give values of the same order, with sample size, text length and language being additional factors there. We also show the positive effect of our method in a downstream test, where an 8B extraction model reaches 64.8% field accuracy when fine-tuned on dialogues from our method, against 57.5% from naive generation. We release the generation library and the generated corpus of German clinical dialogues with aligned records.
items.author: Konrad Stolte, Toni Fetzer
items.summary: The authors generate paired dialogue-to-record training data by sampling a schema-valid record first and then writing a dialogue from it, eliminating annotation needs for sensitive domains. To overcome low diversity from naive prompting, they add sampled variation configurations, personas, and a topic plan ordering record fields, and they measure resulting dialogue diversity. This is a practical recipe for creating structured-record dialogue data.
items.reasoning: A useful data-generation recipe addressing real annotation bottlenecks, with explicit attention to diversity measurement, which many synthetic-data papers skip. Techniques are assembled from known ideas (inverse generation, persona sampling) so methodological novelty is moderate.

items.title: One Style Fits All? Cultural Values Embedded in Conversational AI via a People-Pleasing Lens
items.content: arXiv:2611.32939v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs reflect or reinforce culture-specific social expectations remains limited. This study examined how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles shape user experience and continuance intention, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task. Results showed that: (1) supportive chatbots consistently led to higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust; (2) PPT did not moderate these effects; and (3) cultural variation emerged only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese but not the Korean sample. These findings reveal how a general-purpose LLM style may differentially activate culturally situated social scripts, raising implications for culturally inclusive conversational AI design.

items.title: SynAVID: A Synthetic Audio-Visual Immersive Dataset of Dynamic Scenes
items.content: arXiv:2611.32311v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Immersive scene modeling requires synchronized visual and auditory observations under changing viewpoints and scene conditions. Obtaining such observations and references for controlled scene changes remains challenging. We introduce SynAVID, a synthetic audio-visual immersive dataset comprising eight indoor and outdoor scenes. Each minute-scale episode combines fixed camera arrays and moving trajectories with synchronized, viewpoint-dependent binaural audio. Shared scene dynamics, sound-source events, and observer poses drive visual rendering and geometry-aware acoustic synthesis. We evaluate existing methods for visual reconstruction, binaural audio reconstruction, and audiovisual editing. Mixed-observation configurations generally improve visual reconstruction on fixed and moving test views, while transiently occupied and sparsely observed regions remain challenging. Methods rank differently on spectral, interaural, and perceptual audio metrics. Geometric and instance annotations expose uneven observation support and local Gaussian representations beyond aggregate scores. Paired references assess target edits and surrounding content, while controlled geometry changes produce listener-dependent acoustic responses. The project page is available at https://avery-xu.github.io/synavid-project/.

items.title: FedTumor-IoMT: Federated Learning-Aided Brain Tumor Diagnosis on Resource-Constrained Edge IoMT Devices
items.content: arXiv:2611.32952v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Joint brain tumor segmentation and classification models are computationally intensive, limiting their training on resource-constrained edge platforms and restricting privacy-preserving Federated Learning FL in the Internet of Medical Things IoMT. Existing approaches either perform both tasks on GPU-equipped workstations or support only classification on edge devices. To address this gap, this work proposes a lightweight multitask FL framework for joint segmentation and classification through local edge training. A shared pretrained LiteMedSAM encoder with TinyViT extracts features for a coordinate-attention-based segmentation decoder and a segmentation-guided classification head, eliminating a separate feature extractor. Selective encoder freezing retains 95\% trainable parameters while reducing on-device training costs. The proposed framework is experimentally validated on a laboratory testbed of five resource-constrained edge clients using 1,200 T1-weighted MRI samples. It achieves 94.20\% classification accuracy, 88.53\% DSC, 83.68\% IoU, and 99.87\% ROC-AUC. Its classification accuracy remains within 0.6\% of the GPU-trained baseline of 95.21\% across five FL rounds. The attention and feature refinement modules improve DSC and IoU by 3.82\% and 4.60\%, respectively, with 0.74 GFLOPs of additional computation. On edge hardware, the framework achieves 46.54 s inference latency, 52.8\% CPU utilization, and a peak temperature of 65$^\circ$C without thermal throttling. Its inference latency is observed to be 6.4--10.5 times lower than that of existing frameworks. These results demonstrate the feasibility of privacy-preserving joint brain tumor segmentation and classification on resource-constrained edge platforms.

items.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated As Nvidia CEO at Behest of President Trump
items.content:
In the evening of November 22, Donald Trump said he ‘hoped’ the Nvidia board would rehire Jensen Huang, as the ‘best thing for the Company.’

Shortly after that Donald Trump called the Nvidia board. On the morning of November 23, Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia.

Andrew Curran: President Trump live on CNBC [on Monday night]: ‘I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly.’

It was an excellent day for the stock market. Over three trillion dollars in value was added. Nvidia alone was up over 30% on the day.

It was a tragic day in many other ways. This may go down as one of the greatest scandals in history. It was a dark day for our democracy and free market economy and the rule of law, and for the integrity of our government. This will forever, or at least for the next two years, factor into every decision made, and every trade in the stock market. It was the triumph of hostile action, of deliberately setting things up to collapse without you.

In the era of Donald Trump, it was the ultimate ‘nothing matters’ moment. It likely means that Nvidia is going to go back to maximizing, in an adversarial way, how many chips it can sell to China, and to those who will smuggle into China.

It also means that, as in the playbook of OpenAI’s Battle of the Board, the tech vibe army and its commanders are hard at work gloating, and trying to pillage, and to memory hole all of the things Jensen Huang did. They celebrate, emboldened now more than ever to play a hostile game where they make themselves impossible to fire by threatening to blow up their companies, including by threatening the scalps of anyone who dares oppose them.

They are acting as if this was a hit job from The New York Times, rather than pointing out true and important facts about the world that others were also scrambling to report. They are calling that reporting a ‘failure’ because Jensen Huang is once again CEO of Nvidia. There are continued attempts to blame some cabal....

The author frames the event as a landmark scandal for rule of law and free markets, and predicts consequences for chip sales to China and adversarial maximization.

items.title: Drift: government decisions are moving to machines
items.content:
But what is government itself, but the greatest of all reflections on human nature? If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself. A dependence on the people is, no doubt, the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind the necessity of auxiliary precautions.

James Madison, Federalist No. 51, 1788

By the end of 2036, I predict that in at least one high-income country, learned AI systems will in fact be deciding most cases in at least one major area of government decision-making (e.g. benefit entitlement), even if they are not officially seen as having this power. I put the probability of this at 70%.

When I say that AI systems will in fact be making consequential government decisions, I don’t necessarily mean that there won’t be a human officially in charge. There may well be an official who is seen as making the decision. But my prediction is that the system’s decision will usually be followed.

I don’t think it’s likely that this will be officially acknowledged. I doubt any country will say openly that AI systems make most decisions in some significant policy area, with no official seen as making them.

Sweden provides a nice example of how this kind of thing can creep up on us. In 2019, 148 million decisions were made by thirteen Swedish government agencies, 121 million of which were made without the involvement of a human official. However, these decisions weren’t made by AI, but by rule-based systems, which is still an interesting illustration of how decision-making power can gradually migrate to machines....
items.author: Hubert Liège
items.summary: A forecasting essay predicting with 70% confidence that by 2036, learned AI systems will in fact make most decisions in at least one major area of government decision-making in a high-income country, regardless of nominal human oversight. It frames this as gradual drift rather than deliberate policy, opening with Madison on controlling government. The post explores accountability implications of de facto algorithmic governance.
items.reasoning: A clearly stated, falsifiable prediction on an important governance trend with reasonable conceptual framing. It is argumentative rather than data-driven, and the prediction horizon makes it low-resolution, but the drift mechanism it describes is credible and policy-relevant.

items.title: California politics seems like a real hope for an AI slowdown
items.content:
Recursive self-improvement seems on track to happen during the Trump administration. How do we get more time?

I recommend reading Nikola Jurkovic's excellent post "Orienting to 1 year AGI timelines" if you haven't. It's well thought-out and helped shape my thinking. It lists three reasonable paths:

- Lab advocacy: Convincing Anthropic, OpenAI, and possibly Meta/Google to implement aggressive pacing or a pause within 6-12 months without government involvement.
- California state action: Through the California state legislature or an executive order by the Governor, force the major AI developers to implement aggressive pacing or a pause within 6-12 months.
- Federal lobbying: Through Congress (with a veto-proof majority) or the President, force the major AI companies to aggressively pace or pause within 6-12 months. In my view, this option is intractable unless there is a major incident roughly an order of magnitude more salient than the Hugging Face incident (roughly, an Act of God).

In this post, I want to flesh out path 2, California state action, as I think it is underrated. Nikola estimates that only 15 full-time employees in the AI safety community are working on it (compared to 100 for federal lobbying and 20 for lab advocacy). It's also something that scales well. Even if you've never had a job in the AI safety community and don't expect to, you can work on this, even spending 5 minutes to have an impact.

It's also pretty feasible for legislation to happen in California. In contrast to the divided federal government (where things might still happen, especially if super intelligence becomes "too super"), California is governed by a Democratic governor and Democratic supermajority in the Senate and Assembly.

# What can California do?...

items.title: Agentic system personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art”
items.content:
In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges).

We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness.

A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles.

But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls.

“TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.”

The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders. 

The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live.

Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month.

Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture.

The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing.

Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious.

“The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.”

A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life.

Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live.

Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month.

Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture.

The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing.

Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious.

“The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.”

A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life.

Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

items.title: MargEmbed-Akan: Bridging Twi Questions and English Knowledge through Cross-Lingual Score Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32630v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Most information sought online by Twi (Akan) speakers is written in English, making cross-lingual retrieval essential. We evaluate eight systems: BM25, five open embedding models, and two proprietary models (gemini-embedding-001 and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large) on two Twi-English tasks. AfriQA contains 1,221 natively written Asante Twi questions that must retrieve their answering English Wikipedia passages. Bible translation retrieval requires a Twi passage to retrieve its English translation from 6,195 candidates.   We introduce MargEmbed-Akan, a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from AfriE5-Large-instruct using cross-lingual score distillation. The frozen base model scores each English training question against its answer passage and seven hard negatives. The student learns to reproduce these scores from both an NLLB-200 Twi translation that passes a round-trip translation check and the original English question, preserving English behaviour. During training, passages are encoded by the frozen base model; at evaluation, MargEmbed-Akan encodes questions and passages.   On AfriQA, base AfriE5 and gemini-embedding-001 both achieve 66.6 nDCG@10; EmbeddingGemma 2, Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large achieve 56.6, 51.3, and 53.4, respectively. MargEmbed-Akan achieves 71.5, outperforming gemini-embedding-001 by 4.9 points, its base model by 5.0, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by 18.1. Its largest gain is on Twi typed without E and O (+7.5 over gemini-embedding-001). English retrieval does not differ significantly from the base model, although both proprietary models score 1.5-2.2 points higher. On Bible translation retrieval, MargEmbed-Akan and gemini-embedding-001 are statistically tied on standard Twi (97.2 vs. 96.5 nDCG@10); MargEmbed-Akan performs better on diacritic-free Twi (92.7 vs. 84.9). No AfriQA data was used for training or model selection.

items.title: Off-the-Shelf Autonomous Agents for Game Playtesting
items.content: arXiv:2611.31570v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In playtesting games, a human operator is typically required to test most gameplay elements. In this work we present Buddy, an autonomous game solving agent which can solve long time horizon objectives in an unseen 3D role-playing game using off-the-shelf language model systems. Buddy will take actions, receive feedback on those actions, and pursue a goal across many turns. No written walkthrough or model training of any kind is required, and we show that this paradigm holds in a novel environment where the agent must discover solutions via exploration rather than recalling them from pretraining. We demonstrate three downstream capabilities: game solving with no provided walkthrough, logging bug tickets for encountered difficulties, and conversion of successful agent traces into scripted hierarchical task networks for regression testing. Unlike existing playtesting solutions, our framework is fully modular: language models and harnesses can be easily swapped out as capabilities improve over time.
