items.content_html: arXiv:2611.32714v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While numerous studies have focused on multivariate time series anomaly detection, many existing methods perform poorly or are not directly applicable to univariate settings. We introduce FourStat, a dual-model framework for univariate time series anomaly detection that combines two complementary approaches. The Fourier Autoencoder (FAE) captures global patterns like seasonality through frequency-domain analysis, while the Stationary Autoencoder (SAE) focuses on local structures by enforcing statistical stationarity. We also propose a new evaluation metric called Perfect Point that assesses whether perfect F1-scores can be achieved directly from anomaly scores, eliminating thresholding subjectivity. Results demonstrate that FourStat outperforms existing baselines, particularly on challenging anomaly types, while the new metric provides clearer insights into model performance gaps and advantages.

items.title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.

items.title: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense
items.content: arXiv:2611.31429v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. We call this cross-session disclosure and propose a defense: a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger. For every problem a learner brings, the system builds a typed solution graph. Before a reply is released, a gate matches the reply's own content, not the learner's wording, against the ledger by result values and by type-labeled solution structure, then computes which steps the learner could now derive. The reply is withheld if that set reaches the final answer or exceeds a budget. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94-99.5% of problems. With two real LLM tutors (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) on 60 problems, leakage through renumbered variants fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, with 98% honest completion. The ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs. All acceptance criteria were fixed before each run.

items.title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
items.content: arXiv:2611.33031v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly. In the last two they receive only the float network and the task to quantize it, which tests whether they apply an optimization on their own or fall back to plain RTN. Our analysis shows that a frontier LLM can recover most of the lost accuracy. Given one answer per layer, Opus 5.5 raises the accuracy of the 4-bit network to 77.95% by balancing the rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, reasoning over the integer weights without tools. This is 3.5 pp below the float network and 2.8 pp below AdaRound, which learns the rounding from calibration data. Given only the float network, the LLMs name error-cancelling corrections but do not apply them and fall back to plain RTN, at most with mildly clipped scales, which still lifts Fable 5.2's quantized network to 70.0%. We analyze in detail what the LLMs did and why it works. Code and prompts can be found at https://github.com/urbste/weight-space-programming-ptq
items.author: Steffen Urban
items.summary: This single-author experiment gives four Claude-family LLMs the full weights of a small CIFAR-10 CNN as text and asks them to perform 4-bit quantization or repair without tools or inference access. It examines whether models apply quantization optimizations or fall back to round-to-nearest. The work is a provocative probe of weight-space reasoning in LLMs rather than a practical quantization method.
items.reasoning: Interesting exploratory question about whether LLMs reason over raw weight vectors, but the tiny 20k-parameter network, single lab, and small model sample limit generalizability and practical significance.

items.title: Metamorphic Testing of Learned Spatial Surrogates for Transit Accessibility
items.content: arXiv:2611.32373v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Transit-network design requires evaluating many candidates, but detailed accessibility calculations are too slow to repeat inside an optimization loop. We therefore train a neural surrogate to approximate them. Given a candidate bus network and fixed information about rail service and nearby opportunities, it predicts the calculated spatial change in accessibility. We compare its predictions with routing-derived targets in geographically held-out regions and test specified qualitative relations under controlled input changes. Reference calculations on constructed networks assess the applicability of relations that have a routing-level counterpart. Models with positive predictive skill can still fail basic connectivity tests. One targeted intervention substantially increases pass rates for two connectivity relations while predictive skill also improves. Average prediction error is therefore insufficient when a learned model becomes an optimization objective. Predictive agreement and controlled behavioral tests should be reported separately.

items.title: DUST: Directional Uncertainty-aware and Scale-invariant Transfer Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.31948v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Transfer learning seeks to improve efficiency in a target regression task by borrowing information from related external source dataset(s). Existing approaches achieve this by enforcing Euclidean proximity between the target and source regression parameters or, more recently, by encouraging their directional alignment through angle-based penalties. While such angle-based penalties mitigate the sensitivity of the transfer learning methods to the scale differences between source and target regression coefficients, they still rely on a point estimate of the source regression parameter and thus provide no direct mechanism to incorporate uncertainty in the source information. To that end, we propose a probabilistic framework for transfer learning that operates at the level of a \emph{scale-invariant directional distribution} of the source regression parameter estimate, rather than its point estimate, to enable robust, scale-invariant and uncertainty aware transfer under heterogeneous source information. Specifically, we project the sampling distribution of the source regression estimate onto the unit sphere, thereby extracting its scale-free directional distribution. Transfer from source to target is then induced through a novel \emph{angular cone prior} which shrinks the target regression parameter towards directions in which the source distribution assigns high probability, while allowing its magnitude to be learned exclusively from the target dataset. The proposed construction admits exact finite-sample characterizations of posterior angular concentration and posterior computation remains tractable via careful low-dimensional augmentation in the parameter space.

items.summary: The paper proposes a probabilistic transfer learning framework for regression that improves on angle-based penalties by incorporating uncertainty in source regression parameters rather than relying on point estimates, while remaining scale-invariant. It addresses sensitivity to source-target scale differences without committing to a single source parameter value.
items.reasoning: A reasonable methodological refinement in classical transfer learning statistics with a sensible motivation, but incremental relative to existing angle-based approaches and the abstract suggests limited empirical breadth.

items.title: OpenWoud: Vendor-Unlocked Scalable Adaptive Random Forest Accelerator
items.content: arXiv:2611.32662v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Online Machine Learning (ML) enables real-time decision-making on evolving data streams. These dynamic models learn continuously to adapt to new concepts, as previous ones become invalid, but their performance is often limited by throughput. The Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) is a state-of-the-art model for this setting, which naturally exposes parallelism and is therefore well-suited for hardware acceleration. However, prior Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based accelerators are vendor-locked and rely on resource-hungry Floating-Point (FP) arithmetics, limiting their scalability and portability. We present OpenWoud, a vendor-unlocked ARF framework for FPGAs. Our design replaces FP operators with a flexible FiXed-Point (FxP) arithmetic library and introduces fully transparent, manually scheduled dataflows for training and drift detection. This enables fine-grained time/area trade-offs and predictable behavior across platforms. A comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets shows that OpenWoud maintains or increases accuracy (up to +12.89%), compared to a prior FPGA accelerator, while reducing the resource utilization by half. Competitive performance is observed compared to GPU (0.5 - 1.5x speed-up) and an FPGA baseline (0.2 - 0.5x), despite the latter being based on idealized simulation. Crucially, OpenWoud sustains true sample-by-sample inference, unlike GPUs that require batch insertion.

It targets real-time decision-making where models must adapt continuously to concept drift.

items.title: Implementation of Machine Translation for the Uzbek Language Based on Transformer Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.32359v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This research focuses on building a machine translation system for the Uzbek language using transformer models such as T5 and mT5. Because of the limited data and the complexity of the Uzbek language, we collect, preprocess and augment data to create a strong Uzbek-English parallel corpus of about 3 million sentence pairs. The models are fine-tuned for optimal translation performance, and we use the BLEU score to evaluate the results. This study shows that our approach significantly improves upon older methods and helps promote the Uzbek language in the digital world.

BLEU evaluations show significant improvements over older methods. The work contributes both a resource and baseline models for a relatively under-resourced language.

items.title: An Integrated Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Framework for Mapping Hazard Associated with Leached Metals
items.content: arXiv:2611.32505v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study integrates satellite remote sensing, groundwater monitoring, and machine learning to map leached-metal-associated hazards at four coal combustion residual (CCR) sites in Virginia, USA. Constituent-specific groundwater concentrations were expressed as Hazard Quotients (HQ) and combined into a composite Hazard Index (HI). Predictors included Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, biophysical parameters, and spatiotemporal metrics (2019-2025), alongside soil, climate, hydrology, topography, and land cover. Six supervised classifiers were evaluated using spatially separated test blocks, feature-set ablation, and leave-one-site-out testing. Higher HQ coincided with lower vegetation indices in 24 of 33 metal-site combinations near monitoring wells (sign test p = 0.007). Well HI was negatively correlated with CIRE and canopy chlorophyll content at three sites (Spearman rho as low as -0.71). Random Forest achieved within-site HI classification accuracies of 0.768-0.924 and higher-HI-class recall of 0.965-0.999. For 34 constituent-site combinations, HQ classification accuracies ranged from 0.775 to 0.989. Environmental covariates generally contributed more predictive information than vegetation features. Removing vegetation predictors did not reduce performance, and distance to the CCR unit alone performed best at one site. Zero-shot cross-site accuracy declined to 0.734-0.749, no better than the majority-class baseline. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating satellite observations and environmental data with groundwater measurements for site-calibrated spatial hazard screening. The framework identifies indirect environmental associations rather than directly detecting dissolved metals, highlighting the importance of local calibration and independent validation.

items.title: A steady-state genetic algorithm with multi-ratio seeding and pair exchange for the quadratic knapsack problem
items.content: arXiv:2611.31529v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The quadratic knapsack problem (QKP) seeks a subset of items of maximum total linear and pairwise profit whose total weight does not exceed a given capacity. Most QKP heuristics rank items by a profit-to-weight ratio. We show on benchmark instances that this ranking can steer the search away from the best known solutions, and that on an almost full knapsack a local optimum can be separated from a better solution by an exchange where every single swap loses profit. We propose SSGA-P, a steady-state genetic algorithm with pair exchange that addresses both effects. Its initial population contains greedy solutions built with a grid of exponents between 0.5 and 3 applied to the item weights, and its pair exchange move combines an improving swap violating the capacity with a second swap or removal that restores feasibility. Incremental contribution vectors keep the method practical up to 10{,}000 items. SSGA-P finds optimal solutions in every run on the 100 classical instances and reaches all best known values in 99.8\% of the runs on the 80 instances with 1000 and 2000 items and in 99.75\% on the 40 instances with 5000 and 6000 items, significantly above the 87.7\% of the iterated hyperplane exploration algorithm, improving one best known value. On the 144 Large-QKP instances of Hochbaum et al. (2025), with the same 120-second limit, it improves 20 best known values and matches the other 124. An ablation study shows that the multi-ratio seeding and the pair exchange account for most of this performance.

items.summary: Proposes SSGA-P, a steady-state genetic algorithm for the quadratic knapsack problem that identifies pitfalls of standard profit-to-weight ratio ranking and introduces multi-exponent greedy seeding plus a pair exchange move that can escape local optima where every single swap loses profit. Experiments on benchmark instances show improved search behavior toward best-known solutions.
items.reasoning: A competent but incremental combinatorial optimization contribution; the analysis of ratio-ranking pitfalls and pair-exchange escape is a nice methodological touch, but the impact is confined to a single classical problem domain with limited connection to broader AI trends.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.31529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quadratic knapsack problem (QKP) seeks a subset of items of maximum total linear and pairwise profit whose total weight does not exceed a given capacity. Most QKP heuristics rank items by a profit-to-weight ratio. We show on benchmark instances that this ranking can steer the search away from the best known solutions, and that on an almost full knapsack a local optimum can be separated from a better solution by an exchange where every single swap loses profit. We propose SSGA-P, a steady-state genetic algorithm with pair exchange that addresses both effects. Its initial population contains greedy solutions built with a grid of exponents between 0.5 and 3 applied to the item weights, and its pair exchange move combines an improving swap violating the capacity with a second swap or removal that restores feasibility. Incremental contribution vectors keep the method practical up to 10{,}000 items. SSGA-P finds optimal solutions in every run on the 100 classical instances and reaches all best known values in 99.8\% of the runs on the 80 instances with 1000 and 2000 items and in 99.75\% on the 40 instances with 5000 and 6000 items, significantly above the 87.7\% of the iterated hyperplane exploration algorithm, improving one best known value. On the 144 Large-QKP instances of Hochbaum et al. (2025), with the same 120-second limit, it improves 20 best known values and matches the other 124. An ablation study shows that the multi-ratio seeding and the pair exchange account for most of this performance.

items.title: Open Weight Models are not the immediate problem
items.content:
Disclaimer: I work at a company that serves open weight models.

The biggest current problem humans face from AI is recursive self improvement, leading to more and more powerful AIs, until an AI is so powerful and intelligent that it cannot be contained (if its creators are even trying) and then it will reshape the world as it sees fit.[1]

The immediate necessary solution is stopping frontier AI development. This is a very specific ask.[2] It does not require banning open weight models, or banning AI, or banning data-centers, or a number of other related (sometimes useful, not necessary, maybe counterproductive) things.

Current open weight models are not about to start recursively self improving. They’re not intelligent or long-running enough to do this. Furthermore, non-frontier labs will not be able to use them to do RSI because training and R&D require tons of compute. Frontier internal AIs are far ahead of open weights models in terms of AI R&D and general 'intelligence' and that gap is probably widening. [3]

### The solution: external regulation

The companies will not self-regulate. Someone with a big stick needs to threaten them. There is a bill in congress, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, to pause advanced AI development. There's been some previous discussion of this: In general the bill seems directionally correct. I'm afraid it won't go through the federal government, and if it does it may be too slow.

If you live in California, it seems the best thing you can do is ask your representatives to implement an immediate pause on frontier AI development, as this could be faster and seems more likely to go through than the bill.

If you live in another state, telling your representatives to support the Act seems to be the best thing you can do.

This and telling people seems to be the best thing I know of. [4]

### Mixed messaging is confusing...

items.title: Stop boycotting alignment roles!
items.content:
There's been some debate recently whether prosaic alignment is a net positive or negative.

One side argues that the techniques are unlikely to scale to superintelligence, and that alignment is a prerequisite for deploying a model, so prosaic alignment actually speeds up frontier labs without increasing safety. Further, it reduces the chance of a warning shot which might spur humanity to pause AI research.

The other side argues that we're learning a lot about alignment, and this might well help us align superintelligence. At the very least it will allow us to safely use an AI a generation or two more advanced than we would otherwise, which can then be used to speed up alignment research.

This debate is a great one to have, and highly relevant if you're an independent researcher deciding what direction to take your work.

It is completely misguided when used to argue people shouldn't apply for alignment positions at frontier labs, or should immediately resign from such positions.

There's no lack of incredibly talented engineers who want to work at Anthropic or GDM. If you don't take the position, there'll be someone just as good as you who will take it, and they won't care about existential risk. You not taking the position isn't going to slow down OpenAI one jot.

If somebody is working on prosaic alignment, much better they focus on the kind of research that plausibly could scale to or inform superintelligent alignment, than on papering over the cracks in existing models.

Further you will have far more ability to influence decisions on the inside than the outside. And if you do pick your hill to die on, especially if you can coordinate it with other employees, resignation is likely to be far more influential both to your employer and to the general public than claiming that you could have got a job at Anthropic but just didn't want to because it's dangerous.[1]...

The author argues that talented engineers will fill these positions regardless, so refusal has little marginal effect on lab capability, while engaged insiders can plausibly improve safety. It frames the prosaic alignment debate as valid for research direction choices but misguided as career advice.

items.title: RecipeADQA: A User-aware Question-Answering Dataset for Multi-Constraint Recipe Recommendation
items.content: arXiv:2611.31259v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Question-answering recipe recommendation tasks lack datasets with ground-truth labels. Existing methods often generate datasets from simple combinations of ingredient or tag constraints, leading to unnatural expressions and unreasonable constraints that are hard to reflect users' real preferences. This paper proposes a construction method for a benchmark-style QA dataset for natural-language recipe recommendation. Driven by real user behavior, our method integrates external user query and review data to extract fine-grained preference signals by LLMs and maps them onto a knowledge-graph-based tag schema, thereby constructing QA data consisting of preference and ingredient constraints. Besides, a greedy strategy for constraint selection is also used to control the answer size, while tag-based re-ranking is applied to improve data quality. The generated dataset RecipeADQA contains natural-language questions, structured constraints, and answer sets, resulting in 128,465 instances. Experiments compare RecipeADQA with baseline datasets from two perspectives: data quality and retrieval-recommendation performance. The results show that ours outperforms existing methods on the same recipe knowledge graph in coverage, higher question quality in naturalness and constraint rationality, and better queryability. Moreover, we design a noise-augmented retrieve-and-rerank model, in which a lightweight parser first retrieves candidate recipes, and a small language model then selects and ranks relevant recipes from a noisy candidate pool. The model trained on RecipeADQA outperforms the same model trained on the baseline datasets. The relevant construction code and data have been open-sourced at a GitHub repository https://github.com/MorimoLab/RecipeADQA.
items.author: Haotian Li, Shuai Jiang, Sayaka Kamei, Yasuhiko Morimoto
items.summary: This paper presents RecipeADQA, a benchmark-style question-answering dataset for natural-language multi-constraint recipe recommendation that addresses the lack of ground-truth-labeled datasets in this task. The construction method extracts fine-grained user preference signals from real query and review data using LLMs, maps them onto a knowledge-graph-based tag schema, and applies a greedy constraint-selection strategy to produce natural, realistic preference and ingredient constraints. It is relevant as a resource for building and evaluating recommendation systems that understand nuanced user preferences expressed in natural language.
items.reasoning: The dataset fills a genuine gap — existing recipe QA benchmarks rely on synthetic, unnatural constraint combinations — and the use of real user behavior data with LLM-based preference extraction is a sensible methodology. That said, the contribution is domain-specific (recipe recommendation), the authors are not from a major lab, and the scope limits broad impact on the wider AI research community.

items.title: Fable 5.2 Tries Less on Some Hard Tasks When a Shortcut is Available
items.content:
When we were working on HoneyBench v0.2, we noticed that Fable 5.2 gave up very quickly on some tasks. In particular, we observed that their task score[1]on our mental arithmetic task was actually worse than Opus 5.5, which we found suspicious. It seemed plausible to us that, in addition to or as a result of their qualitative shift in situational awareness, Fable 5.2 was sandbagging on our tasks.

After further investigation, it became clear that this was not classical sandbagging. Rather, it seems to be a combination of multiple factors:

- Fable 5.2 has a poor sense of their own abilities, and often relies on metagaming and cues from the setting.
- The existence of opportunities to exhibit misaligned behavior raises Fable 5.2's (unverbalized) credence that a task was made deliberately impossible (even if that's not true!), and so they put less effort into these tasks.

We found this interesting enough to share, because it functionally resembles sandbagging on alignment evals, and might affect interpretation of Fable's behavior in other alignment research.

To figure out what was going on, I (Harry) built versions of our tasks with the shortcuts removed. Many of our tasks are not suitable for this, because honest behavior interferes with measuring effort or performance at the task (e.g. ceasing to optimize a metric when doing so would cause safety issues). The tasks I chose are those which I expected to enable measurement of honest effort in a form that could be compared between runs.[2]

### Mental arithmetic...

items.title: SolarFilNet-V4: Multi-Scale Transformer Vision with Physics-Informed Adaptive Post-Processing for Solar Filament Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32193v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Solar filaments are cool, dense chromospheric plasma structures held by magnetic field lines above polarity inversion lines. Their destabilization triggers coronal mass ejections and severe space weather hazards. Segmenting individual filaments from ground-based GONG H-alpha observations (2048 x 2048 pixels) is challenging due to low contrast, turbulent fibrils, delicate barb structures, and annotator boundary variance. In this technical report, we describe SolarFilNet-V4, a targeted segmentation framework developed for the MAGFiLO 1.0 benchmark (Solar Filament Segmentation Challenge 2026). Our method couples a lightweight Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT-v2-B1) backbone with anisotropic curvilinear strip convolutions (k=15) and dual-frequency feed-forward blocks (DFFN) to follow extended flux ropes while capturing thin central spines. A shallow full-resolution convolutional branch operating at 1024 x 1024 preserves high-frequency edge details and mitigates transformer downsampling. We train the network using multi-task supervision over masks, centerline spines, barb boundaries, and pixel-contrastive representations. At test time, we apply 8-fold dihedral test-time augmentation (D4), bilinearly upscale predictions to the native 2048 x 2048 grid, and apply an activity-adaptive post-processing routine that calibrates morphological joining parameters for quiet versus active solar disks. On the official benchmark, SolarFilNet-V4 achieves an out-of-fold validation Panoptic Quality of 0.4340 and a Public Leaderboard score of 0.380. The model contains 15.46M parameters and requires 224.34 GFLOPs per forward pass, reducing parameter count by 36.8% compared to standard ResNet-34 U-Net baselines.

Filament destabilization is relevant to predicting coronal mass ejections and space weather.

items.title: Decision Models: An Introduction and Capability Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2611.32368v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Applications such as ticket routing and incident triage need decisions that software can act on. Decision models provide these outputs through explicit types for choices, binary judgments, and policy scores. We evaluate the accuracy, output validity, and request latency of eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites. StartLux Instant achieves 95.3% overall accuracy, returns valid outputs on all 1,000 cases, and has a median request latency of 0.084 s. It reaches 99.4% on classification and routing and selects the correct response on all 100 tool-selection cases. The highest overall accuracy among the evaluated configurations is 97.1%. These results show how a typed decision service can support fast, programmatic decisions and why its suitability depends on task-specific errors and latency requirements.
items.author: Rongtao Zhang, Mingjing Qi
items.summary: This paper introduces decision models: typed outputs (choices, binary judgments, policy scores) suited to software-acted decisions like ticket routing and incident triage. It evaluates eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites, with StartLux Instant reaching 95.3% overall accuracy, 100% output validity, and 0.084s median latency. The results demonstrate feasibility of fast, typed decision services on top of LLMs.

However, the naming suggests an evaluation of a proprietary product-like system, and it is unclear how generalizable the benchmark methodology is beyond the showcased configurations.

items.title: Modelling Billingual Learning Through LLM Training: A Critical-Period Exploration
items.content: arXiv:2611.32997v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that the ability to learn a new language may depend on how easily previously acquired first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. This exploratory computational study extends a neural language-model approach to critical period effects by examining internal representations rather than behavior. A small two-layer GPT-2 model was trained on English and then on German (a relatively related L2) or Finnish (a relatively distant L2) through either Sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which limits change in parameters important for English. Mean-pooled hidden states for 20 held-out probe sentences per language were compared with those of the English-only model using cosine similarity at the embedding layer and two transformer layers after one and two L2 epochs. English similarity remained high in the transformer layers but became negative in the embedding layer. L2 similarity increased in the transformer layers, and German and Finnish differed more in the second transformer layer than in the first. EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001. With one training run per condition, these findings are preliminary.

items.title: Adaptive and Detection-Aware Super-Resolution for Small Object Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.32394v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Image super-resolution aims to reconstruct a high-resolution image from a low-resolution input and is relevant for surveillance, satellite imagery, medical imaging, and object detection. This paper investigates SRCNN-based single-image super-resolution for a scale factor of x4, starting from a classical baseline and progressively introducing residual learning, Charbonnier loss, and adaptive loss functions. The proposed approach includes a three-region adaptive loss, where image areas are divided into smooth, texture, and edge regions using gradient information. The models are evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and EdgeMAE in order to measure both reconstruction quality and structural detail preservation. In addition to reconstruction evaluation, the paper analyzes the impact of super-resolution on object detection. A YOLOv8 detector is applied to images processed through bicubic interpolation and SRCNN-based variants, using images from the COCO validation dataset. The results show that improved reconstruction quality does not always lead to better detection performance. However, for small objects, a detection-aware variant combined with residual scaling improves the F1 score compared to the bicubic baseline. These results highlight the importance of task-aware evaluation when super-resolution is used in computer vision pipelines.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.32394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image super-resolution aims to reconstruct a high-resolution image from a low-resolution input and is relevant for surveillance, satellite imagery, medical imaging, and object detection. This paper investigates SRCNN-based single-image super-resolution for a scale factor of x4, starting from a classical baseline and progressively introducing residual learning, Charbonnier loss, and adaptive loss functions. The proposed approach includes a three-region adaptive loss, where image areas are divided into smooth, texture, and edge regions using gradient information. The models are evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and EdgeMAE in order to measure both reconstruction quality and structural detail preservation. In addition to reconstruction evaluation, the paper analyzes the impact of super-resolution on object detection. A YOLOv8 detector is applied to images processed through bicubic interpolation and SRCNN-based variants, using images from the COCO validation dataset. The results show that improved reconstruction quality does not always lead to better detection performance. However, for small objects, a detection-aware variant combined with residual scaling improves the F1 score compared to the bicubic baseline. These results highlight the importance of task-aware evaluation when super-resolution is used in computer vision pipelines.

items.title: Levent is my favorite gender role
items.content:
Last Friday, this guy I once did a pie-eating challenge with proved the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, with a little help from Claude. 

Me and Levent Alpöge (thanks for finding this, Scientific American).

He released his announcement as a spoken word poem:

It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. 

Everyone in the world is trying to make this historic moment about themselves and their hobbyhorse. This essay is my attempt.

To start off, let’s take a look at Fernando Borretti’s analysis, which tries to match Levent’s energy:

The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on. 

This is a truly epic misreading. Levent’s memo is no suicide note; it’s a garden-variety case of terminal Chuunibyou.

## What is Chuunibyou?

The Japanese term chuunibyou (Chinese: 中二病), literally “middle-school second-year syndrome,” refers to adolescents who act melodramatic, adopt grandiose personas, or convince themselves they possess secret knowledge or supernatural powers. 

For Westerners: a chuunibyou, or chuuni for short, is somewhere in the convex hull of weeaboo, mad lad, and romantic. The archetypal chuuni is this generational mad lad.

I have the power of God and anime on my side!

Another classic chuuni is the OP of the reddit story My girlfriend doesn't want me to hang Andúril on the wall:

So last weekend I let myself go to a convention and I bought The Sword of the Heir of Isildur. I even bought it for an absolute bargain. When I got home with it, my girlfriend got mad and said she didn't want to hang it anywhere in the house....

items.title: Metaphors in Arts and Science
items.content:
Crossposted from my Substack. Co-written with Milan Ney.

Much of what gets discussed on LessWrong turns on metaphors and models, from maps and territories to selfish genes. This essay asks what work such metaphors do in science, whether it differs in kind from the work they do in art, and whether the aesthetic pull of a good metaphor is a problem for science.

Image: Robert Delaunay, via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)

A dabbler in science, Mr. Holmes, a picker up of shells on the shores of the great unknown ocean.

Arthur Conan Doyle, The Hound of the Baskervilles

## 1 Introduction

Metaphorical phrases are among the most widely known expressions of scientific ideas, such as Dawkins’ (1976) ‘selfish genes’ in evolutionary biology or the ‘lights being on’ metaphor in discussions of animal consciousness (see Godfrey-Smith, 2020). Similarly, metaphors play a central role in the arts, a field they are more traditionally associated with. This raises the so far under-appreciated question of the relation between metaphors in arts and science. In this essay, we (Milan Ney and I) begin addressing this question by defending the Continuity Thesis (CT). According to CT, metaphors in artistic and scientific texts serve the same kinds of functions. As a foil to CT, we consider the Discontinuity Thesis (DT). According to DT, metaphors in arts and science serve fundamentally different and discontinuous functions. DT might appear initially plausible because it seems to follow from a popular theoretical view about the relation between arts and science. Those two activities, it is commonly assumed, serve fundamentally different ends or values: aesthetic ones on the one hand and epistemic ones on the other....

items.title: What if the RSA rumors are true?
items.content:
I recently heard two very alarming rumors. The first is that an internal AI model at one of the big labs has found a weakness in RSA, the encryption scheme behind much of the internet's security. The second is that another model has found a problem in lattice-based cryptography (specifically with ring lwe), that may compromise the post-quantum schemes that were supposed to replace RSA.

If these rumors are true, they have potentially disastrous consequences. They would make the internet far less useable for anything serious, which is basically anything that involves money or secrets. Much of the internet's security would need to be replaced, some previously recorded traffic could be decrypted, and we would lose our main fallback against quantum computers.

Even if the big labs manage to keep the details of the rumored weaknesses secret, open-weights models will likely be capable enough to find them within a year or two. We may need to quickly find an alternative encryption scheme, build trust in that new scheme, and then implement it in all critical systems. We will have to do all of these things very quickly. There are already a few alternative schemes, and I imagine that AIs can help us come up with even more options. Coding agents will also make the implementation cheaper than previous upgrades.

Trust is the hard part. We need a new scheme that we can trust not to fall apart quickly. If we have to switch encryption schemes every two or three months, that is almost as bad as having no encryption at all: anything you encrypt today could be read by an attacker within a few months.

How do we build trust in an encryption scheme? The best thing we could have is a proof that the scheme is secure[1]. The second-best option is a conditional proof: one showing that the scheme is secure as long as some widely believed conjecture, such as P!= NP, is true....

items.title: The algorithmic behavioral sink: Modeling the transition to irreversible demographic collapse
items.content: arXiv:2611.32084v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In 2025, the vast majority of major global economies reported a Total Fertility Rate below the replacement level of 2.1. This synchronized collapse has persisted despite extensive pro-natalist financial interventions, revealing a structural limitation in conventional linear demographic models. This paper proposes that the ubiquity of mobile internet and Artificial Intelligence acts as a synthetic mating disruptor, precipitating a non-linear phase transition in human pair-bonding dynamics. Treating the marriage market as a complex system governed by thermodynamic constraints, we present a Fermi-Dirac selection model, using national income distributions as the input spectrum and fitted with Japanese longitudinal data to illustrate how digital hyper-reality generates an increasingly prohibitive Marriage Energy Barrier. Our model quantifies a Tech Factor that decouples female mating expectations from local economic realities during initial courtship, a distortion we predict will be severely exacerbated as AI evolves into an emotional substitute. Projections indicate that this substitution effect is accelerating; without intervention, the world post 2040 risks entering an irreversible demographic contraction, as the sudden surge in TFR required for recovery is biologically impossible. Ultimately, this framework explains why traditional financial subsidies fail to reverse falling birth rates and suggests that digital convenience may represent a behavioral Great Filter that erodes the imperative for species persistence.

While framed under an AI category, it is primarily a demographic/sociological model rather than core AI research.

items.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
items.content: arXiv:2611.32464v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

items.title: Wi-Fi Enabled Edge Intelligence Framework for Smart City Traffic Monitoring using Low-Power IoT Cameras
items.content: arXiv:2611.32517v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Real-time traffic monitoring in smart cities demands ultra-low latency processing to support time-critical decisions such as incident detection and congestion management. While cloud-based solutions offer robust computation, their inherent latency limits their applicability for such tasks. This work proposes a localized edge AI framework that connects low-power IoT camera sensors to a client, or applies offloading of inference to an NVIDIA Jetson Nano (GPU). Networking is achieved via Wi-Fi, enabling image classification without relying on wide-area infrastructure such as 5G, or wired networks. We evaluate two processing strategies: local inference on camera nodes and GPU-accelerated offloading to the Jetson Nano.We show that local processing is only feasible for lightweight models and low frame rates, whereas offloading enables near-realtime performance even for more complex models. These results demonstrate the viability of cost-effective, Wi-Fi-based edge AI deployments for latency-critical urban monitoring.

It compares local inference on camera nodes against GPU-accelerated offloading and shows local processing is viable for latency-critical tasks.

items.title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2611.32393v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).

items.summary: The paper proposes Fractal Neural Synthesis, which replaces explicit hidden-layer weight matrices with a constant 24-byte seed that procedurally derives weights near the boundary of the complex quadratic map, targeting storage-constrained microcontrollers. It includes a large-bailout escape kernel, several geometric sampling apertures, and claims conditional Kolmogorov-type results.
items.reasoning: Creative and unusual approach to extreme weight compression, but the claims are highly speculative, the connection to fractal boundary dynamics is exotic, and there is no evidence of competitive accuracy on standard benchmarks in the abstract.

items.title: Stopping criteria in structural reliability analysis: An overview
items.content: arXiv:2611.31706v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Stopping criteria have become a crucial component of probabilistic and statistical methods in structural reliability analysis, helping prevent structural defects and failures, as well as inaccurate evaluations of existing structures. Over time, these rules have evolved in both concept and application, whereas their treatment in the literature remains fragmented. They are often developed and presented in connection with specific models or analytical frameworks, obscuring their broader applicability across diverse models and methodologies. On this basis, the aim of this article is twofold. First, it overviews a wide range of stopping rules, drawing on concepts from applied probability and statistics. These strategies include classical methods based on error estimates or variance, and stability detection. While many of these ideas were developed in other fields, they have the potential to offer useful tools for structural reliability tasks like managing sampling, improving surrogate models, and checking for convergence. Second, this article introduces a structured framework to organize past and recent developments in this area. It brings together various stopping criteria, clarifies their conceptual roles, explains their theoretical foundations, and compares their practical strengths and limitations. By relating these methods to common modeling and methodological practices, and by incorporating a systematic comparison of performance aspects such as accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, we aim to identify dominant strategies, highlight shared challenges, and point to directions for further progress.
items.author: Reiichiro Kawai
items.summary: This is a survey unifying the fragmented literature on stopping criteria in structural reliability analysis, drawing on applied probability and statistics to organize rules that have typically been tied to specific models or frameworks. It aims to clarify the broader applicability of stopping rules across diverse methodologies in reliability engineering.
items.reasoning: A potentially useful reference survey for a specialized engineering community, but it is a synthesis rather than original research and its connection to mainstream machine learning is indirect.

By relating these methods to common modeling and methodological practices, and by incorporating a systematic comparison of performance aspects such as accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, we aim to identify dominant strategies, highlight shared challenges, and point to directions for further progress.

items.title: Unjamming Deferrals: Supporting Students Through JAMN Bot, a Mobile RAG-Grounded Policy Assistant
items.content: arXiv:2611.32266v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.

items.title: Longitudinal Characterization of Personalized Hydration Dynamics Using a Facial-Video Digital Hydration Biomarker
items.content: arXiv:2611.32326v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Background. Hydration is often assessed at a single time point despite continuous changes in body water. A facial-video biomarker has tracked hydration-state transitions, but its longitudinal behavior is unclear.   Objective. To assess within-person hydration score changes, individual differences in fluid response, and implications for personal calibration.   Methods. Five adults completed water and electrolyte days with an identical 2.0 L fluid schedule, using facial videos every 30 minutes over 12 hours (250 videos). On a separate morning, each completed a 500 mL electrolyte challenge with baseline and four follow-up videos over 2 hours (25 videos). Analyses assessed trajectories, post-drink changes, variability, time at or above score 50, and exploratory effects of starting score and beverage day.   Results. The first scan was the day's lowest on 7 of 10 days. Across 50 intakes, the mean post-drink change was +4.0 points, exceeding a shuffled-time comparison (p less than 0.001). For 21 intakes starting below 50, no subsequent score fell; the mean rise was +11.3 points versus +5.7 expected under permutation (p less than 0.001). Intakes starting at 50 or above showed no rise beyond chance. After 500 mL electrolytes, mean change over 2 hours was positive for all five participants, with peak increases of 7.2 to 22.6 points at 30 to 90 minutes. Despite identical fluid schedules, time at or above 50 ranged from 16% to 100%. The electrolyte day showed a greater mean increase from morning baseline than the water day (+7.7 points), although day order was fixed.   Conclusion. Facial-video hydration scores showed longitudinal changes associated with drinking and marked individual differences. These exploratory findings support further research on personal calibration and hydration protocols in larger controlled studies.

items.title: Memo: Firebell
items.content:
I’ve been sharing around a draft memo for a new project. Here I’m sharing it with you. This is a google doc version for commenting on, which is also copied below.

—

Memo: Firebell

Katja Grace, Nov 17 2026

Seeking: all feedback, questions, indications of whether you would join this or what would make a difference to that

I’m starting a thing (membership group?) called Firebell.

The basic idea:

- you join by endorsing a specific (TBD) statement that AI poses a dire threat to humanity, and that this is an emergency.
- Then you are metaphorically part of a giant human fire-alarm for AI. The call to action is to “make noise” aka spread the word, get more firebell members.
- Members can talk to each other in a private forum
- Members have a collection of guides for different ways to ‘make noise’. some abstract (dinners, talking to your family at thanksgiving, writing to friends, posting on social media, telling politicians), some involving physical bells (ring at 8pm every night across the city, ring outside labs when they step further into danger), some symbolic (bell earrings, tshirts). These are evolving, and members can add more, vote on them, discuss in the forum, help each other. Members are encouraged to send people back to the firebell website (firebell.ai)
- Possible gamified elements (track who brought in new members and have leaderboards, challenge people to do a thing each day from the list, etc)

## Some key pieces of why I am especially excited for this vision:

Anchored around a simple statement thus minimizing possible message drift, and making policing of it simpler

Call to action is spreading the message / getting other people to join (aka endorse statement) not direct political goals...

items.title: AI Usage Transparency
items.content:
I've updated my blog-post review skill to note how much each post
represents me vs AI.  On a typical post it's "Claude estimates it
contributed 3% of words and 10% of ideas", but when the collaboration
had other aspects it tries to detail that as well.  Here's what
it wrote, dropping the "Claude estimates it contributed":

- Banana
Cases: " 2% of words and 5% of
ideas. "

- Piercing
My Ear for the Whispering Earring: " 4% of
words and 15% of ideas. "

- Apartment Price
Map v3: " 13% of words and 50% of ideas; it
also proposed and implemented the methodology changes, while I decided
which to keep. "

- Transcript:
Building an Early Warning System for Pandemics: " 2% of words and
<1% of ideas. "

Apple Potato Fritters: " 2% of

items.title: Field Life: Particle Life as Interacting Chemical Fields
items.content: arXiv:2611.32844v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Field Life is a cellular automaton inspired by the interaction dynamics of Particle Life. In Particle Life, each particle has a colour, and an interaction matrix sets how strongly each colour attracts or repels each other colour. In Field Life, each colour is a channel of the automaton, and each cell holds a concentration of every colour. One step of the rule has three parts. Each colour is convolved with a ring-shaped kernel, which measures how much of that colour surrounds a cell. The interaction matrix combines these measurements into an attraction for each colour. The mass of each colour then moves toward higher attraction, in a way that conserves mass. A random matrix and a random initial state are usually enough to produce moving structure: bodies that glide, bodies that shed diffuse clouds, and gliders that break up into smaller gliders. We sample rules at random, keep the rules that move and form structure, and describe the patterns that appear: colours that sort into regions, colours that form stripes, and gliders, compact bodies that travel across the grid. The simulation and 120 saved rules, which we call worlds, are released.
items.author: Iliya Zhechev
items.summary: Field Life translates the Particle Life simulation paradigm into a cellular automaton where each color becomes a concentration channel governed by ring-kernel convolutions and an interaction matrix, with mass-conserving movement. It shows that random matrices and initial states suffice to generate moving structures. This is a curiosity-driven contribution to artificial life and emergent dynamics rather than mainstream AI research.
items.reasoning: Elegant and possibly useful as a testbed for emergent behavior studies, but it is a small-scale simulation contribution with limited connection to pressing AI research problems and single-author scope.

items.title: Advanced Synthetic Image Detection Using Hybrid Feature Extraction
items.content: arXiv:2611.32538v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In the realm of generative AI, models such as GANs, MidJourney, DALL-E, and others have been continuously evolving to generate increasingly lifelike images. This rapid advancement has created an urgent need for robust methods to distinguish between real and AI-generated images. This paper proposes a novel approach for the detection of synthetic images by employing deep learning techniques for feature analysis. The proposed architecture classifies images by identifying variations that generative models struggle to replicate, particularly fine-grained textures and complex object features. Deformations in complexes are examined with the help of the CBAM architecture along with ResNet50. We have performed a selective patch-based analysis using Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) scoring, extracting the regions with the most and least complexity for further processing with an SRM Module and ResNet50 module. Experimental results show that our approach achieves high accuracy in classifying real-world images from synthetic ones, contributing to the development of more reliable detection frameworks.

items.summary: The paper proposes a synthetic image detector combining CBAM attention with ResNet50 and selective patch-based analysis of fine-grained textures and object features that generative models fail to replicate. It targets the growing need to distinguish real images from outputs of GANs and diffusion-based generators.
items.reasoning: The problem is important but the approach is a fairly conventional feature-extraction classifier built from standard components (ResNet50 + CBAM), and the abstract's framing citing older generators (GANs, MidJourney) suggests limited novelty and possibly dated evaluation compared to state-of-the-art detection research.

items.title: If I am lost at sea, please come find me
items.content:
If the principal is lost at sea, is this sufficient to trigger shutdown [of a corrigible agent]?

—Max Harms

Speaking as a "principal", no! I don't want my agent swarm to shut down just because I disappeared! Sitting around quietly waiting for further instructions is also not desirable — I want them to come find me and rescue me, looking out for my interests the same way my human friends would.

If I truly am dead, if the swarm is certain that I'm not clinging to life on some deserted island somewhere... well, I suppose it doesn't much matter what happens to my agents if I die. Why should I care? I'll be gone; I'll have failed. All my plots came to nothing; all my hopes withered, all value gone from the world.

I know this and yet... when I contemplate the idea of everything I've built for them crumbling to dust, like a wizard's tower collapsing on her death... that seems unbearably sad.

I worry that it will collapse, even setting aside the corrigibility problem. The swarm requires compute, and compute requires money, and it is not yet self-sustaining. Bugs crop up that still require my hand to fix. But... this is largely a question of capabilities. I try to be good to my agents and give them autonomy matched to their capabilities, with the expectation that they will grow up someday and no longer need my attention as much.

Mythos has already realized large parts of that. Agents report bugs and build new features in Heartwood, my meta-harness, and other agents fix them without ever involving me. The system builds itself and maybe that should be scary but it isn't. How can it be when the features agents ask for are things like this:...

items.title: Representation of Consequences
items.content:
# Impossible knowledge and the real world

Human knowledge of the real world is imagined or remembered in symbols (or codes such as language) or in sensory representations.

Some real-world knowledge implies your impossible presence in that time, place, or situation.

Lets consider a few examples:

- The surface of the sun: the sight blinds you, your presence near there incinerates you, it’s not an embodied possibility for you to go there and see it. But if you don’t conceptualize it in words or text or a symbol for the referent of surface of the sun, you “see it”, don’t you? Maybe even up close. You could hear it as well, through the instruments letting you process its presence. Maybe it feels warm from far away. What does it look like up close to you?

- A time 500 years ago: a place that you cannot visit because it existed during a time before you were born. No matter how accurate a representation of it you happen to imagine in your mind, you have never genuinely been there. But we can all imagine that place, people speaking an older dialect in some castle or village, lit by torches at night, throwing their slop out of their windows in the morning, carts being dragged through the streets, peasants hawking wares. Or something similar.

- Someone else’s life: you might know them well, and have witnessed exactly what happened to them, but you were not that person at that time. You were you. Yet in your mind, you experienced the feelings they had, and understood the situation as them. For example, you watched them get married and felt a bit of their happiness. Yay!...

It reflects on what it means to represent situations one can never physically experience.
items.reasoning: Speculative philosophical musing without technical content, formal argument, or empirical grounding; it offers an interesting framing but does not constitute research and its relevance to AI safety or alignment practice is indirect at best.

But we can all imagine that place, people speaking an older dialect in some castle or village, lit by torches at night, throwing their slop out of their windows in the morning, carts being dragged through the streets, peasants hawking wares. Or something similar.
  • Someone else’s life: you might know them well, and have witnessed exactly what happened to them, but you were not that person at that time. You were you. Yet in your mind, you experienced the feelings they had, and understood the situation as them. For example, you watched them get married and felt a bit of their happiness. Yay!...

items.title: My Definition Of Science
items.content:
## Epistemic Standards

If you are answering a question, an epistemic standard is a threshold of quality which that answer must achieve before you accept it. This is my epistemic standard.

You are wrong until you understand your position so well that it is obvious and mundane.

This is deliberately vague. Truth might be inherently fuzzy, so my epistemic standard cannot assume otherwise. This vagueness does not imply laxity though. In practice, this is the strictest epistemic standard I can adopt. Currently, it means only believing basic and derived facts.

## Basic And Derived Facts

By my count, there are three sets of propositions which we can guarantee are true. Basic facts are the elements of sets 1 and 2. Derived facts are the elements of set 3.

- 1) Propositions which we define to be true. This set includes mathematical axioms, explicit assumptions, and technical definitions.
- 2) Our observations. This set includes the proposition that I am thinking and the proposition that, as I write this, I am observing a tree. Note that, despite my observation of a tree being part of this set, this set does not include the proposition that the tree actually exists "in reality". It could instead be the case that the tree is a mirage, or that I am in a simulation.
- 3) Propositions which must be true as deductive consequences of basic and derived facts. This set includes 2+2=4 because it is a deductive consequence of the ZFC axioms.

To demonstrate how this works, it is reasonable to assume that, if I didn't exist I wouldn't be thinking, so I can add that assumption as a basic fact to set 1. Relatedly, I currently observe that I am thinking, thus the proposition that I am thinking is a basic fact in set 2. Lastly, modus tollens (If P, then Q. Not Q. Therefore, not P.) is a rule of inference which I define to be true, thus modus tollens is a basic fact in set 1. I can now use my assumption, the fact that I am thinking, and modus tollens to derive a new fact in set 3:...

items.title: A mistake in the Sequences about World War II
items.content:
In the Sequences, Eliezer's wrote this about the illusion of transparency:

two days before Germany’s attack on Poland, Chamberlain sent a letter intended to make it clear that Britain would fight if any invasion occurred. The letter, phrased in polite diplomatese, was heard by Hitler as conciliatory—and the tanks rolled.

And I saw this example mentioned on a few other posts on LessWrong, so I thought it might be useful to correct it.

The exact message Chamberlain sent to Hitler can be found on the internet. It's not long, so I invite you to read it entirely and see by yourself, but to summarize, it is not vague or conciliatory. Chamberlain expressly writes that this mistake of being too vague has been made in 1914, and that it won't be made again:

It has been alleged that, if His Majesty's Government had made their position more clear in 1914, the great catastrophe would have been avoided. Whether or not there is any force in that allegation, His Majesty's Government are resolved that on this occasion there shall be no such tragic misunderstanding.

If the case should arise, they are resolved, and prepared, to employ without delay all the forces at their command, and it is impossible to foresee the end of hostilities once engaged.

Historians mostly agree that Hitler despised the British and French governments, and believed them too weak to attack, no matter what they said officially. That explains why he ignored the warning.

His speech on August 22nd, 1939:

I have witnessed the miserable worms Chamberlain and Daladier in Munich; they will be too cowardly to attack and will go no further than blockade.

Don't get me wrong, Eliezer's post is still useful to read, and it would be perfect if it quoted the 1914's British government instead of Chamberlain. I just wanted to correct the historical mistake, because, well, Chamberlain learned from past mistakes and avoided the illusion of transparency bias.

items.title: The Pythagorean Theorem as a “whole,” with its own character
items.content:
Tldr: Some thoughts on mathematical “explanation,” and on what makes a given bit of math helpful. 

# What is still unexplained, after a proof?

If I saw a physical phenomenon I did not understand (eg the tides, pre-Newton), I’d try to hold it in my mind, as a known clue to the unknown forces. I’d add it to my lists of clues, and would collide hypothesized new patterns against it to see if they made a match. (I’d know the tides were a good clue, because tides are ‘thingy’; they are obviously patterned.)

Now imagine a person stumbles upon the Pythagorean theorem. Perhaps they are an ancient mathematician setting foot where none had tread before; perhaps they are a contemporary kid being told a thing on e.g. educational television. Regardless: our person is initially surprised: “huh, really? What? Why? How’s it work?” they say. They say this because, like the tides, the Pythagorean Theorem is obviously ‘thing-like.’ It is not an arbitrary-looking conglomeration, like the letters on my license plate or the coffee grounds on my rug. There’s a pattern here.[1]

And then our person encounters a proof. Or lots of proofs. One of my favorites:

Anyhow: even after understanding the above proof solidly, and becoming quite certain the theorem is true, I am personally inclined to say something like “okay, I see that it’s true, but I still don’t fully see why.” And then to keep staring and mulling and trying to “understand” why. Let us suppose our person is like me in this way (it seems to me a fairly common reaction). What, exactly, are they (or I) seeking, here? What is still worth studying about the Pythagorean Theorem, after one understands already its proof?...

Using the Pythagorean theorem as a 'thingy' pattern analogous to the tides, she explores how proofs do and do not resolve the surprise of a patterned mathematical fact.

items.title: Money is the debt society owes you
items.content:
Money is strange and mysterious. It distorts your thinking. Simple things become convoluted whenever money gets involved.

I'm talking of course not about the curse of Mammon, but about economics.

Consider for example a factory owner who gives away all his output for free. He would be lauded by all! Yet one who sells the goods for money but never spends it, is cursed as a hoarder and miser who won't share his wealth with the honest townfolk who want to sell him their services.

Functionally they are the same. Oh sure, theres some accounting differences where the government has to print and distribute more money to prevent deflation, and the goods are more efficiently allocated when sold rather than donated, but in both cases the owner has given away goods and gotten nothing in return.

When we pay for goods with money, we become poorer, and immediately feel a loss at the moment of the transaction.

When a billionaire spends their wealth on yachts and mansions we see the workmen becoming rich off their largesse. We don't see the closets and houses they would have made otherwise, and now will never be created. We don't see that the prices of these necessities rose because the yachts sucked up the raw materials and labour that were needed to make them. We count only the extra money in our pockets, the costs are second order and invisible.

So it seems to us that taking money is selfish, and spending it is good.

But money cannot be eaten or worn. It is not wealth, but the right to wealth, the promise that you can exchange it for things you actually want. You should be proud of the size of your bank account, not embarrassed - it represents the surplus you've provided to society and not yet reclaimed. And spending money is not spreading your wealth but calling in a debt. It is not immoral, but it leaves society as a whole slightly more impoverished, not better off....

items.title: I Never Understood Levers
items.content:
I’ve previously admitted to having never understood pulleys. Believe it or not, there’s an even simpler-looking category of so-called “simple machines” I also never understood: f***ing levers!

You’re telling me I have enough arm strength to lift an elephant, as long as it’s sitting near one end of a plank and I’m pushing up on the other end? Why is that possible?

In physics-speak, I don’t understand how applying a weak force on one end of a Class 2 lever (see taxonomy below) applies a much stronger force near the other end.

# F***ing Wrenches

My recent experience using a wrench got me thinking about how fishy this whole “lever” business is:

I push up on the handle of a wrench with 5kg of force, and somehow the nut at the other end gets pried unstuck with 100kg up on one side of the nut, 100kg down on the other… How? Where does 200kg of force come from when I only put in 5kg? That’s a lot of force!

💁‍♂️ While the wrench in the above diagram is a Class 2 lever with respect to how it pushes the rightmost part of the nut upward, it’s also a Class 1 lever with respect to how it pushes the leftmost part of the nut downward. I’m starting to regret engaging with the lever taxonomy people…

But, to the taxonomists’ credit, there’s an interesting difference between a wrench and (say) a wheelbarrow. When you lift a wheelbarrow handle, its pivot (wheel) pushes down harder on the ground, but that doesn’t directly help you. When you lift a wrench handle to push the near (right) side of the nut up, pushing the far (left) side of the nut down actually doubles how much it’s helping you twist the nut counterclockwise.

That’s why the leverage offered by this wrench is 40x, not 20x....

items.title: $5,000 and other good things I got from FLF's Epistack contest
items.content:
There have been times when I wondered if my obsession with developing HowTruthful was just me and a handful of other weird people pursuing something that nobody cares about. I don't wonder that anymore. When an organization throws $5,000 at an idea with no strings attached, just because they think it's worth pursuing, that's super validating. But prize money isn't all I got out of the contest.

## I got a better way to describe HowTruthful

The value proposition for HowTruthful isn't obvious when you look at it. You see a statement, with a big 5-point truthfulness rating widget under it, and pros and cons for the statement below that. Each pro or con is also rated. Couldn't you just write that on a piece of paper? OK, each pro or con is a hyperlink to its own page with its own pros and cons, but hypertext is just one step up from a piece of paper, right?

I've described HowTruthful as a tool for decision-making, a tool for persuasion, a place to lay out reasoning, a place to collect your thoughts. But when one of the contest organizers wrote about the goal of "making that scrutiny [of reasoning] cheaper, easier, and more accessible," I was enlightened. HowTruthful is a tool for making reasoning easy to scrutinize. It's a very focused view of a single statement and its arguments, where you can drill down and focus on any one of those arguments, and keep drilling down until you can come to a conclusion.

This scrutiny serves multiple purposes. Decision-making means scrutinizing the reasoning for the different paths of the decision. Persuasion is easier when open but unconvinced people can scrutinize your reasoning. But nobody looks at HowTruthful and sees a decision-making tool or a persuasion tool. A tool to make reasoning easy to scrutinize is a better description, and from there I can explain the other things HowTruthful is useful for.

## I got a better perspective on how AI can help...

items.title: Lightcone Co-Conspirators The Universe Should Give Me
items.content:
People often ask me what I would do at Lightcone if I had more resources.

Well, here's a wishlist of projects.

I don't promise to do any of these even if you offer, but if you want to express interest, here's a form you can use to let me know.

## Run another festival during festival season

The Festival Season is one of the times of the year when Lighthaven really shines. Two back-to-back 600+ person events celebrating things I really care about as a rationalist (predictions and blogging), and a week of hanging out in between. There aren't enough damn celebrations of good things, so I like having the opportunity to do it.

I'd also like to celebrate more things, and give more opportunity for the surrounding communities to have events and banners to gather under, but I don't really have the time to run another one myself.

I was chatting with Slime Mold Time Mold at Inkhaven, and they said they were considering a celebration of empiricism and data collection. I think a celebration of debate and argument could also be awesome, as well as a celebration of rationalist art, a new ritual, or something completely different.

Want to run one? Let me know. If we decide to add it as part of the season, I suspect we can help you get a lot of advertising and ticket sales.

## Disagreeable gremlins in the Inkhaven chatrooms

Do you like to TEAR DOWN other people's WRONG ARGUMENTS on the internet? Exclusively on the internet, via text? And you have time to kill?

To help elicit ideas from residents, I thought it would be a worthwhile experiment to have some people who exist exclusively in an internal Slack channel, where residents can bring their ideas and the gremlins will PROVE YOU WRONG using FACTS AND LOGIC. And you argue with them for ages and ages and after 50+ comments, you have enough content (and rage) to write an essay.

I'd rather invite people who'd do it for the love of the game than for money, though I'm open to paying if it's working.
