items.content_html:
People often ask me what I would do at Lightcone if I had more resources.

Well, here's a wishlist of projects.

I don't promise to do any of these even if you offer, but if you want to express interest, here's a form you can use to let me know.

Run another festival during festival season

The Festival Season is one of the times of the year when Lighthaven really shines. Two back-to-back 600+ person events celebrating things I really care about as a rationalist (predictions and blogging), and a week of hanging out in between. There aren't enough damn celebrations of good things, so I like having the opportunity to do it.

I'd also like to celebrate more things, and give more opportunity for the surrounding communities to have events and banners to gather under, but I don't really have the time to run another one myself.

I was chatting with Slime Mold Time Mold at Inkhaven, and they said they were considering a celebration of empiricism and data collection. I think a celebration of debate and argument could also be awesome, as well as a celebration of rationalist art, a new ritual, or something completely different.

Want to run one? Let me know. If we decide to add it as part of the season, I suspect we can help you get a lot of advertising and ticket sales.

Disagreeable gremlins in the Inkhaven chatrooms

Do you like to TEAR DOWN other people's WRONG ARGUMENTS on the internet? Exclusively on the internet, via text? And you have time to kill?

To help elicit ideas from residents, I thought it would be a worthwhile experiment to have some people who exist exclusively in an internal Slack channel, where residents can bring their ideas and the gremlins will PROVE YOU WRONG using FACTS AND LOGIC. And you argue with them for ages and ages and after 50+ comments, you have enough content (and rage) to write an essay.

I'd rather invite people who'd do it for the love of the game than for money, though I'm open to paying if it's working.

Have a merch store...

items.title: Why do intense writing
items.content:
Feedback on a party party we hosted where you had to write or edit 400 words per hour or be kicked out

Scott Alexander is very good at blogging. He also, surprisingly, talks like he writes. Before meeting him for the first time at a meetup five years ago, I had thought that writing was a job he was very good at, but that it still took quite a lot of time for him to get posts to the level where they’re written so well. But in real life, he sounded pretty much the way he wrote, in real time, with no editing.

I think this cuts both ways. If you can talk, writing can be awesome and not hard. You can actually just do it!

There’s an issue, though, that @Chris Lakin talks about: sometimes, to get to an awesome thing, there’s some activation energy required, and if people only do local optimization, they don’t get to awesome things. Starting and actually doing writing can be hard/non-straightforward, even though the process of writing is awesome.

One can backchain, and be super-intentional about writing, but I think this can make it harder to get to start actually producing words in some easy and inspired way. They imagine the enormity of the scope of intended writing and become on some level afraid of it.

One could talk for 40 minutes successfully explaining their favorite subject to someone; yet writing down all of what they’d say to someone, without having a clear picture of an audience in mind or being able to track and manage attention with short feedback loops, can be much harder.

Unlike speaking, though, writing allows you to improve at producing words: you can look at the entirety of what you wrote, and edit it, and recursively improve it on many levels, and then, the next time, become slightly better at figuring out how to put words together somewhat nicely immediately, before the editing pass; and the next editing passes will also be somewhat better; and so you’ll improve at how good you’re at producing words, in this self-play RL-like fashion....

items.title: 2026 Petrov Day house party retrospective
items.content:
Note: there are spoilers in this post (marked [Spoiler]); these details are fun, but if you want to have fun playing similar future Petrov Days yourself, you might not want to skip them!

Continuing the longstanding LW tradition of celebrating September 26 with buttons that can, but maybe shouldn’t, be pressed, we hosted a party at Arkhipov — our London group house (named after another guy who also did not end the world).

We wanted to celebrate the Petrov Day virtues

The obligatory part of the party was that we would have a big red button, and if anyone pressed it, the party would end immediately.

The button

We really did not want it to be pressed; the event is about celebrating the virtues of Petrov Day, and it would be sad if someone demonstrated being unvirtuous in this way, and it would be sad if the party ended early. So we tried to select hard for the people we invited, and extended the invitations and approved the sign-ups from only a few people we weren’t certain about.

This wasn’t the most interesting part of the party, though.

The core activity of the party was largely modeled after the 2024 LessWrong Petrov Day, which was great, and which I remember fondly. On LW, anyone who singed up in advance (not quite knowing the details yet), got sorted into WestWrong and EastWrong; people above a certain LW karma could apply to be a core participant. Core participants became the generals of two sides and a Petrov of each side; the generals each had a button that would nuke the other side, and Petrovs all saw a number of incoming missiles (normally zero) and had buttons to report an incoming strike or to say that all is clear. If your side is nuked, you (as a citizen or a core participant) lose a lot of karma; if two sides nuke each other, they also lose access to the LessWrong frontpage for a day. So, serious consequences. (Petrovs gained or lost karma depending on the accuracy of their reports.)...
